docs.text:
File What it is Loads into Backbone parameters scannet-semseg-litept-small-v1m1.pth (SHA-256 4fc1c778…) LitePT-S trained for ScanNet semantic segmentation LitePT (the defaults) 12.71 M scannet-insseg-litept-small-v1m2.pth (86408c63…) LitePT-S* trained for ScanNet instance segmentation (PointGroup) LitePT with dec_depths: [2, 2, 2, 2], dec_conv: [true, true, true, false], dec_attn: [false, false, false, true] 15.99 M structured3d-semseg-litept-base-v1m1.pth (53b18ba6…) LitePT-B trained for Structured3D semantic segmentation LitePT with enc 3-3-3-12-3, 54–576 ch, heads 3-6-12-24-32, dec_channels: [72, 108, 216, 432], dec_num_head: [4, 6, 12, 24] 45.11 M structured3d-semseg-litept-large-v1m1.pth (e50bd216…) LitePT-L, same task LitePT with enc 3-3-3-12-3, 72–864 ch, heads 4-8-16-32-48, dec_channels: [72, 144, 288, 576], dec_num_head: [4, 8, 16, 32] 85.88 M

Released by the Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing Lab of ETH Zurich on Hugging Face (revision a8e76e9; each file is <name>/model/model_best.pth there). Code and weights are MIT: the repository's LICENSE, and license: mit on the model card, both read on 2026-10-12. The files are Pointcept training checkpoints: the backbone is in state_dict under the prefix module.backbone., next to a task head and the optimiser state. All four

  • expect 6 input channels, colour and normal as the authors' data pipeline prepares them (reproducing it is the caller's job). A backbone built with another in_channels has a stem convolution these weights do not fit;
  • were trained on rooms at 0.02 m voxels, with float16 attention (see LitePT: two reference outputs);
  • attend only in the two coarsest stages, on voxels of 8 and 16 grid cells. At a 5 mm grid those are 4 cm and 8 cm, and the fixture scene is 308 and 80 voxels there: fewer than one patch of 1024, so the attention is global.

The repository also offers LitePT-S for nuScenes and Waymo (4 input channels, 0.05 m voxels), LitePT-L for nuScenes, a ScanNet200 instance model and a Waymo detection model. None of those was downloaded or checked.

model:
  backbone:
    type: LitePT                  # LitePT-S, untrained, on GSNet's grid
    in_channels: 3
    grid_size: 0.005

Also used for verification: the ScanNet segmentation checkpoint of PTv3 (scannet-semseg-pt-v3m1-0-base/model/model_best.pth on Hugging Face, MIT, SHA-256 40206376…, backbone keys under module.backbone.), and the GraspNet-baseline RealSense checkpoint (checkpoint-rs.tar, non-commercial research licence, backbone keys under view_estimator.backbone.).

No checkpoint of OA-CNNs has been released by its authors: on 2026-10-12 the Pointcept organisation on Hugging Face held PTv3, Sonata, Concerto and Utonia only, and the Pointcept model zoo lists a training command for it. OACNNs is therefore tested with parity against the official code, not weights-verified.

Checkpoints of SpUNet-v1m1 are released, by works that use it as their backbone, and they load into SpUNet key for key after convert_pointcept_state (tests/integration/test_backbone_released_weights.py; files loaded on 2026-10-13):

Release Files loaded here Licence SpUNet options RayYoh/GaussianCross (GaussianCross, ACM MM 2025) scannet/semseg-spunet-base-lin (157 MB), scannet/semseg-spunet-base (470 MB) MIT (model card) out_channels: null for the linear-probing file, defaults for the fine-tuned one KadirYilmaz/Volt teacher_weights/ (the distillation teachers of Volt, ECCV 2026) scannet_unet_teacher.pth (470 MB) MIT (model card) defaults

The MSC archives the Pointcept README links (Masked Scene Contrast, CVPR 2023, on the author's SharePoint) were not downloaded here. SpUNet stays tested: the loads prove names and shapes, and no activation comparison with the official model was recorded for these files. A ScanNet SpUNet converted by a third party into another library's layout also exists (torch-pointcloud/spunet-v1m1.scannet20.pointcept, MIT according to its card, SHA-256 11658b4d…); its card does not say which checkpoint it was converted from, and it was not used here.

How to start a grasp model from any of these files, and the full table of released weights that load into SpUNet, PTv3, PTv3Sonata, LitePT and MinkUNet: Scene encoders: sparse-voxel networks and released weights.

docs.title: Where the implementations deliberately differ from upstream
docs.text:
Each difference exists for the backbone contract and is exact for a single cloud.

Topic Upstream Here Why PTv3 attention backend flash-attention in half precision; without it, the patch size shrinks to the smallest cloud of the batch scaled_dot_product_attention in the input precision with the fixed-patch layout of the flash path No extra dependency; a cloud's result does not depend on its batch neighbours PTv3 serialisation depth one depth for the batch, from its largest cloud; the Hilbert curve depends on it one depth per cloud Batch independence PTv3 order shuffling every forward pass, in evaluation mode too training mode only Deterministic evaluation PTv3 voxel representative a random point of each voxel (training transform) the first point of each voxel Deterministic; features go back to exactly the points that produced the voxel PTv3 multi-dataset norms (pdnorm_*, PPT) one set of normalisation layers per training dataset, chosen per sample by a condition one set, chosen when the weights are loaded (pretrained_condition); the model is a plain PTv3 The Backbone contract carries no per-sample dataset condition. The released ppt checkpoints load with the statistics of the chosen dataset; the other sets are dropped PTv3 cls_mode (encoder without decoder) returns the coarsest level enc_mode: true returns the deepest concat_stages encoder stages concatenated on every input voxel A scene encoder returns one feature per point; encoder-only checkpoints load strictly LitePT attention backend flash-attention on float16 queries, keys and values; there is no other path scaled_dot_product_attention in the input precision, on the same patches No extra dependency. Measured: with the released weights the official output itself moves by 6e-4 to 2e-3 between the two precisions LitePT PointROPE a CUDA extension, or a PyTorch fallback that looks the rotations up in a table computed in PyTorch from the grid coordinates No compiled code; equal to both (the evidence was recorded with each) LitePT serialisation depth one depth for the batch, from its largest cloud one depth per cloud Batch independence LitePT order shuffling at every pooling, on every forward pass, in evaluation mode too; the model's shuffle_orders only reaches the input level training mode only, at every level, switched by shuffle_orders Deterministic evaluation LitePT patch size of a decoder stage that attends ignored: the level keeps the layout its encoder stage computed has to equal the encoder's; anything else is an error An argument that silently does nothing is a trap LitePT voxel representative a random point of each voxel (training transform) the first point of each voxel As for PTv3 LitePT enc_mode (encoder without decoder) supported not implemented No released checkpoint uses it, and the model then returns its coarsest level instead of dense features PointNet++ sampling below the first level searches again takes the first rows of the previous sample Identical result (furthest point samples are nested), about half the sampling time OA-CNNs sparse grid the bounding box of the batch, so which voxels a cloud loses at an odd axis (crop_odd_extent) depends on its batch neighbours the bounding box of each cloud Batch independence OA-CNNs voting weights exp(logit - m) / (sum + 1e-6) with m the largest logit of the batch; because of the constant, m changes the result m is the largest logit of the cloud Batch independence OA-CNNs pooling grids anchored at the lowest occupied cell of the batch at each level anchored at the lowest occupied cell of the cloud Batch independence OA-CNNs voxel representative a random point of each voxel (training transform) the first point of each voxel As for PTv3 OA-CNNs arguments without effect (groups, enc_num_ref, dec_depth, down_ratio) accepted; none enters the computation, the decoder has no blocks not parameters A config key that changes nothing is a trap SpUNet 1×1 convolutions (the final layer, the projected shortcuts) spconv convolutions of kernel size 1, stored as (out, 1, 1, 1, in) and applied as that memory viewed as (in, out) facade Linear layers with an (out, in) weight The facade defines a 1×1 convolution as a linear layer; convert_pointcept_state re-lays an official state dict, changing no value SpUNet enc_mode (no decoder, one pooled vector per cloud) supported not implemented Not a scene encoder SpUNet voxel representative a random point of each voxel (training transform) the first point of each voxel As for PTv3

Two upstream behaviours are kept as named constructor arguments because checkpoints depend on them: PointNet2.fps_skip_near_origin (the PyTorch sampling kernel never selects a point within 3.2 cm of the frame origin) and PTv3.fuse_before_decoder_cpe (in PT-v3m1 the first positional convolution of each decoder stage reads the skip features only). PTv3 follows the serialisation-depth rule of the original release, which its weights were trained with; Pointcept ≥ 1.6 adds one to the largest coordinate first, which differs only when that coordinate plus one is a power of two.

OACNNs.crop_odd_extent keeps a third: the way the official model treats the border of its grid. It declares the sparse grid as the exact bounding box of the voxels, and a stride-2 convolution without padding cannot place the last cell of an axis with an odd number of cells. At every level the voxels in that cell are left out of the down-sampling and get zeros back from the up-sampling, and a cloud thinner than 16 voxels along any axis runs out of cells (the official code then stops inside spconv with "out spatial shape reach zero"; here the error names the cloud and says what to change). crop_odd_extent: false keeps every voxel and has no such limit; the two agree whenever every extent is a multiple of 16. A tabletop cloud is easily thinner than 16 voxels at the published 0.02 m grid (the fixture scene is 15 deep), so a grasp detector needs a finer grid or crop_odd_extent: false. The batch dependence that the per-cloud evaluation removes is not small: batching the fixture scene with its own left half moves the official features of the two clouds by up to 1.1 on features of magnitude 10.6 (published configuration), where a batch here reproduces the clouds run alone to 2e-5.

At a 5 mm grid, what has to be re-tuned in OACNNs is point_grid_size: the pooling grids are counted in cells, so the published 8 to 16 cells of the first stage shrink from 0.32–0.64 m to 0.08–0.16 m. SpUNet has nothing counted in metres or cells besides the grid itself; its receptive field shrinks with the grid, as that of SparseUNet14 does. The official SpUNet pads its sparse grid, loses no voxel and does not depend on the batch (measured as for OACNNs: 3.4e-5 on features of magnitude 13.9, which is rounding).

docs.title: Reproducing the evidence
docs.text:
# unit suite: contracts, written-out oracles, published sizes (CPU, no files needed)
pytest tests/unit -k "backbone or ops"

# oracle comparisons; the analytic ones run anywhere, the others need the checkpoints
GRASPPANDA_WEIGHTS=/path/to/weights pytest tests/integration/test_backbone_oracle.py -rs

$GRASPPANDA_WEIGHTS holds graspnet_baseline/checkpoint-rs.tar, components/concerto_{tiny,small,base,large}.pth, components/utonia.pth and components/scannet-semseg-pt-v3m1-0-base.pth. A test is skipped when its file is absent and fails when the file's SHA-256 is not the recorded one.

The fixtures themselves are re-recorded with tools/make_backbone_fixtures.py, which runs the official code and is documented in its docstring. It never imports grasppanda; the packages an oracle needs (torch_scatter, timm, addict, the compiled extensions of graspnet-baseline and openpoints) belong in a separate environment.

LitePT has its own test file and four more checkpoints, all MIT:

# components/{scannet-semseg-litept-small-v1m1,scannet-insseg-litept-small-v1m2}.pth,
# components/structured3d-semseg-litept-{base,large}-v1m1.pth
GRASPPANDA_WEIGHTS=/path/to/weights pytest tests/integration/test_backbone_litept_oracle.py -rs

Its fixtures were recorded in an environment built for the purpose: PyTorch 2.4.1 + cu118 (the newest release flash-attention publishes a cu118 wheel for), flash-attention 2.6.3, spconv 2.3.8, torch_scatter, timm, addict, colorhash, NumPy 1.26, and the official PointROPE extension compiled out of tree for the GPU at hand, as its README instructs. Without flash-attention and the extension make_backbone_fixtures.py litept still runs, on the official PyTorch PointROPE and a plain softmax attention, and writes into the fixture which backend it used.

The sparse CNNs of Pointcept have their own test file, which needs no checkpoint:

pytest tests/integration/test_backbone_sparse_cnn_oracle.py -rs

Their fixtures were recorded from Pointcept at commit 1342eda (MIT), unpacked from the GitHub archive, with spconv 2.3.8, timm, torch_geometric 2.6.1 and torch_cluster 1.6.3 (torch_geometric 2.8 moved the grid clustering OA-CNNs uses into pyg-lib). The recorder imports the official model file without pointcept/models/__init__.py, which would pull in every model of the zoo and its compiled extensions; no upstream code is stubbed or modified.

docs.title: Reviewed, not implemented
docs.text: Licences were read from the repositories on 2026-10-12 (GitHub licence metadata, and the licence file where GitHub could not classify it). "Pointcept" means the model is available inside Pointcept under MIT; the dependencies listed for those rows are the imports of the Pointcept implementation. "Not checked" means exactly that.

docs.title: Point-cloud and voxel encoders
docs.text: Encoder Paper Code, licence Extra dependencies Why not yet, and what it would take DGCNN (segmentation form) Wang et al., TOG 2019 WangYueFt/dgcnn, dgcnn.pytorch (both MIT) none On the list for this round, dropped for time. Needs a k-NN operator in feature space (the reference knn takes 3-D coordinates only), chunked: at 20 000 points every EdgeConv layer compares all pairs of points. The PyTorch port needs no compiled code, so it can serve as an oracle directly. SPVCNN Tang et al., ECCV 2020 spvnas (MIT, archived), torchsparse (MIT) torchsparse A third sparse backend for one model. Port the point-voxel branch onto the facade instead. KPConv Thomas et al., ICCV 2019 KPConv-PyTorch (MIT) its compiled C++ wrappers (cpp_subsampling, cpp_neighbors) Neighbourhoods are precomputed on the CPU in the data loader. That pipeline has to become a transform, or be redone on the GPU with the reference operators. KPConvX Thomas et al., CVPR 2024 ml-kpconvx (MIT) not checked Successor of KPConv; review together with it. OctFormer Wang, SIGGRAPH 2023 octformer (MIT); Pointcept ocnn (MIT), dwconv (no licence file) Octree attention. PTv3 covers the same niche with fewer dependencies; a port needs an octree structure and a depth-wise octree convolution. Swin3D Yang et al., arXiv 2304.06906 Swin3D (MIT); Pointcept MinkowskiEngine, the Swin3D package, timm Tied to MinkowskiEngine. Not worth a port before the sparse facade can express its attention. Point Transformer V1 Zhao et al., ICCV 2021 Pointcept. The widely copied POSTECH-CVLab reproduction carries no licence and cannot be a source pointops (Pointcept's compiled library), einops k-NN vector attention is feasible on the reference operators but slow without a compiled k-NN. Point Transformer V2 Wu et al., NeurIPS 2022 Pointcept pointops, torch_geometric, torch_scatter, timm, einops Grid pooling already exists here (PTv3Sonata); grouped vector attention needs k-NN grouping. Superseded by PTv3. Stratified Transformer Lai et al., CVPR 2022 Stratified-Transformer (MIT); Pointcept pointops2 (compiled), torch_geometric, torch_scatter, timm Same dependency problem as PTv2. PointMamba Liang et al., NeurIPS 2024 PointMamba (Apache-2.0) mamba-ssm (Apache-2.0, compiled CUDA) An object-level model. The serialisation operators here are the ones it needs; blocked on a compiled dependency and on scene-scale evidence. Point Cloud Mamba Zhang et al., 2024 PCM (no licence) not checked Unlicensed code cannot be a source; implement from the paper only. PointMLP Ma et al., ICLR 2022 pointMLP-pytorch (Apache-2.0) not checked Published for classification and part segmentation; no scene-scale configuration to reproduce. PointNet++ with multi-scale grouping, as in Contact-GraspNet Sundermeyer et al., ICRA 2021 contact_graspnet (an NVIDIA licence shipped as License.pdf; read it before use) none A small extension of PointNet2: several radii per level, features concatenated. Take the configuration from the paper, not from the code.

docs.title: Image encoders used by RGB-D grasp methods
docs.text:
None of these is a Backbone in the current contract, which maps a point set to features on points. They need an image-encoder slot and a lifting step from pixels to points; both belong to the design of the image-to-region family (HGGD). Checkpoints of several of them are already in the local weight store.

Encoder Paper Code, licence Extra dependencies Note ResNet encoder-decoders He et al., CVPR 2016 torchvision (BSD-3-Clause); the encoder inside HGGD (MIT) torchvision The obvious first image encoder: permissive, small, the one HGGD-style methods are built on. DINOv2 Oquab et al., TMLR 2024 dinov2 (Apache-2.0) not checked Strong frozen RGB features. DINOv3 Siméoni et al., 2025 dinov3 (the custom "DINOv3 License") not checked The licence has to be read before anything depends on it. EfficientViT Cai et al., ICCV 2023 efficientvit (Apache-2.0) not checked A fast encoder for real-time use. FastViT Vasu et al., ICCV 2023 ml-fastvit (a custom Apple licence) not checked Custom licence; read before use. MambaVision Hatamizadeh and Kautz, CVPR 2025 MambaVision (NVIDIA Source Code License-NC) not checked Non-commercial code: cannot be a source of code here. SAM 2 image encoder Ravi et al., 2024 sam2 (Apache-2.0) not checked More useful as a provider of instance masks than as a scene encoder.

docs.title: Add a component
docs.text: You can add a backbone, grouper, head bundle, detector, transform, hook or evaluator without forking: write a class, register it, and point a config at it. The example project does exactly this and is the best starting point.

docs.title: 1. Write and register it
docs.text:
# my_components.py
from torch import nn

from grasppanda.models import Backbone
from grasppanda.registry import BACKBONES


@BACKBONES.register()
class MyBackbone(Backbone):
    """One sentence that says what it is: the catalogue shows it."""

    output = "dense"                      # the contract: features live on the input points
    status = "tested"                     # what you proved, not what you hope
    source = "My method (Me et al., 2026)"  # the paper, method or library it implements
    extras = ("spconv",)                  # optional dependencies, if any

    def __init__(self, in_channels: int = 3, out_channels: int = 256, depth: int = 4) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.out_channels = out_channels
        ...

status, source, extras and the first sentence of the docstring are what grasppanda components and the catalogue print. Components inside the grasppanda package must declare source on the class itself (a subclass does not inherit a citation), add one tiny configuration to tests/unit/test_swap_matrix.py if they are stages of the seed-based skeleton, and regenerate the pages with python -m tools.make_component_docs; the unit suite fails until all three are done.

Rules that keep configs checkable:

  • Annotate every constructor parameter. The annotations are what config values are validated against.
  • No **kwargs. Registration refuses it: a component that swallows arbitrary keys would turn typos into silent no-ops.
  • Import annotation names at runtime, not under TYPE_CHECKING.
  • Subclass the slot's base class (Backbone, Grouper, HeadBundle, …). The base decides which registry and which config slot the component belongs to.

docs.title: 2. Use it
docs.text:
custom_imports: [../my_components.py]     # or an importable module name

model:
  backbone: {type: MyBackbone, depth: 6}

grasppanda print-config my_config.yaml --check

docs.title: Slots that hold other components
docs.text:
Annotate the parameter with Cfg[Base] and build it yourself, so you can hand the child what you already know:

from grasppanda.models import Backbone, BaseGraspDetector, HeadBundle
from grasppanda.registry import BACKBONES, DETECTORS, HEADS, Cfg


@DETECTORS.register()
class MyDetector(BaseGraspDetector):
    def __init__(self, backbone: Cfg[Backbone], head: Cfg[HeadBundle]) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.backbone = BACKBONES.build(backbone)
        self.head = HEADS.build(head, in_channels=self.backbone.out_channels)

Cfg[Backbone] tells the validator which registry owns the slot, so nested configs are checked without constructing anything.

docs.title: Injected arguments
docs.text:
A child should not make the user repeat what the parent knows. Declare such a parameter with the INJECTED default:

from grasppanda.registry import HEADS, INJECTED


@HEADS.register()
class MyHead(HeadBundle):
    in_axes = ("seed", "channel")

    def __init__(self, num_angle: int = 12, in_channels: int = INJECTED) -> None: ...
  • The config may omit in_channels; the parent supplies it through HEADS.build(...).
  • If the config sets it and disagrees with the parent, building fails. Nothing is silently overridden.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
Declare what your component consumes and produces as class attributes; the base classes document which ones exist, and the catalogue explains each next to the components that declare it:

Slot Contract attributes backbone output, output_channels(options) proposal requires, seed_scores, needs_supervision view stage seed_scores, label_formats, needs_matched, applies_seed_weights assigner label_format, optional_outputs, needs_supervision grouper support, out_axes, required_seed_channels(options) head bundle in_axes, label_format, score_kind, applies_seed_weights, needs_supervision, required_seed_scores(options)

The seed-based skeleton compares them for every detector built on it, on the config and again on the built stages (stage_contract_problems in grasppanda.models.detectors.seed_based). A stage of that skeleton therefore needs no checking code of its own: declare the attributes truthfully and an illegal combination is refused with a message that names both sides. Say only what the code does: a head that sets applies_seed_weights = True without reading MatchedLabels.weight turns a config error into a silently wrong model.

Two of them reach beyond the pair of stages next to each other:

  • output_channels(options) is the width a backbone returns, told from its options alone; return the same number the built module has as out_channels (tests/unit/test_swap_matrix.py compares them for your tiny config and for your defaults). The default reads an integer out_channels option, so an encoder that has one needs nothing more. Return None only where the width is known once the encoder is built (a bridge whose width is that of a library model): the config check then builds the encoder once, without released weights, and the test asks for the reason (WIDTH_KNOWN_ONCE_BUILT). A grouper that fixes the width of the seed features states it with required_seed_channels(options) and names in projected_variant the grouper that takes any width, which grasppanda compose puts in its place.
  • needs_supervision lists what a stage reads from the training Supervision, by where it sits (objects, objects.tolerance, point_labels.<name>, extras.<name>), each with the option that makes the stage read it, or None when it always does. A dataset reader says what a config makes it serve with served_supervision(node), and the config check refuses a training dataset that does not serve what the model reads. tests/unit/test_supervision_contract.py trains every legal stage set on a batch that carries exactly the declared fields and without each of them in turn, so a stage that reads more than it declares fails there. A detector that is not built on the skeleton declares needs_supervision on itself.

A component that owns slots of another kind can compare its children's contracts before anything is built by implementing check_config:

@classmethod
def check_config(cls, node):
    grouper = GROUPERS.get(node["grouper"]["type"])
    head = HEADS.get(node["head"]["type"])
    if grouper.out_axes != head.in_axes:
        yield f"{grouper.__name__} emits {grouper.out_axes}, but {head.__name__} expects {head.in_axes}."

Each yielded message becomes a config error at that node.

docs.title: Head bundles
docs.text: A head bundle is one class that owns the prediction module, the target encoder, the loss and the decoder. They share one grasp parameterization (angle and depth grids, width scale, score meaning), so they are swapped together or not at all. There is no way to configure a head with another bundle's decoder.

docs.title: Optional dependencies
docs.text:
Import heavy dependencies inside the component, through require, so that import grasppanda keeps working with the core install:

from grasppanda.utils.imports import require

class SparseThing(Backbone):
    def __init__(self, ...) -> None:
        spconv = require("spconv.pytorch", extra="spconv-cu118", purpose="SparseThing")

A user without the extra gets SparseThing needs 'spconv.pytorch' … pip install -e ".[spconv-cu118]".

docs.title: Sharing it
docs.text: Put it under projects/<your_project>/ with a README that states a support level; see projects/README.md. A pip-installable plugin can expose a grasppanda.plugins entry point to be imported automatically.

docs.title: Data contracts
docs.text: Stages exchange small typed structures instead of a shared dictionary. Each structure checks its own invariants, so a mismatch fails where it is introduced, with a message that names the stage.

docs.title: Observation and Supervision
docs.text:
losses = model.loss(observation, supervision)     # training
grasps = model.predict(observation)               # inference: no ground truth in reach
  • Observation holds what a model may see: depth, RGB, intrinsics, points, per-point features, and masks.
  • Supervision holds labels and is only ever passed to loss.
  • A mask carries its Provenance (sensor, calibration, predicted, ground_truth). observation.gt_assisted() lists inputs derived from ground truth, and results are stamped with that list. The workspace crop that most GraspNet-family pipelines apply at test time is derived from the ground-truth segmentation; here that is visible instead of implicit.
  • The dense grasp labels of an object (ObjectGraspLabels) hold their score and width grids either as tensors or as a reader that leaves them in the label store. Code that consumes them calls gather_grids and gets the same values either way; see Data loading.

docs.title: Points and features
docs.text:
Structure Invariant PointSet (N, 3) coordinates with batch offsets, a reference frame and an identity. A sub-sampled set remembers its parent. PointFeatures (N, C) features bound to a PointSet. feats.expect(points, user=...) raises if they belong to a different set.

This is what stops per-point features of a sub-sampled cloud from being indexed as if they lived on the full cloud, and what stops a voxelisation's inverse map from being reused with another point set.

docs.title: Stage outputs
docs.text: Structure Produced by Notes SeedSet proposal Seeds, optional features, named scores (graspness, objectness, …) and a validity mask. No score is mandatory. ApproachSet view stage One approach direction per seed, optionally a crop frame and a template index. GroupFeatures grouper Features with named axes, e.g. ("seed", "channel") or ("seed", "depth", "channel"). A head states the axes it expects. GraspGroup head bundle The single output type of every detector.

docs.title: GraspGroup
docs.text:
Geometry follows GraspNet-1Billion; all lengths are metres.

Field Meaning translation Grasp point. rotation Proper rotation. Column 0 approach axis, column 1 closing axis, column 2 finger-height axis. width Jaw opening. depth How far the fingers reach past the grasp point along the approach axis. Not a camera depth. score Ranking score, higher is better; score_kind says what it means. frame, gripper, key Reference frame, gripper geometry, sample identity. 
grasps.validate()                       # finite, orthonormal, det +1, widths ≥ 0
grasps.sort_by_score()                  # stable: ties keep their order on every platform
grasps.to_graspnet_array()              # (G, 17), only at the I/O boundary

GraspNet label scores are friction coefficients: lower is better and −1 means invalid. They are labels, not confidences, and exist only inside Supervision.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text: grasppanda.ops holds pure-PyTorch reference implementations that run on CPU and define correct behaviour: furthest point sampling, ball and cylinder query, kNN, grasp NMS, voxelisation, view templates. Their conventions (first sample is index 0, first hits in index order, strict thresholds, 0-based indices) are documented in the API reference and pinned by tests against brute-force oracles.

docs.title: Data loading: where the label grids are read
docs.text:
A seed-based detector of the GraspNet family is trained on dense grasp labels: for every annotated point of an object, a friction score and a gripper width for each of 300 views × 12 angles × 4 depths. That is 14 400 grasps and 57.6 kB per grid and point. This page explains what a training batch used to carry, what it carries now, why nothing changed in the numbers, and what the change is worth on a clock.

Nothing here has to be configured: the shipped dataset configs use the fast path. Read on if you write an assigner, train on your own label store, or want to know where an iteration spends its time.

docs.title: What a batch carried
docs.text:
A training frame of GraspNet-1Billion shows about nine objects. The Graspness recipe keeps a quarter of each object's annotated points, at least 300: about 3 300 label points per frame, each with a score grid and a width grid. The reference pipelines copy all of them into the sample, and so did SampleGraspLabels:

per frame per batch of 4 label points kept 3 300 13 300 their score and width grids 350 MiB 1.4 GiB label points the 1024 seeds of a frame are matched to 600 2 500 what label matching reads of them 34 MiB of scores, 0.2 MiB of widths 140 MiB

The grids were read from the label store in a dataloader worker, pickled to the training process and copied to the GPU, where label matching looked at a tenth of them. On the development machine the copy to the GPU alone took 0.3 s per batch, and four workers delivered 8 frames per second to a model that can train on 16.

docs.title: Deferred grids
docs.text:
SampleGraspLabels has an option that says where the grids are read:

transforms:
  - type: SampleGraspLabels
    point_fraction: 0.25
    min_points: 300
    collision: zero_scores
    grids: deferred        # or: dense
grids: dense grids: deferred The worker draws the label points and copies their grids out of the store draws the same label points and writes down which rows of which files they are The sample carries ObjectGraspLabels.scores, .widths (.collision, .tolerance) as tensors ObjectGraspLabels.deferred: file names, rows, collision mode; a few kilobytes per object batch.to(device) moves the grids moves poses and label points The assigner indexes the tensors at the matched rows reads the matched rows from the store

The label points, the object poses, the point labels and every random number drawn are the same in both. Only the moment at which the grids are read moves: from "before the forward pass, all of them" to "inside it, the ones that are needed". They cannot be read earlier, because which label points are needed depends on the seeds, and the seeds are chosen by the network.

The read is one pass per batch (DeferredGraspLabels.gather):

  1. the matched (object, label point) pairs of all frames come to the host in one transfer and are grouped by object;
  2. every distinct row is copied once, in file order, from the memory-mapped store into one page-locked buffer (np.take, which copies straight into the buffer);
  3. the buffer goes to the device in one transfer; so do the bit-packed collision rows, which are unpacked there and written into the scores as zeros;
  4. on the device the rows are expanded to the seeds that share them and the views are re-indexed.

Widths and tolerance at the chosen view are 48 numbers per seed and are read cell by cell. An assigner that needs the widths of all views (GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp) reads them like the scores.

docs.title: The numbers do not change
docs.text:
Deferring is a change of storage, and it is held to that:

  • A deferred reader returns the stored values: zeros where collision: zero_scores would have written them, the tolerance radius of each stored level, collisions bit for bit. tests/unit/test_data_deferred_labels.py compares every grid, every collision mode, with and without tolerance, repeated and unsorted requests, against the arrays the store was built from, on a label grid whose size is not a multiple of eight. Seven deliberately broken readers (bit order, row offsets, a forgotten zero) each fail that file.
  • The same file builds the synthetic dataset twice, once per storage, and requires identical samples and bit-identical MatchedLabels for all 32 combinations of the options of NearestLabelAssigner, for ScaleBalancedAssigner, and for the scale statistic.
  • tests/integration/test_deferred_labels.py repeats this on real training frames for the shipped GSNet, GraspNet-baseline and Scale-Balanced-Grasp recipes: three batches each, all tensors of MatchedLabels identical on the GPU; and on GraspClutter6D frames in which one object model occurs twice.
  • A whole training step, losses and gradients of every parameter, is bit-identical between the two storages for GraspNet-baseline and Scale-Balanced-Grasp (under PyTorch's deterministic kernels, without which their backward pass does not repeat itself).
  • A whole training, too. GraspNet-baseline was trained for 100 iterations (runtime.deterministic: true, two loader workers, shuffling and augmentation on) three times: with the code before this change, with the code after it, and with the first half run by the old code and the second half resumed by the new. All three end with the same weights and the same optimizer state, bit for bit.

GSNet is a special case, and not because of the labels. Its sparse convolutions do not repeat themselves: two training steps on the very same batch, with the same seed, differ in the last bits of some loss terms and in every gradient, with dense labels and with PyTorch's deterministic switches on. Two trainings of 25 iterations with the same code and seed end with weights that differ by 3 · 10⁻³ on average; old code against new differs by the same amount. A loss curve of GSNet is therefore not reproducible to the last bit on this stack, whatever the labels. What is shown for GSNet is everything that can be identical: the batches, the random draws, the labels matched inside one forward pass, and the view and head losses computed from them.

Two things follow for runs:

  • grids is not part of a transform's config(), so assets derived from a data recipe (the scale statistic) are shared by both storages.
  • It is part of the resolved config, so the config hash of a run changes with it, and resuming a run started with dense grids under a config that says deferred needs runtime.allow_config_mismatch=true. The resumed run draws the same batches, in a run directory of its own.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text:
tools/bench_data.py runs a training config on the real dataset and reports the loader alone, an iteration part by part (the device synchronised around each part) and the plain training loop. With --grids dense deferred both storages run back to back in every repeat, on the same frames, with the same sampling and initial weights.

python -m tools.bench_data gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --grids dense deferred --scenes 8 --iterations 24 --warmup 16 --repeats 3

On the development machine: an RTX A6000 and 16 cores, both shared with other jobs (load average 20 to 30 during the runs), the label store on a network file system and in the page cache, four workers, 24 batches after 16 of warm-up, the first eight scenes of the training split. Cells are best / median over three repeats. before is the code before this change (commit ccb8704), run right before or after; dense and deferred are the two storages on the current code.

GSNet, batch 4 (before: two repeats)

best / median before dense deferred loader, frames/s 7.88 / 7.77 7.80 / 7.15 35.9 / 34.8 batch as it leaves a worker, MiB 1409 1409 2.77 first batch after, s 9.12 / 9.17 4.92 / 5.75 1.22 / 1.27 batch.to(device), ms 286 / 305 341 / 353 2.94 / 3.00 forward, ms 72.4 / 75.9 68.1 / 73.2 102 / 108 of which the assigner, ms 20.5 / 22.5 18.9 / 20.0 50.8 / 51.9 backward, ms 74.4 / 78.7 79.5 / 80.6 77.2 / 78.1 optimizer step, ms 3.00 / 3.01 2.78 / 2.84 2.73 / 2.98 iteration, s 0.86 / 0.87 0.97 / 0.99 0.22 / 0.24 of which waiting for the loader, s 0.45 / 0.46 0.51 / 0.54 0.05 / 0.05

GraspNet-baseline, batch 2

best / median before dense deferred loader, frames/s 6.28 / 6.27 7.35 / 7.20 39.1 / 29.6 batch as it leaves a worker, MiB 805 805 1.17 first batch after, s 6.61 / 6.91 3.61 / 3.84 1.37 / 1.52 batch.to(device), ms 158 / 176 155 / 181 2.31 / 2.59 forward, ms 81.1 / 85.4 77.8 / 79.2 103 / 109 of which the assigner, ms 17.2 / 17.2 14.4 / 15.3 40.9 / 43.6 backward, ms 51.9 / 54.8 49.0 / 50.5 49.2 / 49.4 optimizer step, ms 1.89 / 2.24 2.33 / 2.45 2.26 / 3.13 iteration, s 0.54 / 0.56 0.51 / 0.52 0.16 / 0.17 of which waiting for the loader, s 0.29 / 0.30 0.26 / 0.27 0.02 / 0.02

Scale-Balanced-Grasp, batch 2 (with a scale histogram of 64 frames instead of the shipped 3200, which changes the weights and not the timings)

best / median before dense deferred loader, frames/s 6.96 / 6.57 7.37 / 7.03 31.7 / 28.4 batch as it leaves a worker, MiB 805 805 1.18 first batch after, s 8.41 / 9.33 5.59 / 5.83 1.82 / 1.94 batch.to(device), ms 154 / 171 149 / 159 3.57 / 4.09 forward, ms 141 / 144 134 / 139 169 / 173 of which the assigner, ms 18.5 / 20.3 18.5 / 18.7 53.1 / 55.7 backward, ms 158 / 159 132 / 136 130 / 135 optimizer step, ms 2.46 / 2.62 2.90 / 3.15 2.25 / 2.80 iteration, s 0.54 / 0.56 0.48 / 0.53 0.31 / 0.31 of which waiting for the loader, s 0.22 / 0.23 0.20 / 0.22 0.02 / 0.03

An iteration is 3.7 times shorter for GSNet, 3.3 times for GraspNet-baseline and 1.8 times for Scale-Balanced-Grasp, whose model is the heaviest of the three. The deferred assigner costs 30 to 40 ms more than the dense one, because it reads; the copy to the device and the wait for the loader, which it replaces, cost 0.4 to 0.8 s. On the full training split the loader keeps the model waiting somewhat longer than on eight scenes (60 to 75 ms per iteration instead of 20 to 50) while the workers share their cores with the model and with other jobs.

Ten epochs of GSNet on GraspNet-1Billion are 64 000 iterations: about 15 hours at 0.87 s, about 4.5 hours at 0.25 s. These totals follow from the iteration times above; a full run was not timed.

The model is now the larger part of an iteration; before, an iteration waited for the loader and for the copy to the device.

docs.title: On a cold page cache
docs.text:
All of the above is with the label store in the page cache, which is where it is after the first minutes of a run. Before that, a deferred read is at a disadvantage: the dense path reads rows in four workers, the deferred path in the training process, which waits for every row that is not cached. On the network store of the development machine (a gigabit link) a cold row costs about 4 ms, so the rows of one batch cost about 10 s; the same store delivers a file read front to back at 85 to 105 MiB/s, six times faster than it delivers scattered rows.

So the first time a deferred reader opens a label file, the file is also read once, front to back, on one of two background threads (two sequential streams fill the link). The threads end when their queue is empty. A dataloader worker forked while they are still reading starts without them and without the memory maps of the training process.

Measured on a private copy of the label files of four scenes (18 objects, 2.67 GiB) on the same network store, dropped from the page cache before every run; 30 batches of four frames, seconds from the start of the loader:

loader and label matching GSNet training loop dense grids 51 73 deferred, without read-ahead 81 to 93 66 deferred, with read-ahead 34 to 36 52

With the read-ahead the first batch is slow (22 to 34 s: its rows are fetched while the files are read) and the cache is warm from the fifth batch on. Without it, batches are still two to three times slower than warm after thirty.

The files a GSNet training on GraspNet-1Billion reads are 7.5 GiB (scores 2.7, scene collisions 2.1, widths 2.7; tolerance levels add 0.7 for GraspNet-baseline). At the 105 MiB/s of this link that is a good minute, so expect the first one to two minutes of a run on a completely cold cache to be slow. This last figure is an estimate from the file sizes; a cold start of the whole training set was not measured.

Other ways of reading cold rows were measured on the same copy (loader and label matching, 30 batches) and not adopted: asking the kernel for the rows of a batch before copying them (madvise, 72 s), copying on eight threads (87 s), both together (61 s), and letting the workers ask for the rows they sampled (59 s). They all read scattered rows, at the speed of scattered rows.

GRASPPANDA_LABEL_READ_AHEAD=0 switches the read-ahead off. Do that on a machine whose memory cannot hold the label files next to everything else: there the cache never becomes warm, reading files ahead only displaces other pages, and a faster disk for $GRASPPANDA_CACHE is what helps.

docs.title: Reading labels in your own code
docs.text:
An assigner, or any code that consumes Supervision.objects, reads grids through one function and does not care how they are stored:

from grasppanda.structures.observation import gather_grids

# request k reads label point rows[k] of objects[owner[k]]
scores = gather_grids(objects, "scores", owner, rows)             # (K, V, A, D)
widths = gather_grids(objects, "widths", owner, rows, views)      # (K, A, D) at views[k]
mask = gather_grids(objects, "collision", owner, rows)            # (K, V, A, D) or None

objects can be the objects of every frame of a batch; one call reads them all. For a single object there are labels.gather_scores(rows), gather_widths(rows, views), gather_collision(rows) and gather_tolerance(rows, views). labels.dense() turns deferred labels into tensors, which reads everything and is meant for inspection.

Indexing labels.scores directly still works on dense labels and fails on deferred ones (scores is None): an assigner written that way either moves to gather_grids or runs with grids: dense.

A label store of your own can be deferred by returning, from the defer(rows, collision=...) method of its label source, an object that implements grasppanda.structures.observation.DeferredGrids: three properties and one class method, gather(readers, name, owner, rows, views), which reads for a group of readers at once.

docs.title: Decisions, with the measurements behind them
docs.text:
Why not read in the workers? A worker knows the label points but not the seeds. It could ship the rows of every label point that is the nearest one of some scene point, a superset of whatever the seeds will match. Measured on 24 training frames: 3 300 label points sampled, 1 390 in that superset, 610 matched by 1024 furthest-point seeds; the nearest-neighbour search costs a worker 15 ms per frame. The superset would still put 150 MiB of scores and widths per frame through the loader and onto the device (the deferred path reads 34 MiB and ships 0.04), and it needs a fallback for a seed whose float32 match on the GPU falls outside a float64 superset. Not worth its complexity.

Distinct rows, expanded on the device. Of 4096 seeds about 2 500 distinct label points are matched. Reading per seed, or per object with a transfer each, loses to reading each row once into one buffer: with one transfer per object the assigner took 110 to 500 ms on a GPU that other jobs share, because every small transfer waits for the device; with one pass per batch it takes about 50 ms.

np.take into a reused, page-locked buffer. Copying 146 MiB of rows out of the memory maps takes 18 ms with np.take(..., out=buffer, mode="clip") and 24 ms with fancy indexing into a fresh array; the transfer of 190 MiB to the GPU takes 9 ms from page-locked memory and 19 ms from ordinary memory. Reading on three or four threads was faster in the best case (7 ms) and slower in the median on a busy machine, and was left out.

Opening files. A dataloader worker starts every epoch without open files. NumPy resolves a Path it is asked to memory-map component by component, a dozen lstat calls that are round trips on a network file system: 61 of the 84 ms it took to open one label file. The store now opens maps by string path, and hands out labels without opening their grid files at all, so a worker that defers never opens them. The first batch of a run arrives after about 1 s instead of 7 to 9 s.

docs.title: The rest of an iteration
docs.text:
With deferred grids, a GSNet iteration (batch 4) looks like this on the development machine; the device is synchronised around every part, mean over the 30 iterations of one run:

part ms wait for the loader 67 (median 0.7) batch.to(device) 2.7 forward: backbone 25.9 forward: proposal (seed selection) 7.2 forward: view stage 0.6 forward: assigner 47.9 forward: grouper 3.9 forward: head 0.2 forward: losses and the rest 5.5 backward 52.3 optimizer step 2.8

What was changed besides the label storage, each with its measurement:

change before after measured on Box workspaces work on one table-frame coordinate at a time, in contiguous memory 54.9 ms 23.5 ms SegmentationBoxWorkspace.inside, mean of 320 calls on 160 real frames; the 480 masks compared are identical align gathers the valid pixels with np.take 7.9 ms 3.1 ms a 1280 × 720 cloud, 60 % valid One training sample in a worker (both of the above, and no grids) 280 ms 92 ms GSNet recipe, median of 24 frames, files open Label files opened by string path, and only when a grid is read 6.7 to 9.2 s 1.1 to 1.3 s time to the first batch, GSNet, two pairs of runs Poses and label points of a batch moved to the device stacked 22.1 ms 3.7 ms mean of 60 batches from the loader, old and new interleaved (medians 4.5 and 1.8 ms)

Looked at and left alone:

  • pin_memory, non-blocking transfers. A deferred batch is 3 MiB and moves in 3 to 5 ms. There is nothing left to gain.
  • persistent_workers. Starting the workers of an epoch now costs about a second. Workers that persist would carry their random state from one epoch into the next, which breaks the rule that the samples of an epoch depend on the seed and the epoch only, and exact resume with it.
  • prefetch_factor. Measured at 2, 4 and 8 on the full training split: the mean wait for a batch was 64, 72 and 99 ms. The waits come from how fast the workers are, not from how much they may queue.
  • Graspness maps. Reading the map of a frame takes 17 to 21 ms (one member of a compressed archive, and the check that it labels exactly the pixels of the frame). It is the next thing to look at in a worker.
  • More workers. A worker now needs about 92 ms per frame of an otherwise idle core; four of them deliver 30 to 37 frames per second alone and about as much as GSNet consumes (15 to 17) while the model competes for the same cores. On a machine with free cores num_workers: 8 should remove the remaining waits; that was not measured here, because the benchmarks were limited to four workers.

Where the time now is, and what would move it:

  • The assigner. Of its 48 ms, about 25 are the copy of 145 MiB of score rows out of the page cache and 9 their transfer. The scores take eleven values and 93 to 98 % of them are −1: a lossless one-byte code per score, as a derived asset, would quarter both, a sparse row format more. Neither is built.
  • The model. Backbone, proposal, grouper, head, losses and the backward pass are about half of the iteration. Mixed precision, torch.compile and channels-last memory change numbers and were out of scope. None of them was measured; as expectations only: the sparse convolutions and the point operators are C++ and CUDA kernels that torch.compile does not see, so it can only help the small MLP heads; mixed precision could shorten the sparse U-Net's forward and backward, but its sparse convolutions would have to be checked for stability in half precision first; channels-last concerns dense 2-D convolutions, which among the shipped methods only HGGD has.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Open files. A deferred reader keeps one memory map, and with it one file descriptor, per label file it has read: 220 for a training on GraspNet-1Billion (two per object model of its 40, one per scene of its 100, one more per object with tolerance labels). It keeps at most half of the limit on open files (ulimit -n), 4096 at most. A dataset with more label files than that reopens maps, which is slow on a network file system: raise the limit.
  • Memory. The page-locked buffer grows to the largest read, about 300 MiB for 4096 seeds, and is kept. The label files themselves are not copied: they are file-backed pages shared with every other process that maps them.
  • Dense is still there. grids: dense is the reference path and the component's default; the identity tests compare against it.

docs.title: Learns like the reference?
docs.text:
Measured combinations says that an option composes, builds, trains for 20 iterations without blowing up and predicts. This page asks the next question: does the option learn like the stage it replaces? Every cell is trained for 250 iterations and its losses are put beside those of the method as shipped (its reference), trained under exactly the same settings.

One run per cell, 250 iterations on 8 frames of one scene. An outcome is a statement about training dynamics on that budget, not an accuracy measurement: a cell on a par may still detect worse grasps, and a cell that is worse here may catch up with a full schedule. No number on this page is an AP.

docs.title: How a cell is judged
docs.text:
• Settings, the same for a cell and its reference: 250 iterations on the 8 frames of the split sample (scene 0), seed 0, prediction on 4 frames, grasppanda probe --schedule constant: no scheduler, every parameter group at the recipe's peak rate, scaled by the batch ratio when the probe's batches are smaller than the recipe's (FineGrasp: 0.008 for 32 frames becomes 0.002 for 8), so that methods compare. A cell whose request sets the schedule runs it (as at level 1): there the schedule is what is measured.
  • FineGrasp runs under --schedule recipe, its reference and its cells alike: at the constant 0.002 without the recipe's 800-iteration warm-up, the two post-norm transformer layers that fuse FineGrasp's four crop scales give every seed one feature (the reference implementation's fusion does the same), so the head learns the label distribution and every grasp gets one score until about iteration 530; under the warm-up the fusion recovers by iteration 80.
  • mean: the mean of a loss term over the last 25 of the 250 iterations (reported, finite values; the total loss is not judged, it sums terms whose definitions may differ).
  • ratio: the cell's mean divided by the reference's mean of the same term.
  • rise: over the last half of the run (iterations 126 to 250), the mean of its second half divided by the mean of its first half, minus 1 (the middle iteration of an odd count in neither half): +0.30 means the term ended 30 % higher than it was half-way.
  • tolerance: per method: 1.25, or the first multiple of 0.05 above the largest ratio between two seeds of its reference (any term but the total, either way round), when that is larger.
  • rising: a rise above the rising threshold of the method that also exceeds the reference's rise of the term by more than it (the rise alone for a term the reference does not report); the threshold is 0.1, or the first multiple of 0.05 above the largest difference between the rises of one term under two seeds of the reference, when that is larger.
  • lower: a comparable term below 1/tolerance of the reference's: reported, not judged.

Outcomes, in order of precedence:

Outcome Meaning fails the run did not finish: an exception, a crash, a timeout, or no real frame read. A run that died of GPU memory is not recorded (it says nothing about the config) and is run again no reference the method as shipped has no finished run under the same settings: nothing to compare with diverging a loss term is rising over the last half of the run (see rising), a loss or a weight became non-finite, or no grasp was predicted on any of the 4 frames while the reference predicts some worse not diverging, and a comparable loss term ends above the tolerance of the method times the reference's (mean of the last 25 iterations), or a part of the model that holds trainable parameters received no gradient in any iteration not comparable not diverging, nothing worse, but the cell changes the definition of every term the reference has: there is no term to compare on a par every comparable loss term ends within the tolerance of the method, at least one term is comparable, nothing rises, every value is finite and a frame has a grasp. A term far below the reference's is reported (lower), not judged

A term is not comparable when the cell changes its definition; the cell is judged on the others:

  • loss: a loss preset replaces the function of the term it is put in.
  • head: a head bundle defines the targets and the loss of every head term (score, width, angle, depth, tolerance).
  • assigner: an assigner changes the labels the view stage and the head see (a view stage sees the labels through the assigner only): every view and head term.
  • stage code: a proposal or view stage owns its targets and its loss: one whose class computes them with other code (its own loss or target methods, not inherited from the reference's stage) defines every term of that stage anew; one that computes them as the reference's does, with the same loss options, keeps them (a proposal that changes only how it samples).
  • presence: a term only one of the two runs reports.
  • sign: a term whose mean is not positive (a weighted loss can go below zero).

The tolerance and the rising threshold of a method. A cell and its reference are two runs, so a ratio away from 1 means something only beyond what two runs of the very same config show. Every reference was therefore trained twice, under seed 0 and seed 1 (The noise floor). Under the five seed-based methods, a term that has settled (it rose or fell by less than 10 % over the last half) agrees within 7 % between the seeds; a term still falling steeply at the end differs more (EconomicGrasp's graspness by 1.32x), and HGGD at its peak rate differs by up to 1.55x (angle, offsets). One tolerance for all would be blind under the stable methods or trigger-happy under HGGD, so each method gets its own: 1.25 (the plan's value, more than three times the spread of a settled term) unless its references spread more, then the first multiple of 0.05 above their largest ratio. The rising threshold follows the same rule from the rises. The spread comes from one pair of runs per method: a third seed would firm it up.

docs.title: Not on this page
docs.text:
• post: post-processing trains nothing, so a training run says nothing about it; its check is to compare the grasps in and out of the chain (and the evaluator) on 20 frames of a trained method, which is not part of this page yet.
  • stage-set, cross: several slots replaced at once: no single stage of the reference to compare with.
  • Accuracy of any kind: see the method pages of the model zoo.
  • More than one run per cell: the noise floor above is the only repeat.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
python -m tools.learn_check references --seeds 0 1 --scale-statistic-sha <SHA-256>
python -m tools.learn_check run --kind encoder --scale-statistic-sha <SHA-256>
python -m tools.learn_check status    # selected, run and pending cells; time left
python -m tools.learn_check export    # compare -> learns_like_reference.json
python -m tools.learn_check page      # this page

The runs are those of tools/probe_grid.py (--iters 250 --predict-frames 4), one run directory per kind, so an interrupted run continues where it stopped. The SHA-256 is that of the imported width histogram of Scale-Balanced-Grasp (see Measured combinations). The losses of every run are in learns_like_reference/losses_per_iteration.json (the mean of every 5 iterations).

docs.title: Measured combinations
docs.text:
Which component works under which method, measured: every cell of this page is a recorded run of grasppanda compose and grasppanda probe, and nothing is inferred from a contract or from another cell. The contract tables of Swapping components say what the config check accepts; this page says what happened when the accepted combinations were built, trained and asked to predict. A refused cell is the verdict of the config check on that config: nothing was built. The combination explorer answers a selection of method and options from these records; the slot pages say what each option is.

A cell is one run, and a run is not repeatable. The two recorded commands repeat the experiment, not its numbers: the config hash and the parameter count repeat exactly and the losses of the first iteration to the digits given; later losses, the share of real and of supervised seeds, the grasps per frame and, for a combination near the edge, the split between runs and runs-unstable are those of the recorded run and differ in the next one. A record is bound to the commit of its run: it is replaced when its config changes, not when the code of a component does.

No AP appears on this page, and none follows from it. A probe trains 20 iterations on 8 frames. It shows whether a combination works: it builds, its losses are finite, seeds reach its head, it predicts. It says nothing about how good the combination is; that takes a full training run and an evaluation on a benchmark split. Whether a cell that runs also learns like the stage it replaces (250 iterations, term by term): Learns like the reference?.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
• Grid: 1262 recorded cells (1014 runs, 174 runs-empty, 29 runs-unstable, 41 refused, 4 fails): every shipped method config as it is, every registered scene encoder under every seed-based method, every variant of every other stage with one stage replaced at a time, a sample of the legal sets of stage variants, HGGD as it is, every image-encoder preset under HGGD, every post-processing preset under all six methods, every recipe preset under every method it applies to, every loss preset in one term of every kind it accepts under every seed-based method with such a term, and a few requests that replace several slots at once. The variants of a stage are its presets plus every component whose constructor defaults no preset states. A component that needs an option only a preset supplies (DepthEmbedGroup, DepthPoolGroup, MultiRadiusGroup, MultiScaleGroup) has no cell under its type name: that request is refused for the missing option before any contract is compared, which says nothing about a combination. Its presets have cells.
  • A cell: grasppanda compose <method config> --set <slot>=<choice>, so that an encoder is fitted and adapters are inserted exactly as a user gets them, then grasppanda probe <composed config> --iters 20 --frames 8 --schedule constant: the real trainer with the method's own recipe on the split sample of GraspNet-1Billion (RealSense; scene 0, frames 0, 32, …, 224), then prediction on two of those frames. Both commands of every cell are in the measured file.
  • The learning rate: grid probes train at the recipe's peak rate without its schedule (--schedule constant: the optimizer's rate, or max_lr of a one-cycle schedule, at every step, scaled by the ratio of the batch sizes when the probe's batches are smaller than the recipe's, so FineGrasp's 0.008 for 32 frames trains at 0.002 on 8; optimizer, weight decay, clipping and hooks as the recipe has them, except that a batch-norm momentum the recipe decays per epoch is held at its first-epoch value, as the rate is held at its peak: a probe's epochs are a few iterations long). Run over the few epochs of a probe, the schedules would decay GSNet to 0.63 and EconomicGrasp to 2.4 % of its rate and keep FineGrasp in its warm-up, and the trends of different methods would not compare. A cell whose request sets the schedule (a schedule preset, a schedule-free optimizer, a recipe preset) runs that schedule. grasppanda probe --schedule recipe runs a recipe as shipped. Of the 1182 probes on this page, 1103 held the peak rate (schedule: constant in the record); 79 ran the recipe's schedule (schedule: recipe).
  • One exception to "as a user gets them": configs that read the width histogram of Scale-Balanced-Grasp were probed with the reference's own file (scale_statistic.source: legacy_import), because the native histogram is a statistic of the whole training split and a probe reads eight frames. The override is part of the recorded command.

docs.title: Verdicts
docs.text:
Verdict In a table Meaning runs ✓ · ✓ own · ✓ in Adapter On real frames: the detector was built, every requested training iteration ran with finite losses and at least one real seed, every top-level part of the model that holds trainable parameters received a gradient in at least one iteration, the weights stayed finite, and prediction returned one valid grasp group for every probed frame, at least one of them with a grasp. runs-empty ∅ · ∅ in Adapter As runs, except that no probed frame has a grasp: prediction returned one valid grasp group for every probed frame and every group is empty. Every stage ran; a model trained for a few iterations often keeps no seed. A run that is also unstable is runs-unstable. runs-unstable ≈ (n) On real frames: the detector was built, trained and predicted, but a loss or a weight became non-finite (a non-finite loss ends the training there), or an iteration had no real seed (no scene point passed the proposal, so only the proposal was trained), or no iteration supervised a seed, or a top-level part with trainable parameters received no gradient in any iteration, or fewer iterations ran or fewer frames were predicted than were asked for. refused ✗ (n) The config check refused the config (the same check as grasppanda print-config --check --for train). Nothing was built; the report carries the messages. On this page all 41 refusals come from grasppanda compose, which runs that check on the composed config and writes nothing when it fails. fails fails (n) An exception was raised after the config check had passed. The report names the phase (build, data, optimizer, loss, backward, step, hook, predict), the component it came from and the message. wired — No real frame was read. On a synthetic table-top scene with random labels the detector was built, back-propagated a loss through every stage and predicted. This shows that the stages connect; it says nothing about real data. Not used on this page.

✓ in Adapter: the bare swap is refused by the contract between encoder and proposal; compose wrapped the encoder in the one adapter that bridges it, said so, and the adapted config ran. †: compose also fitted the encoder to the method, setting out_channels to the width of the encoder it replaces or in_channels to the point features the method feeds. (n) points to the reason below the table: for a refusal the first sentence of each message of the config check (the whole messages, with the fix they propose, are in the measured file), for a failure the phase, the component and the exception, for an unstable run what was unstable. ‡ marks numbers that depend on the load of a shared machine. § marks what judge 2 flagged in a run that did not stop it from running (Judges). Below the mark of a probe: the grasps it predicted on each probed frame and, for a record of judge 2, the range of the fall of its loss terms and the levels it did not reach (learns ✗ (n)); a probe that predicted no grasp on any frame is greyed. Below a refusal, its kind when the record has one (structural, not-implemented, policy, not-a-combination).

docs.title: Judges
docs.text:
A probe is judged by grasppanda.combine.probe. The verdicts above and the fields below are those of judge 2, from 2026-10-15; 1221 of the 1262 records on this page were judged by it (judge: 2 in the measured file). The other 41 were judged by the first judge. It had no runs-empty, so a run that predicted no grasp on any probed frame is runs (0 probes of this page); it recorded none of the fields below; and from 2026-10-13 on it also checked a run for a top-level part that no gradient reached, which only a record with no_gradient shows (0 of them). A record keeps its judge until its cell is probed again.

Judge 2 also records whether the parts of a model learned, not only whether they ran. None of it changes a verdict, except that a top-level part no gradient reached makes a run runs-unstable (as before) and an empty prediction makes it runs-empty. In a record of judge 2:

Field Meaning judge 2 for a record judged by judge 2, which holds the fields from trend to lr_factor; absent for a record of the first judge, which holds none of them (about.judges) trend per loss term and for the total loss, over the iterations in which the term was active (reported, finite and not exactly 0.0): [first, last_quarter, fall], its value at the first of them, the mean of the last ceil(active / 4) of them, and (first - last_quarter) / |first|, positive when the term fell (0.7: by 70 %), to four significant digits and three decimals; three nulls when the term was never active active per loss term active in fewer iterations than ran: the number it was active in flags per loss term with a flag: the flags of the list below that hold no_gradient the units of the model whose gradient never had an L2 norm above 1e-8 in an iteration, over its trainable parameters. A unit is a registered sub-module at depth 2 (backbone.encoder, head.score_net) or a parameter a top-level part holds itself (head.bias); when no unit of a top-level part was reached, the part is listed instead of its units (backbone: a dead part). Gradients are read before every optimizer step, unscaled under mixed precision. In a record of the first judge (only when its probe had the check): the top-level parts without a non-zero gradient unchanged the top-level parts whose trainable parameters did not change: the L2 norm of the difference between before the first optimizer step and after the last one is at most 1e-6 times the larger of 1 and the L2 norm before checked [units, parts] with trainable parameters, over which no_gradient and unchanged were checked score_quantiles per predicted frame, the smallest, the median and the largest score of its predicted grasps, to 4 significant digits; null for a frame without a grasp. Scores are those the detector returns (their meaning is its score_kind) learning_rate, lr_factor the learning rate of the first parameter group of the first optimizer at the first and at the last optimizer step, as those steps used it; the last of these divided by the first: the decay the schedule applied within the probe. A schedule that steps per epoch decays with the probe's epochs, which follow from the batch size and the number of frames (GSNet's 0.95 per epoch: 0.95^9 after 20 iterations of 2 per epoch); 1 under the schedule constant; null when the first is 0 schedule, rate how the probe set the learning rate (about.schedules): constant, the recipe's peak rate at every step, or recipe, the recipe's schedule run over the probe's epochs (always for a cell whose request sets the schedule); rate is the rate every step used under constant, in the first parameter group of the first optimizer. A record without schedule was probed before the probe had the option, with the recipe's schedule losses_per_iteration not in the record: the side file measured_combinations/losses_per_iteration.json holds, for every record of judge 2 with a probe of its own, every loss term and the total at every iteration, to four significant digits (null where the term was not reported). It is written with the records and holds what the trends are computed from

The flags of a loss term; active iterations are those in which the term was reported, finite and not exactly 0:

  • flat: the term was active in at least two iterations, and the mean of its last quarter differs from its first active value by less than 5 % of that value.
  • rising: the term was active in at least two iterations, and the mean of the last half of its active iterations exceeds the mean of the first half by more than 10 % of the first half's mean (with an odd count the middle iteration is in neither half).
  • zero_at_end: the term is exactly 0.0, or not reported, at the last completed iteration.
  • constant: the term was reported in at least two iterations with the very same value in every one of them, zeros included.

The schedules of a probe (schedule in a record):

  • recipe: the config's own scheduler, run over the probe. The probe sets train.epochs to ceil(iterations / iterations per epoch), so a schedule that steps per epoch is compressed into those few epochs (GSNet's 0.95 per epoch ends at 0.95^9 = 0.63 after 20 iterations of 2 per epoch, EconomicGrasp's cosine at 2.4 % of its start) and one that steps per iteration runs its first steps only (FineGrasp's warm-up of 800 iterations keeps a probe of 20 at no more than 2.5 % of its rate).
  • constant: no scheduler: every parameter group of every optimizer trains at the recipe's peak rate for the whole probe. The peak is the rate the optimizer gives the group (the configured lr, with the multipliers of ParamGroups), except for a schedule that sets a peak of its own: max_lr of OneCycleLR and CyclicLR, the larger factor of LinearLR. Every other schedule of the toolbox starts at that rate or reaches it at the end of its warm-up. When the probe's batches hold fewer frames than the recipe's, the peak is scaled by their ratio (the linear scaling rule: FineGrasp's 0.008 for 32 frames trains at 0.002 on batches of 8). A batch-norm momentum that the recipe decays per epoch (BNMomentumHook: GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, HGGD) is held at its first epoch's value likewise (hooks.<i>.decay=1): decayed over epochs of a few iterations it can reach its floor of 0.001 within the probe (Scale-Balanced-Grasp's at iteration 73), and the running statistics, which prediction normalises with, then stop following the weights; training itself does not read them. The optimizer (its weight decay and its momentum as configured), clipping, accumulation and every other hook are the recipe's.

Fall per loss term §, a column of the tables of what the probes saw, gives the fall of every term (the term without loss/; active n where it was active in fewer iterations than ran), and Learns, predicts § whether the run reached those levels (Measured classes) and what kept it from them: the flags, the units no gradient reached, the parts that did not change, frames without a grasp or with one score for all; not checked for a record of the first judge. A flag is a statement about one short run, a reason to look, not a verdict. Under schedule: constant every step of that run used the recipe's peak rate, so flags compare across methods; a record without schedule ran the method's own schedule over the probe's epochs, which may have lowered the rate within the probe (lr_factor) by very different amounts from one method to the next.

docs.title: Measured classes
docs.text:
One run, seed 0, 20 iterations, 8 frames of one scene; a class counts verdicts, not accuracy. A cell (one option under one method) is decided at four levels, each from its record alone; every level needs the one before it:

  • composes: the contract rules and the config check accept the composed config: grasppanda compose writes it (any verdict but refused). A refusal by policy is undecided (needs consent), and so is a request that is not a combination.
  • runs: the probe ran clean on real frames: the verdict runs or runs-empty. A runs-unstable probe counts as not running only when its repeat (repeat in the record: the same config, seed and schedule) was unstable too; without a repeat the level is undecided (unstable, not repeated); when the repeat ran clean the cell runs, and learns and predicts are read from the repeat. fails does not run.
  • learns: judge 2 only. Every loss term was active (reported, finite, not exactly 0) in at least 50 % of the iterations and fell by at least 5 % (fall = (first - mean of the last quarter) / |first| over its active iterations), and no term is flagged flat, rising or constant; a term that is 0 at the last iteration (zero_at_end) is judged on its active iterations. Every unit with trainable parameters received a gradient (no_gradient is empty) and every part changed (unchanged is empty).
  • predicts: judge 2 only. Every predicted frame has at least one grasp, and on every frame the smallest and the largest score differ (score_quantiles): a model whose scores collapsed to one value ranks nothing.

A level that cannot be decided from a record says why:

  • not checked: the record was judged by the first judge, which recorded neither the trend of the loss terms nor the scores of the predicted grasps.
  • unstable, not repeated: the probe was runs-unstable and has not been repeated: an unstable run counts as not running only when a second probe of the same config is unstable too.
  • needs consent: refused by a policy that waits for the user's consent (trust_remote_code needs accept_remote_code: true): a rule about this machine, not about the combination.
  • not a combination: the request names a component that lacks an option only a preset supplies: it is refused before any contract is compared, and is no combination.
  • not probed: the grid has the cell, but no record yet.
  • not reached by the method as shipped: the method as shipped, probed the same way, does not reach this level either (for example FineGrasp at the constant rate, whose fusion of crop scales gives every seed one feature in a short run, so every grasp gets one score): under that method the level says nothing about the option at this budget.

The class of an option at a level counts the methods under which it reached that level. For a stage of the seed-based skeleton decided under all five seed-based methods (GSNet, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp):

  • universal: it reached the level under all five seed-based methods.
  • most: under three or four of them.
  • some: under two.
  • specific: under exactly one.
  • none: under none of them.

An option of another slot (post-processing, loss, recipe, image encoder) is universal only when it reached the level under every method it applies to and those include the five seed-based ones. Every other class reads N of M probed: it reached the level under N of the M methods where the level was decided, and the methods where it was not are named after it (+2 not checked). A level that no method decided is named by the reason. A level decided only where the level before it failed is not checked: the class says so instead of counting the failures again.

A class is a statement about this grid: these presets, the methods' own recipes, this dataset, one stage replaced at a time. A stage that is refused alone may work together with the stage it depends on (a head bundle with its assigner and its labels); those are the sets of stages. The classes of the scene encoders and of the other stages, level by level:

An adapter wraps an encoder and is not one itself, so it has no row above: compose inserts it where the contract between encoder and proposal asks for it (✓ in Adapter). What was measured with each, over all groups of the grid:

docs.title: The training recipe
docs.text:
A recipe preset changes what is around the model: the optimizer, the schedule, the hooks of the training loop, the point augmentation. Each is applied alone to every method as shipped and probed like a stage; an augmentation a method's data contract does not accept is refused there. —: the preset names the scene encoder of the seed-based skeleton, which HGGD does not have. A preset that sets the schedule (the schedule presets, the schedule-free optimizers, the recipes) is probed with that schedule, schedule: recipe in its record, since the schedule is what its cell measures; the others with the schedule of the grid (A cell above). What each preset is and how to use it: the recipe slot.

docs.title: Sets of stages
docs.text:
The contract rules accept 9104 sets of stage variants, too many to probe each: 95 were probed (86 runs, 9 runs-empty) and 9009 were not. The probed sets were picked so that a stage variant that occurs in a legal set occurs in a probed one, under a dense and under a sub-sampling encoder: 118 of the 118 pairs of variant and kind of encoder are in a probed set. That a set runs says nothing about another set with the same parts. The sets that were not probed are the sets of grasppanda.combine.grid.cells(("stage-set",)) without a record (about.stage_sets_not_probed of the measured file counts them); python -m tools.probe_grid run --only '<id>' probes one.

A set states all five stages and the encoder: the preset named, under which the set needs no adapter. It was composed onto the method config whose data recipe serves its labels (last but one column), so the optimizer, the schedule and the data pipeline are that method's.

docs.title: Post-processing
docs.text:
Every post-processing preset as the evaluation variant post of every method (grasppanda compose <config> --set post=<preset>), applied by the probe to the predictions of its two frames: grasps predicted → grasps left. A post-processor reads grasps and the observation, never a network, so it needs no training of its own: a cell is the method's prediction plus the chain. The grasps are those of a detector trained for the iterations of the probe; the page of the slot has the same steps on the predictions of released weights.
