docs.title: Losses
docs.text:
Every loss preset in every kind of loss term it accepts, under every seed-based method that has a term of that kind (grasppanda compose <config> --set <stage>.<loss option>=<preset>). Which loss fits which kind of term is a contract (Heads and losses); the unit tests run every loss in every term of its kind on tiny models. A method has several terms of some kinds, so a cell replaces one representative term per kind and method: the last term of that kind in the order of the pipeline (proposal, view, head; within a stage, the order the stage declares its terms in). That is the term nearest the grasp, where the methods differ; GSNet, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp share their proposal. The representative terms:

docs.title: Adding a component
docs.text:
A new encoder or stage appears in the grid by being registered. Give it a preset if its options cannot be guessed (Try a combination), probe its cells and regenerate:

python -m tools.probe_grid run --only 'encoder/*/MyEncoder' 'stage/*/*/my-preset'

tests/unit/test_combine_grid.py fails until every cell of a registered component has a record in the measured file.

docs.title: Operators and their backends
docs.text:
grasppanda.ops holds the geometric operators the models are built from. Each has a pure-PyTorch reference implementation that runs on any device and defines the result. Four of them can also run on optional compiled kernels (C++/OpenMP and CUDA), which are used only where they return exactly what the reference returns.

Nothing on this page is needed to use GraspPanda: after a plain pip install without a compiler every operator runs on the reference. The kernels make inference and training faster; they never change a result.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
The conventions are part of the contract: which point wins a tie decides which seeds a checkpoint sees, so a ported checkpoint only reproduces if they are kept.

Operator Result Rules a backend must reproduce furthest_point_sample(points, num_samples, skip_near_origin, tie_break) (B, num_samples) indices The first sample is index 0. The squared distance is x² + y² + z² added left to right. tie_break="lowest_index" takes the first of several equally far points; "pointnet2_cuda" takes the one the PointNet++ CUDA kernel takes (bit-reversed thread id, then index, with min(512, 2^⌊log₂N⌋) threads). skip_near_origin never picks a point with squared norm ≤ 1e-3 after the first. ball_query(query, support, radius, nsample) (B, M, nsample) indices, (B, M) hit counts Strictly inside: d² < radius². The first nsample hits in index order; missing slots repeat the first hit; a query without hits returns index 0 in every slot and a count of 0. cylinder_query(query, support, rotation, radius, hmin, hmax, nsample) as ball_query With d = Rᵀ(p − q): hmin < d.x < hmax and d.y² + d.z² < radius², all strict; the axis is column 0 of rotation. Same ordering and padding. knn(query, support, k) (B, M, k) distances and indices Ascending Euclidean distance; equidistant neighbours in index order (a stable sort); indices start at 0.

three_interpolate, inverse_distance_weights, voxelize, grasp_nms, the view templates and the serialisation codes have a single implementation.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
Backend What runs When reference The pure-PyTorch operator. Always available. compiled The kernels of grasppanda._ops. A library has been built and its self-check passed on the device. Selecting it explicitly is an error otherwise. auto (default) compiled where it is available and passed its self-check, else reference.

The kernels take float32 tensors on a CPU or a CUDA device. Other floating types always run the reference, as does knn when gradients are requested or k > 64, and cylinder_query under autocast or with TF32 matrix products (see below).

docs.title: What "identical" means, and how it is ensured
docs.text:
A kernel has to return the same integers as the reference for every input, and the same distances bit for bit. That is checked three times:

  1. By construction. Every kernel expression mirrors one expression of the reference (grasppanda/_ops/src/common.h):
  2. no fused multiply-add: a fused a·b + c rounds once where PyTorch rounds twice (-ffp-contract=off on the host, __fmul_rn / __fadd_rn on CUDA);
  3. three-term sums in PyTorch's order. Where the reference spells the order out (furthest point sampling) so do the kernels. Where it calls sum(-1) (ball query, kNN) PyTorch adds left to right on the CPU but (x + z) + y on CUDA, and the kernels follow the device;
  4. thresholds are rounded to float32 the way PyTorch rounds a Python number that is compared with a float32 tensor;
  5. the root of a kNN distance is taken by PyTorch, not by the kernel: PyTorch's float32 square root on the CPU is accurate to one unit in the last place but is not the correctly rounded one (it differed in 18 % of a million random values);
  6. NaN and infinite coordinates behave as in torch.minimum, argmax and sort.
  7. At run time. The first time an operator runs on a device, its kernel is compared with the reference on small random and lattice clouds (ties, repeated points, empty and oversized neighbourhoods, points exactly on a surface), and the kernels' squared distances are compared with PyTorch's bit for bit. A kernel that differs is not used; one log line says so.
  8. In the test-suite. tests/unit/test_ops.py runs every oracle test on both backends; tests/unit/test_ops_equivalence.py and tests/integration/test_ops_cuda.py compare the backends on some 2 700 (CPU) and 4 700 (CUDA) randomized calls; the GSNet stage-parity and backbone-oracle tests run with the kernels as default.

docs.title: The cylinder query
docs.text:
The reference rotates the offsets with a batched matrix product, that is through a BLAS whose rounding is not specified: MKL and cuBLAS return different last bits for the same input. No kernel can reproduce that. The cylinder kernel therefore computes its own rotated offset together with a bound on how far any correct float32 evaluation can be from it, and gives a verdict only for support points that are further from the cylinder surface than that bound. A query that meets a point inside the band before it is complete is handed back and answered by the reference itself. On recorded GraspNet-1Billion frames that happens to 2 of 4096 queries, on synthetic table tops to 13 of 65 536; the result is the reference's in every case.

Under autocast, or with torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32, the reference's matrix product runs in half precision or TF32. The kernel is then not used, because a float32 kernel would be more accurate than the reference and so disagree with it.

docs.title: Selecting a backend
docs.text:
In a config, per operator (fps, ball_query, cylinder_query, knn); operators that are not mentioned use auto:

runtime:
  ops: {fps: reference, knn: compiled}

The values are validated when the config is loaded. The selection is applied by grasppanda.ops.backends.configure, which is also the Python interface:

from grasppanda.ops import backends

backends.configure({"fps": "reference"})      # for this process
with backends.override(knn="reference"):       # temporarily, for a comparison
    ...
print(backends.report())

grasppanda train, test and infer apply runtime.ops when the run starts, and the backend each operator settled on is written to env.json in the run directory.

The environment variable GRASPPANDA_OPS overrides the configuration for one process, either with one backend for all operators or with a list:

GRASPPANDA_OPS=reference grasppanda test ...
GRASPPANDA_OPS=fps=reference,knn=compiled python my_script.py

grasppanda env --json and the env.json of every run record what each operator uses on the CPU and on the current CUDA device, and why if that is not what auto would prefer:

"ops": {
  "fps": {"requested": "auto", "cpu": "compiled", "cuda": "compiled"},
  "knn": {"requested": "auto", "cpu": "compiled", "cuda": "reference",
          "note": {"cuda": "the compiled library has no kernels for 'cuda' tensors: ..."}},
  "library": {"path": ".../grasppanda_ops_3a33d4588d6dade9.so", "cuda": false,
              "detail": "CPU kernels only (no CUDA 11.x toolkit ...)"}
}

docs.title: Building the kernels
docs.text:
The kernels are compiled the first time an operator needs them, with PyTorch's own extension tooling (torch.utils.cpp_extension), and cached. The build takes a few seconds: the kernels use no PyTorch headers and are called through ctypes.

Needed For Without it A C++ compiler ($CXX or c++) and ninja (pip install ninja) CPU kernels One log line per process; every operator runs on the reference. Selecting reference (GRASPPANDA_OPS=reference) silences it. A CUDA toolkit of the major version PyTorch was built with CUDA kernels CPU kernels only; operators on CUDA tensors run on the reference. 
python -m grasppanda._ops.build            # build if needed, then report
python -m grasppanda._ops.build --force    # rebuild, also after a recorded failure
python -m grasppanda._ops.build --cpu-only
  • Cache. $GRASPPANDA_OPS_CACHE, by default <cache root>/ops ($GRASPPANDA_CACHE or ~/.cache/grasppanda). One directory per PyTorch version, variant (CPU or CUDA), platform and source revision, so several environments share a cache without clashing and an upgrade rebuilds. Nothing compiled is ever part of the package.
  • Toolkit. $CUDA_HOME, nvcc on the path and /usr/local/cuda* are examined; a toolkit of exactly PyTorch's CUDA version wins, then any of the same major version. The kernels are compiled to PTX for the oldest GPU architecture PyTorch supports and specialised by the driver on first use, so one build serves every GPU of a machine and a build made on a login node serves its compute nodes. TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST overrides the architecture list as for any PyTorch extension.
  • Failures. A failed build is recorded with its log next to where the library would be, reported in one log line, and not retried until the compiler changes or --force is given. A failed CUDA build still yields the CPU kernels.
  • Never on first use. GRASPPANDA_OPS_BUILD=0 uses a library only if it is already built.
  • Forked workers run the CPU kernels on one thread (GNU OpenMP does not survive a fork); the parent uses torch.get_num_threads().

docs.title: Changing an operator or adding a kernel
docs.text:
• The reference comes first. Change behaviour there, with an oracle test written out in tests/unit/test_ops.py.
  • A kernel is accepted when it returns identical integers and bit-identical distances on tests/unit/test_ops_equivalence.py and tests/integration/test_ops_cuda.py, and when the GSNet parity and backbone oracle tests pass with it as default. Add the cases your change makes interesting to the randomized comparisons, and a self-check to grasppanda/ops/backends.py.
  • Where the reference goes through arithmetic that cannot be mirrored (a BLAS, a library function that is not correctly rounded), let PyTorch compute that part, or decide only what is certain and hand the rest back, as the cylinder query does.

docs.title: Swapping components
docs.text:
Replacing one stage of a method is one line in a config. This page says which replacements the toolbox accepts, what each one changes besides that line, and which swaps look harmless and are not. The tables are generated from the contract rules that the config checker runs (python -m tools.make_component_docs), and every cell is exercised by tests/unit/test_swap_matrix.py, so they describe the code as it is.

Nothing here is a result. A swapped model has to be trained and evaluated before it means anything; the configs under configs/experimental/ are starting points with no AP attached.

docs.title: The one-line swap
docs.text:
grasppanda components --slot backbones          # what exists, with its contract
grasppanda components PTv3                      # options, defaults, what it fits
grasppanda print-config gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --check \
    --opts "model.backbone={type: PTv3, in_channels: 3, grid_size: 0.005}"

or, in a file,

_base_: [../gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e.yaml]
model:
  backbone: {type: PTv3, in_channels: 3, grid_size: 0.005}   # the options of the old type are dropped

A swap the contracts forbid stops at the config check, before a dataset is opened, and says what to change:

$ grasppanda print-config gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --check \
      --opts "model.backbone={type: PointNet2}"
✗ 1 config problem in configs/gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e.yaml

  model
    GraspnessFPS requires 'dense' scene features, but PointNet2 returns 'subsampled' ones
    (features on a sub-sampled point set). Wrap the backbone in the explicit adapter
    `{type: FeaturePropagation, backbone: {...}}` or choose a proposal that works on
    sub-sampled features.

grasppanda print-config gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --check \
    --opts "model.backbone={type: FeaturePropagation, backbone: {type: PointNet2}}"   # ✓ valid

docs.title: What the checker compares
docs.text:
A seed-based detector is backbone → proposal → view → (assigner) → grouper → head. Each stage declares a contract as class attributes; the rules below compare them. They belong to the skeleton, so the verdict is the same for GSNet, EconomicGrasp, GraspNetBaseline and ScaleBalancedGrasp, and the same whether the model comes from a YAML file or from DETECTORS.build(...) in Python.

Rule Compares Why it exists Kind of refusal Where features live backbone.output with proposal.requires Features on every scene point and features on a subsample are different objects. Converting is a learned or a sampling step that changes the model, so it is a component you write down, never an interpolation behind your back. fixed-by-compose: the encoder adapter Feature axes grouper.out_axes with head.in_axes A crop with a depth axis and one without feed different heads. An axis is never added or squeezed implicitly: an axis adapter is a component you write down (DepthEmbedGroup repeats a crop over the depth bins with a learned embedding of the bin, as Scale-Balanced-Grasp repeats its seed feature; DepthPoolGroup takes the maximum over the bins). fixed-by-compose: the axis adapter. structural for an axis adapter under the head of the other family; not-implemented for a scene-support crop without a depth axis under a head with one (no adapter repeats a scene crop) Label set assigner.label_format with head.label_format and view.label_formats Dense grids (48 grasps per point and view) and compact labels (one) are different supervision; a grid cannot be recovered from one grasp. structural. Compose writes the label set the head reads into the assigner and the data recipe, so the rule is met when a request sets an assigner of the other set, or a view stage that reads dense grids only under compact labels Fields of the matched labels view.needs_matched, head.needs_matched with assigner.optional_outputs A stage that reads an optional field needs the assigner option that produces it. The error names the option. fixed-by-compose: the option; structural when the assigner never returns the field Seed weights assigner.optional_outputs["weight"] with applies_seed_weights of view stage and head Every shipped view stage and head bundle applies a weight per seed: each of its losses is the weighted mean over its supervised entries, every entry weighted by its seed. A stage that does not would train unweighted next to a weighted assigner. not a refusal: a warning in the report of grasppanda compose and when the model is built Seed scores seed_scores of proposal and view stage; head.required_seed_scores(options) One owner per score (objectness cannot be predicted and supervised twice), and a score the decoder multiplies in must be predicted by some stage. fixed-by-compose where a stage has the option: a scoring proposal predicts graspness only (ScoredSeeds with select_by: graspness_only), the head decodes without the score (OperationHead with score_decode: score_x_tolerance). structural where it has none: a proposal that selects its seeds by objectness Depth bins len(grouper.hmax) with head.num_depth One crop per depth bin of the head. not-a-combination One score definition score_target, max_friction of view stage and head Only when both use the definition of grasppanda.models.heads.friction: the view target is the best grasp score of a view. not-a-combination Loss terms loss_terms of a stage with accepts of the loss in it A classification loss on a regression term, or a loss that scores a set as a whole (DiceLoss) where a weight per element arrives, is not the same supervision under another name. structural

docs.title: Why a pair is refused
docs.text:
Every refusal carries a kind, so that "does not fit" says whether it is a property of the components or of what the toolbox implements today. grasppanda compose prints it in brackets before each message, its --json report lists it in refusal_kinds (in the order of refusal), and the numbered reasons of the tables below start with it.

Kind Meaning structural A genuine incompatibility: the components cannot work together whatever their options (two label sets, two owners of one score and no option to drop one, a classification loss on a regression term). not-implemented The combination makes sense, but the code that joins the two parts does not exist yet; the message names what would lift it. fixed-by-compose An adapter or an option lifts it, and grasppanda compose inserts or sets it and says so. Met in a config written by hand without it, or composed with --no-adapter. not-a-combination The components fit, but the config does not state them fully: a component lacks a required option (a bare DepthEmbedGroup without the grouper it wraps), or two options disagree (a size, a grid, a range, a dataset section). policy Refused on purpose until the config says otherwise: model code from a hub repository runs only with accept_remote_code: true.

What compose lifts, besides the encoder adapters and the projected grouper: the axis adapter between grouper and head; the assigner options a stage reads; the graspness-only option of a scoring proposal next to ObjectnessViewStage; the decode option of a head whose score no stage predicts; and the label set of a head bundle, written into the assigner and the data recipe (--set labels=dense|compact asks for it in so many words). Each is one sentence in its report and in the header of the composed file. A data recipe it does not rewrite gets the exact --set, --unset and --opts that would, in the report (Try a combination).

✓: the features of model.backbone: {type: <Encoder>} live where the proposal of the method needs them. in Adapter: the bare swap is refused with a message that names the adapter; model.backbone: {type: <Adapter>, backbone: {type: <Encoder>}} passes that rule.

Adapters: FeaturePropagation turns any encoder into a dense one; FurthestPointSubsample turns any encoder into a subsampled one.

Width is the number of channels the encoder returns with its constructor defaults, as it declares it (Backbone.output_channels); (out_channels) marks an encoder that has an option of that name to set it. The other stages take whatever width arrives, with these exceptions among the reference models: ScaleBalancedGrasp needs 256 channels (DepthCylinderGroup adds the seed features to its crop features). An encoder of another width is refused there by the config check, with both numbers and the ways out; grasppanda compose takes one of them by itself (the encoder's out_channels, or the projected variant of the grouper). once built: the width follows from a library model or a layout that only the constructor resolves, so the check builds the encoder once, without released weights.

Every encoder can serve every method, but never silently. The two adapters are the only bridges between the two kinds of output, and each changes the model in a way worth knowing:

  • FeaturePropagation (subsampled → dense) invents features for points the encoder never looked at: inverse-distance interpolation over the three nearest kept points, then a shared MLP. A graspness head then scores every scene point from features that carry the resolution of the subsample (1024 points with the GraspNet-baseline layout).
  • FurthestPointSubsample (dense → subsampled) decides which points can become grasps. It samples the scene coordinates, so the seeds are spread evenly over the cloud, table included, where GraspnessFPS spreads them over the points predicted graspable. With the same sampling rules it keeps exactly the points PointNet2 ends on, in the same order (tests/unit/test_backbone_subsample.py): swapping PointNet2 for a wrapped dense encoder changes the features of the seeds and leaves the seeds where they were.

docs.title: What an encoder swap changes
docs.text:
The contract says where features live. It does not say what a feature has seen. These are the constructor defaults, which is what a bare {type: ...} gives you:

Encoder Unit of length What sets the receptive field Seeds under its method Re-tune first SparseUNet14 voxel_size, 5 mm Four stride-2 stages: the coarsest voxel is 16 × the grid, 8 cm at 5 mm 1024 by GraspnessFPS from predicted graspness — (reference of GSNet and EconomicGrasp) SpUNet grid_size, default 2 cm (ScanNet rooms) The same four stride-2 stages, with 2-3-4-6 residual blocks where SparseUNet14 has one: more 3³ convolutions per level, so a feature reaches further in voxels as above grid_size; out_channels (default 20, class scores); in_channels (default 6); learning rate (the training check lost most seeds in two iterations at 1e-3) PTv3 grid_size, default 2 cm (ScanNet rooms) Four stride-2 poolings, and attention over patches of 1024 serialised voxels: counted in points, not in metres as above grid_size (0.005 to keep GSNet's unit); enc_patch_size / dec_patch_size if clouds are small; learning rate and schedule PTv3Sonata, PTv3Utonia grid_size, default 2 cm / 1 cm As PTv3, encoder only: dense features are the pooled stages copied back, no learned decoder as above everything under Traps, items 2 and 3 LitePT grid_size, default 2 cm (ScanNet rooms) 3³ sparse convolutions in the three finest stages, attention only in the two coarsest (8 × and 16 × the grid). At 5 mm a tabletop frame is a few hundred voxels there, fewer than one patch of 1024: attention is global as above grid_size; in_channels (default 6); drop_path (0.3, for long schedules); the 72-channel output OACNNs grid_size, default 2 cm (ScanNet rooms) Four stride-2 stages of 3³ sparse convolutions, plus adaptive pooling grids counted in cells (point_grid_size): the 8 to 16 cells of the first stage are 0.32 to 0.64 m at 2 cm and 0.08 to 0.16 m at 5 mm as above grid_size; point_grid_size; out_channels (default 20, class scores); in_channels (default 9); learning rate (the training check lost its seeds for three iterations at 1e-3) PointNeXt radius, default 0.1 m doubling per stage (S3DIS rooms) Ball radii per stage; stride 4 per stage as above radius (the GraspNet-baseline layout starts at 0.04 m); in_channels (default 4) PointNet2Dense radii, default 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.8 m (rooms) Ball radii and the points kept per level (1024 / 256 / 64 / 16) as above npoints, radii PointNet2 radii, 0.04 / 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 m Ball radii; 2048 / 1024 / 512 / 256 points the 1024 points of its second level, by furthest point sampling of the scene — (reference of GraspNet-baseline) PointNet2Transformer radii, 0.04 / 0.1 m Two levels, each with attention over 16 nearest points as above — (reference of Scale-Balanced-Grasp)

What follows from a different receptive field or seed set, whichever encoder causes it:

  • Label statistics move. The head is trained on the seeds that reach it. GSNet normalises score targets with the extrema of the batch (head.score_target: log_friction_batch_norm); EconomicGrasp supervises only seeds within 5 mm of a label point (assigner.max_match_distance), so an encoder that shifts where seeds land changes how many seeds are supervised at all (metric/supervised_seeds in the log); Scale-Balanced-Grasp weights seeds by a width histogram of the training labels.
  • The recipe was tuned for the reference encoder. Learning rate, schedule, batch size and point budget in configs/_base_/schedules/ are the authors' values for their encoder. They are a starting point for another one, not a claim.
  • Channel widths are injected, and checked when the model is built. The proposal, view stage and grouper take the encoder's out_channels. One stage needs two widths to be equal: DepthCylinderGroup with seed_residual: gated (Scale-Balanced-Grasp) adds seed features to crop features. The error names both numbers and the three ways out; grasppanda train reaches it within seconds, print-config --check does not build the model.

docs.title: View stage and head bundle
docs.text:
view ↓ · head → DecoupledGridHead EconomicHead OperationHead SWADHead DirectionViewStage ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ HealpixViewStage ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ IcosphereViewStage ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ LatticeViewStage ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ObjectnessViewStage ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ RomaRotationViewStage ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ TemplateViewStage ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ TwoVectorViewStage ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓

Reading the tables:

  • Proposal. GraspnessFPS scores every scene point and needs the graspness asset of the dataset (grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness). SubsampledSeeds scores nothing: every point the encoder kept is a seed. Without ObjectnessViewStage behind it, nothing in the model separates object seeds from table seeds, and a grasp is decoded for each of them.
  • View stage. TemplateViewStage samples the training view from its own scores (train_selection: multinomial) and reads either label set. ObjectnessViewStage takes the arg-max in both modes, predicts objectness with the views and reads two optional fields of dense labels.
  • Grouper. A seeds-support crop gathers at most the other seeds of the frame, with their learned features. A scene-support crop gathers raw coordinates of the whole cloud and no learned feature. They are not one crop at two resolutions, and only the second has a depth axis.
  • Head bundle. Prediction layers, target encoder, loss and decoder share one grasp parameterisation and move together. SWADHead and OperationHead read dense label grids, EconomicHead compact labels, which the dataset must serve (compact_labels: in the dataset config, grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --compact-labels); OperationHead also needs the tolerance asset. grasppanda compose writes the label set of the head into the assigner and the data recipe.

The detector type does not change which sets are legal. It names the method whose reference behaviour the config claims to follow; a set that is no reference model is a new model, whatever it is called.

HGGD is not in these tables because it is not in this family. It proposes partial grasps from an image heat-map, has no view stage and no approach-aligned crop, and none of its stages fills a slot above; putting a seed-based stage into it, or its heat-map proposal into a seed-based detector, is not a swap the registries can express. Its parts are options of the detector (grasppanda components HGGD). Its "ResNet-34" is the block layout only, with a base width of 8 and four input channels, trained from scratch: a pretrained three-channel ResNet-34 is a different network with a different input (trap 8 of the survey).

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
Swaps that pass every check above, or look as if they should, and are not what they seem. The numbers are stable identifiers: code comments and error messages refer to a trap by its number.

  1. An object-level pretrained encoder as scene encoder (Point-BERT, Point-MAE, ReCon, Uni3D; trap 1). They turn one normalised object of a few thousand points into patch tokens or a single vector. A scene of 15 000 metric points is neither their input nor their output: there is no per-point feature for a graspness head, and normalising the scene destroys the metres the cylinder radii and depth bins are written in. None is registered as a backbone for that reason.
  2. "PTv3 with Sonata, Concerto or Utonia weights" as "PTv3" (trap 2). The released self-supervised checkpoints are encoder-only, have other depths and widths, expect nine input channels (coordinates, colour, normal; zeros where missing) and were trained on a 2 cm or rescaled grid. They load into PTv3Sonata / PTv3Utonia, not into PTv3; loading one into the wrong type fails on the key report. Changing only a weight path changes all of the above.
  3. Keeping the grid when changing the encoder, or changing it freely (trap 3). The grid is the encoder's unit of length. The same layer sees a fourfold different piece of the scene at 5 mm and at 2 cm. Pretrained weights are tied to the grid they were trained on; a model trained from scratch is tied to the grid it was trained at. No contract checks this: grid_size, voxel_size and radii are yours to set, and the defaults of room-scale encoders are wrong for a tabletop (table above).
  4. One PointNet++ for another (trap 4). Seeds come from furthest point sampling and neighbours from ball queries; the start index, the tie rule and the fill order differ between implementations, so two "identical" networks hand different seeds to the head. Here they are options with names (fps_tie_break, fps_skip_near_origin); an author checkpoint reproduces only with the author's values.
  5. A head trained under one proposal, reused under another (trap 5). Targets depend on which seeds reach the head (see Label statistics move). Retrain the head, and recompute any prior such as the scale-balance histogram.
  6. A seed-support grouper for a scene-support grouper "at another resolution" (trap 6). See Grouper above; the contracts refuse the pair with the wrong head.
  7. View classification replaced by "the same thing with regression" (trap 7). The label files are indexed by the 300 template views; a regressed direction needs one target per seed and a different assigner. There is no such view stage here.
  8. Scale-balanced weights on a model that does not read them. Not in the survey: found by the swap matrix. ScaleBalancedAssigner with SWADHead or TemplateViewStage used to build, train and report losses while the weights were dropped. Every shipped view stage and head bundle now applies MatchedLabels.weight (a weighted mean over its supervised entries); a stage of your own that does not is reported as a warning.
  9. A collision filter "on" compared across methods, and scores treated as one quantity (traps 9 and 14). Post-processors are swappable in evaluation.variants, and every result is reported with and without them. But GSNet's score is an unbounded regressed value, EconomicGrasp's a weighted sum of raw logits and OperationHead's a product with a tolerance (score_kind in the catalogue). Anything that thresholds or fuses scores must be fitted per head bundle.
  10. A checkpoint carried across a swap (trap 12 and ARCHITECTURE §8.3). Nothing claims a checkpoint is portable across components: runtime.load_from fails on missing, unexpected or mis-shaped keys and prints the report. Stages you did not swap keep their weights only if you load them deliberately (allow_weight_mismatch), and they were trained for the features of the old encoder.
  11. A weight file's licence inferred from its code (trap 15). Sonata-family weights are CC BY-NC 4.0 under Apache-2.0 code. Using them makes the trained model non-commercial; the scene encoder page lists each file.

docs.title: What is checked when
docs.text: When What How it fails grasppanda print-config <cfg> --check, and first thing in train / test Unknown keys and types; every rule of What the checker compares, with defaults resolved ConfigError listing all problems, each with the config path and the file that set it Model construction (train / test, seconds later) The same rules on the built stages; channel widths; values a constructor validates ContractError, ValueError or BuildError naming the component and the numbers First batch Shapes that depend on data: seeds per frame against the encoder's subsample, label views against the template, missing label assets ContractError naming both sides Never Whether grid_size, radii and the recipe suit your scenes; whether the swap helps —

docs.title: Ready-made swap configs
docs.text:
grasppanda compose writes such a config for any combination and grasppanda probe trains it for a few iterations on real frames: Try a combination. What that gave for every encoder and stage under every method is on the generated page Measured combinations.

configs/experimental/ holds a small set of encoder swaps that pass the check and were trained for a few iterations on GraspNet-1Billion to prove that data, labels and model fit together. Each file states what must be re-tuned and why. See configs/experimental/README.md.

docs.title: What the matrix test proves
docs.text:
tests/unit/test_swap_matrix.py runs on tiny synthetic scenes (two frames of 96 points, random dense and compact labels, a width histogram) on the CPU, with one tiny configuration per registered component. It proves that:

  • every registered scene encoder under every seed-based method either builds, trains one step with a gradient reaching the encoder and predicts, or is refused with the adapter by name, and the adapted model then does;
  • every grouper under every head bundle combines when the axes agree, and where they do not, the grouper inside its axis adapter trains and predicts, while a pair without an adapter is refused as structural or not-implemented;
  • every proposal under both kinds of encoder output does the same;
  • in the full product of proposals, view stages, assigners, groupers and head bundles under both kinds of encoder output, no set that passes the config check fails later: every accepted set trains one step and predicts under the barest and the strictest detector type, and every refused set is refused by the built detector too;
  • every head bundle applies a weight per seed as a weighted mean (uniform weights give the unweighted losses), the scoring proposal with select_by: graspness_only leaves objectness to the view stage that owns it, and OperationHead decodes without the objectness nobody predicts.

What it does not prove: that a combination learns, or anything about real frames. A cell of Measured combinations is a probe on real frames; a synthetic probe of a composed config (grasppanda probe <config> --synthetic) is the same check as here at the sizes of the config.

docs.title: Adding a component to the matrix
docs.text:
A new stage is interchangeable when it says so in its contract and proves it in the matrix:

  1. declare the contract attributes of its slot (catalogue, Add a component) plus status, source and, if needed, extras;
  2. add one tiny configuration to the tables of tests/unit/test_swap_matrix.py (the test fails until you do);
  3. run python -m tools.make_component_docs to regenerate the catalogue and this page.

docs.title: furthest_point_sample(points, num_samples, *, skip_near_origin=False, tie_break='lowest_index')
docs.text:
Iterative furthest point sampling.

The first sample is always index 0 and ties are resolved by a fixed rule, so the result is deterministic and the same on every device. Which points become seeds decides whether a ported checkpoint reproduces, so faster backends are held to exactly this behaviour (:mod:grasppanda.ops.backends).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default points Tensor

(B, N, 3) or (N, 3).

required num_samples int

Number of points to pick, at most N.

required skip_near_origin bool

Never pick points whose squared norm is ≤ 1e-3 (apart from index 0), as the widely used PointNet++ CUDA kernel does. Needed only for parity with checkpoints trained against that kernel.

False tie_break Literal['lowest_index', 'pointnet2_cuda']

Which point wins when several are equally far from the selected set. lowest_index takes the first. pointnet2_cuda reproduces the order of the PointNet++ CUDA kernel (bit-reversed thread id, then index; the kernel runs min(512, 2^floor(log2 N)) threads). Exact ties are not exotic: clouds from a depth camera lie on a lattice, and 3 of 64 sampled GraspNet-1Billion frames had one among their first 1024 samples.

'lowest_index'

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

(B, num_samples) or (num_samples,) indices into points.

docs.title: generalized_furthest_point_sample(coords, num_samples, *, feats=None, metric='concat', coord_weight=1.0, weights=None, start=None)
docs.text:
Furthest point sampling of one cloud under a feature distance and with point weights.

The generalisation the detection literature uses to make the sampler choose instead of only spread: a distance that includes features (F-FPS of 3DSSD) and a weight on the running distance of every point (S-FPS of SASA). Without features and weights it is :func:furthest_point_sample with tie_break="lowest_index". A picked point is never picked again, so the indices are distinct even on duplicated coordinates.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default coords Tensor

(N, 3) coordinates.

required num_samples int

Points to pick, at most N.

required feats Tensor | None

(N, C) features that enter the distance; None for coordinates only.

None metric Literal['concat', 'sum']

With features. concat: squared L2 distance of the concatenation [coord_weight * xyz, feats] (what the released 3DSSD code computes). sum: coord_weight * |Δxyz| + |Δfeats| with L2 norms (Eq. 1 of the 3DSSD paper, its λ being coord_weight).

'concat' coord_weight float

Weight of the coordinates against the features.

1.0 weights Tensor | None

(N,) non-negative weights; the next pick maximises weight × running distance. The running distance is the squared one unless metric="sum" (the convention of the released SASA kernel).

None start int | None

Index of the first pick. None: the heaviest point when weights are given (SASA), otherwise index 0.

None

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

(num_samples,) distinct indices into coords, in the order they were picked.

docs.text:
Gripper frame from an approach direction and an in-plane rotation.

Column 0 of the result is the normalised approach axis. Column 1 is horizontal ([-a_y, a_x, 0] normalised, or [0, 1, 0] when the approach is vertical), column 2 completes the right-handed frame, and the frame is then rotated by angle about the approach axis.

docs.title: fibonacci_views(num_views=300, *, dtype=torch.float32)
docs.text:
Viewpoints on the unit sphere from a Fibonacci lattice.

This is the view grid of the GraspNet-1Billion grasp labels: view i of the label tensors is row i here. The approach direction of a view is the vector from the viewpoint to the origin, i.e. -views[i].

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

(num_views, 3) unit vectors.

docs.title: healpix_views(nside=4, *, dtype=torch.float32)
docs.text:
Viewpoints at the pixel centres of a HEALPix grid (through healpix).

HEALPix cuts the sphere into 12 · nside**2 pixels of exactly equal area on rings of constant latitude: nside 2, 4, 5, 8 give 48, 192, 300, 768 views. Pixels are in RING order.

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

(V, 3) unit vectors.

docs.title: icosphere_views(subdivisions=2, *, dtype=torch.float32)
docs.text:
Viewpoints at the vertices of a subdivided icosahedron (through trimesh).

subdivisions 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 give 12, 42, 162, 642, 2562 views; the count is 10 · 4**subdivisions + 2. The vertices are almost evenly spaced and, unlike a Fibonacci lattice, come with a mesh (every view knows its neighbours).

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

(V, 3) unit vectors.

docs.text: Angle in radians of the rotation taking first to second ((..., 3, 3)).

docs.title: two_vector_rotation(first, second)
docs.text:
Rotation whose first column is first and whose second lies towards second.

Gram-Schmidt on two free 3-vectors: first is normalised, second loses its component along it and is normalised, the third column is their cross product. This is the mapping of the 6-D rotation representation (Zhou et al., CVPR 2019), and, with the roles of the two vectors exchanged, how Contact-GraspNet builds a grasp frame from a predicted baseline and approach.

Returns:

(..., 3, 3) rotation matrices with columns first, second', first × second'.

docs.title: grasppanda.registry
docs.text:
Component registries.

Every swappable piece of GraspPanda is a class registered in exactly one flat :class:Registry. A config node {type: Name, **kwargs} is resolved against the registry that owns the slot it sits in; the owner is decided by the parent's type annotation (Cfg[Backbone]), never by searching every registry for a name.

Design notes (see docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md §6):

  • Lookup is lazy: the first get imports every module below the registry's package, so adding a file is enough to register a component.
  • Duplicate names raise. A failed lookup lists close matches and says whether the name lives in a different registry.
  • Registered classes may not take **kwargs: every config key must be checkable against a signature before anything is constructed.

docs.title: CompactGraspLabels dataclass
docs.text:
The best grasp of every (annotated point, view) of one object instance in a frame.

The dense label set holds a grid of in-plane angles and depths per point and view (:class:~grasppanda.structures.ObjectGraspLabels). Here that grid is collapsed to its best cell, which leaves four small numbers per point and view; this is the "economic" supervision of EconomicGrasp. Points without any good grasp are absent.

Values are stored the way the label asset stores them, as small integers, and are turned into metric quantities by :meth:quality and :meth:metres. The integers travel through the data loader; only the rows a batch matches are ever converted.

docs.title: GraspPanda Architecture
docs.text: Status Design record (v1.0). Written before the implementation. Where the code or the user guides differ from this document, they are authoritative; the differences are being folded back in. Date 2026-10-12 Scope Design for v1: single-view 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasp detection in cluttered scenes. Evidence Every claim about an upstream repository was read from source at the pinned commit listed in Appendix A. No model was trained, no checkpoint was loaded and no AP was measured while writing this document. AP numbers quoted here are author-reported unless marked otherwise.

docs.title: 1. Goals and scope
docs.text:
One line. GraspPanda is to 6-DoF grasp detection in clutter what MMDetection is to object detection: certified reproductions and controlled component-swap experiments, all scored by one pinned, official-equivalent evaluation.

Four requirements, and how the design answers each.

Requirement Design answer Dataset-driven A benchmark is a protocol: dataset version + split manifest + camera + allowed inputs + pinned evaluator (§11.3). Every result is stamped with its protocol id; only protocol-conformant runs enter the model zoo. GraspNet-1Billion first, GraspClutter6D second. Low-code One YAML file plus one command reproduces a method. First result within five commands after pip install (§12.4). More than reproduction Backbone, seed proposal, approach view, grouping, head bundle, loss, augmentation and post-processing are config slots with typed contracts (§8). An ablation is a base config plus an override. Professional Model zoo with provenance, docs site, CI, PyPI release on tag, changelog, citation file, brand assets (§13, §14).

v1 in scope. Single-view RGB-D or point-cloud input; 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasps; cluttered tabletop scenes; GraspNet-1Billion and GraspClutter6D.

Reserved, not implemented in v1 (the architecture leaves room, §8.7): multi-view fusion track (Generalizing-Grasp; own protocol and own leaderboard), suction (SuctionNet-1B), simulated clearing (pile/packed, GSR/DR).

Out of scope. Planar grasps, dexterous hands, object-centric datasets (ACRONYM, GraspGen), web UI, and wrapping upstream repositories in subprocesses as the core implementation.

docs.title: 2. Design principles
docs.text:
Each rule exists because the previous GraspPanda (v0.62) or an upstream codebase broke it.

  1. Depth before breadth. A method enters the model zoo only after it has been trained and evaluated inside this toolbox (§13.1). v0.62 had 39 method entries and no certified reproduction.
  2. Every number carries its provenance. Three classes, never mixed in one column: reported (paper/README), author-ckpt (author weights evaluated here), reproduced (trained here).
  3. Observation and supervision are separate objects. predict(observation) cannot reach ground truth. Any GT-derived input (workspace mask from GT segmentation, GT instance masks) is an explicit, named config attribute and is stamped on the result (§7.1).
  4. Slots have typed contracts. A swap is allowed only when contracts match. A mismatch is a config-check error with an explanation — never a silent interpolation, projection or axis squeeze (§8.3).
  5. One owner per constant. num_view, num_angle, num_depth, depth bins, gripper width, voxel size and seed count each live in exactly one object; everything else receives them by injection (§8.6).
  6. The head bundle is atomic. Head, target encoder, loss and decoder share one parameterization and are swapped as a unit (§8.4).
  7. Share on second use. A component becomes a public, registered slot only when two in-tree methods use it. Until then it stays private to its detector.
  8. Small core, optional weight. Core depends on torch, numpy and a few pure-Python packages. Sparse convolution, visualisation, logging backends and accelerated ops are extras. No sys.path edits, no top-level packages named pointnet2/knn/models/utils.
  9. A run is fully described by its snapshot. No behaviour is reachable only through a CLI flag (§5.6).
  10. Clean room. Upstream logic is studied; code is written here. No file is copied (§14.3).

docs.title: 3. Lessons from reference frameworks
docs.text:
Verified against source on 2026-10-12: PaddleSeg release/2.10, MMEngine main, Detectron2 main, Pointcept main.

Framework Borrow Avoid (with evidence) PaddleSeg YAML + _base_; every component is {type: Name, **kwargs} built recursively; a rule-based ConfigChecker that runs at load time; decorator registration; one-command train/val/predict. --opts only asserts that intermediate keys exist and then assigns the leaf unconditionally, so a misspelt leaf key silently creates a new entry (cvlibs/config.py:228-235). Top-level keys are read with dic.get, so unknown keys are ignored. The builder resolves a type by scanning all registries in order (cvlibs/builder.py:82-87), so equal names in two registries collide silently. Duplicate registration only warns and overwrites (cvlibs/manager.py:112-115). The checker mutates the config to sync num_classes (allow_update=True). Unbounded _base_ depth. Components register only if someone remembered to import them in __init__.py. Build errors are re-raised as RuntimeError(str(e)), dropping the traceback (builder.py:65-75). More than ten run settings exist only as CLI flags (--do_eval, --save_interval, --resume_model, --seed, --use_ema, --log_iters, --keep_checkpoint_max, … in tools/train.py). MMEngine Registry(locations=[...]) lazily imports its modules on first lookup; duplicate names raise unless force=True; custom_imports; _delete_; hook-based engine; dumping the resolved config. Dict merge keeps stale base keys when a child changes type unless the user remembers _delete_=True (config.py:_merge_a_into_b). No key validation: an unknown kwarg fails only inside a constructor, possibly hours into a job. A failed lookup returns None and the error offers no candidate names (registry/build_functions.py:98-106). Scope hierarchy and DefaultScope switching add a lot of machinery for a single-package toolbox. Python configs execute arbitrary code and exist in two dialects (text and lazy-import). {{_base_.x}} is substituted before child overrides apply, so overriding x does not propagate. runner.py is 2413 lines. Detectron2 tools/plain_train_net.py: a complete training loop in 221 readable lines. ShapeSpec: children are built with the parent-computed input shape instead of the user repeating channel counts. Instances: one typed container for predictions. yacs CfgNode requires every key of every component to be pre-declared in one central defaults.py. Pointcept Run snapshot: resolved config dumped into the experiment directory, code copied alongside (scripts/train.sh:87). Offset-based batching for variable-size point clouds. spconv/PTv3 integration patterns. The launcher executes the copied code via PYTHONPATH, so what runs is not what is installed. Config values are rewritten implicitly at load (data.train.loop = epoch // eval_epoch, num_worker=None → cpu_count(); engines/defaults.py:122,133).

Resulting choices: YAML with strict three-layer validation (§5.3), type-aware merge (§5.2), one flat registry family with lazy auto-import and nearest-name errors (§6), build-time injection instead of repeated channel counts (§6.3), a ~300-line trainer with hooks (§12.1), and a snapshot that records code without running from the copy (§5.6).

docs.title: 4. Repository layout
docs.text:
GraspPanda/
├── configs/
│   ├── _base_/
│   │   ├── datasets/            graspnet1b_realsense.yaml, graspnet1b_kinect.yaml, graspclutter6d_d435.yaml
│   │   ├── models/              gsnet.yaml, economicgrasp.yaml, hggd.yaml, …   (full default model per method)
│   │   ├── schedules/           one file per training recipe
│   │   └── default_runtime.yaml
│   └── <method>/                README.md, metafile.yaml, <method>_<backbone>_<dataset>-<camera>_<schedule>.yaml
├── grasppanda/
│   ├── config/                  loader, schema, validation, cross-field checker, snapshot
│   ├── registry.py              Registry, build(), lazy auto-import, plugin discovery
│   ├── structures/              Observation, Supervision, PointSet, PointFeatures, SeedSet, ApproachSet,
│   │                            GroupFeatures, GraspGroup, Gripper, ReferenceFrame, SampleKey
│   ├── datasets/                manifest, derived-asset store, graspnet1b/, graspclutter6d/, samplers
│   ├── transforms/              point-cloud and RGB-D preprocessing and augmentation
│   ├── models/
│   │   ├── backbones/           PointNet++, SparseUNet (spconv), PTv3, 2-D ResNet …
│   │   ├── proposals/           graspness / objectness + FPS, OBS (HGGD's heat-map proposal stays in its detector until reused)
│   │   ├── views/               300-view classification, regression, anchors
│   │   ├── groupers/            cylinder crop: single / multi-scale / multi-depth
│   │   ├── assigners/           seed ↔ grasp-label matching shared by the GraspNet family
│   │   ├── heads/               head bundles: head + target encoder + loss + decoder
│   │   ├── losses/              primitive losses used inside stages
│   │   ├── postprocessors/      collision filter, grasp NMS, width clip, re-rankers
│   │   └── detectors/           GSNet, EconomicGrasp, HGGD, …
│   ├── ops/                     FPS, ball/cylinder query, kNN, grasp NMS: pure-PyTorch reference + optional backends
│   │   └── sparse/              sparse-conv facade: spconv | warpconvnet | minkowski (legacy)
│   ├── _ops/                    compiled extension namespace (built only if a kernel proves necessary)
│   ├── evaluation/              graspnet1b/, graspclutter6d/, protocols/, result records, statistics
│   ├── engine/                  trainer, hooks, optim builders, checkpoint, distributed helpers
│   ├── apis/                    GraspInferencer and friends
│   ├── cli/                     `grasppanda` entry point, one module per sub-command
│   ├── hub/                     weight index, download, sha256 verification
│   ├── visualization/
│   └── utils/
├── tools/                       repo-only scripts: dist_train.sh, gen_model_zoo.py, make_parity_fixtures.py, convert_checkpoint.py
├── projects/                    example_project/ and experimental or third-party methods, each with a support-level badge
├── docs/                        MkDocs Material site; design/ holds this file
├── tests/                       unit/, contracts/, parity/, smoke/
├── resources/                   logo, banner, architecture diagram, demo GIF sources
└── pyproject.toml  README.md  README_zh-CN.md  LICENSE  NOTICE  CITATION.cff  CHANGELOG.md  CONTRIBUTING.md

Packaging notes:

  • Configs ship in the wheel. configs/ stays at the repository root for visibility and is mapped to grasppanda/_configs at build time. grasppanda train gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e resolves a config by name whether the package was installed from PyPI or in editable mode. Without this, "one command after pip install" would require cloning the repository.
  • The CLI lives in the package, not in tools/, for the same reason. tools/ keeps only scripts that make sense inside a checkout.
  • Method folders are organised by method, benchmark is in the file name (<method>_<backbone>_<dataset>-<camera>_<schedule>.yaml), matching PaddleSeg and MMDetection. The benchmark-first view is generated: the model-zoo page is grouped by protocol.

docs.title: 5.1 Format and top-level schema
docs.text:
YAML, loaded with yaml.safe_load. The top level is a closed set of keys:

Key Content _base_ List of relative paths to parent files. custom_imports Out-of-tree components, imported before validation: module names, or .py paths relative to the config that lists them. model The detector: {type: GSNet, backbone: {...}, ...}. data train, val, test, each {dataset: {type: ...}, batch_size, num_workers, sampler}. optimizer, scheduler {type: ...}. train epochs, amp, grad_clip, accumulate, ema, sync_bn. evaluation interval, evaluator, variants (post-processing chains, §11.4), save_best. hooks Extra hooks beyond the defaults. runtime work_dir, seed, deterministic, resume, load_from, log, checkpoint, ops (backend selection), dist.

Target user experience — the whole file a user writes for a backbone ablation:

_base_:
  - ../_base_/models/gsnet.yaml
  - ../_base_/datasets/graspnet1b_realsense.yaml
  - ../_base_/schedules/gsnet_10e.yaml
  - ../_base_/default_runtime.yaml

model:
  backbone: {type: PTv3, in_channels: 3}     # was SparseUNet14; the old kwargs are dropped, not merged

docs.title: 5.2 Inheritance and merge rules
docs.text:
1. Depth ≤ 2. A leaf may inherit from a file that itself inherits from _base_/ primitives; a third hop is an error. Deep chains are where readers lose track of what a config means.
  2. Sibling bases must not conflict. If two files in one _base_ list define the same leaf path, loading fails and names both files. There is therefore no order-dependence to remember (PaddleSeg resolves such conflicts by list position).
  3. Dict onto dict: deep merge — unless type changes. When the child node sets a type different from the parent's, the parent node is replaced. This removes MMEngine's stale-kwargs trap and makes "swap one component" a one-line edit. The log lists the dropped keys.
  4. _delete_: true replaces an untyped dict explicitly.
  5. Lists replace wholesale. Individual elements are reachable through overrides (hooks.0.interval=5).
  6. Interpolation ${a.b.c} refers to another config path and is resolved after all merges and overrides, so overriding the source propagates to every reference.
  7. Dataset roots are not interpolated from the environment. A dataset resolves its root from the config value, then $GRASPPANDA_DATA, then ./data. Machine paths and runtime.work_dir are excluded from the config hash.

docs.title: 5.3 Strict validation
docs.text:
Validation runs before any dataset is opened or any module is constructed. grasppanda print-config --check runs exactly the same code.

Layer What is checked Failure example 1. Schema Top-level and fixed-structure keys (train, runtime, loader blocks) against a declared schema. unknown key 'runtim'. Did you mean 'runtime'? 2. Component signatures For every {type: X, ...} node: X exists in the registry that owns that slot; every kwarg is a parameter of X.__init__; every required parameter is present or injected (§6.3); scalar types match annotations. Registered classes may not accept **kwargs. SWADHead has no parameter 'num_angles'. Did you mean 'num_angle'? 3. Cross-field rules Relations between components (§5.5). CylinderGroup emits axes (seed,) but OperationHead expects (seed, depth).

All problems found in one pass are reported together, each with its config path and the file it came from.

docs.title: 5.4 Command-line overrides
docs.text:
--opts model.backbone.type=PTv3 train.epochs=20 hooks.0.interval=5

  • Values are parsed as YAML scalars, so true, null, 1e-3, [1, 2] mean the same as in a file.
  • Overrides are applied to the merged tree and the full validation of §5.3 then runs. An override cannot create a key that validation would reject in a file.
  • Overriding type follows merge rule 3: kwargs of the previous type are dropped and listed.
  • The override list is stored in the snapshot.

docs.title: 5.5 Cross-field consistency checker
docs.text:
The checker never edits the config. A value is either stated once and injected where needed, or stated twice and required to agree. PaddleSeg's auto-sync is convenient but leaves the user unsure which value won.

Rule Must agree across Mechanism Grasp parameterization: num_view, num_angle, num_depth, depth bins, angle range view stage, head bundle (head / targets / loss / decoder), label grid of the dataset Owned by the head bundle's codec and the view template; the dataset declares its label grid; mismatch is an error unless an explicit re-binning transform is configured. Gripper: max width, finger height, depth base decoder clamp, collision filter, evaluator Owned by one Gripper object referenced by all three. Camera dataset, evaluator, metadata of loaded weights Compared; mismatch on weights is an error unless runtime.allow_camera_mismatch: true. Point budget: sampled points ≥ seeds; voxel size sampler transform, proposal stage, sparse backbone Compared; voxel size is owned by the backbone. Preprocessing fingerprint transforms that precede label alignment, derived-label assets Asset manifest hash must match (§10.2). Inputs model.required_inputs ⊆ what the dataset's observation provides Missing input is an error. GT-provenance inputs set gt_assisted on the run and are rejected by protocols that forbid them. Stage contracts backbone output kind ↔ proposal requirement; grouper axes ↔ head axes; channel counts Checked statically from class metadata, again at build time from real modules. Splits val scenes disjoint from train scenes; save_best never monitors a test split Compared on scene ids from the manifests. Protocol conformance evaluator constants, split manifest hash, post-processing declared Non-conformant runs are stamped protocol: custom and cannot enter the zoo.

Rules are small classes registered in a list, so a project can add its own.

docs.title: 5.6 Run snapshot
docs.text:
Every train, test and sweep run writes into work_dir/<run_id>/:

File Content config.resolved.yaml Fully expanded config, interpolations resolved, defaults of every component filled in. config.sources/ The original leaf file and each base, unmodified, plus overrides.txt. run.json Command line, start time, host, seed, config_hash, protocol id, parent run on resume. git.json, diff.patch Commit, dirty flag, uncommitted diff. For a wheel install: package version and RECORD hash instead. code.tar.gz Tracked files of grasppanda/ and configs/. Stored for the record; the run never executes from it. env.json Python, torch, CUDA, cuDNN, GPU, driver, selected op/sparse backends, pip freeze. data.json Dataset fingerprint, split-manifest hashes, derived-asset manifest hashes.

grasppanda print-config <cfg> [--opts ...] prints config.resolved.yaml to stdout without creating a run.

docs.title: 6.1 Registries
docs.text:
DATASETS, TRANSFORMS, BACKBONES, PROPOSALS, VIEWS, GROUPERS, ASSIGNERS, HEADS, LOSSES, DETECTORS, POSTPROCESSORS, EVALUATORS, HOOKS, OPTIMIZERS, SCHEDULERS.

OPTIMIZERS and SCHEDULERS are pre-populated from torch.optim so that {type: AdamW, lr: 1e-3} works without wrappers.

docs.title: 6.2 Behaviour
docs.text:
• One flat Registry class. No scopes, no parent/child hierarchy.
  • Lazy auto-import. Each registry declares the package it owns (BACKBONES → grasppanda.models.backbones). On first lookup every module below that package is imported. Adding a file is enough; nobody edits __init__.py. import grasppanda stays cheap.
  • Optional dependencies never break import. A module that needs spconv imports it lazily. If the extra is missing, building the component raises SparseUNet14 needs spconv: pip install -e ".[spconv-cu118]".
  • Out-of-tree code. custom_imports: [my_pkg.my_heads] or custom_imports: [../my_components.py] in a config, or a grasppanda.plugins entry point for pip-installed plugins. A .py path is loaded as a standalone module, so a single-file plugin next to its config needs neither installation nor a sys.path edit. projects/ uses the same mechanism; no fork is needed.
  • Duplicate names raise. Overriding requires an explicit force=True.
  • Helpful failures. A failed lookup lists the registered names, the closest matches by edit distance, and whether the name exists in a different registry ('SWADHead' is registered in HEADS, not in GROUPERS).
  • Metadata on the class. Each component may declare status (experimental / tested / reproduced), requires (extras), and its contract attributes (§8.3). grasppanda print-config --list backbones and the docs tables are generated from these.

docs.title: 6.3 Building and injection
docs.text:
A slot's registry is determined by the parameter annotation of the parent class, not by searching every registry for a name:

@DETECTORS.register()
class GSNet(SeedGraspDetector):
    def __init__(
        self,
        backbone: Cfg[Backbone],
        proposal: Cfg[Proposal],
        view: Cfg[ViewStage],
        grouper: Cfg[Grouper],
        head: Cfg[HeadBundle],
        assigner: Cfg[Assigner],
    ):
        self.backbone = BACKBONES.build(backbone)
        self.proposal = PROPOSALS.build(proposal, in_channels=self.backbone.out_channels)
        self.view = VIEWS.build(view, in_channels=self.backbone.out_channels)
        self.grouper = GROUPERS.build(grouper, in_channels=self.backbone.out_channels)
        self.head = HEADS.build(
            head, in_channels=self.grouper.out_channels, view_template=self.view.template
        )
        ...
  • Cfg[Backbone] tells the static validator which registry owns the slot, so layer 2 of §5.3 can walk the whole tree without constructing anything.
  • REGISTRY.build(node, **injected) fills only parameters the user left unset. If the user set one and it disagrees with the injected value, that is an error — never a silent override. This is Detectron2's ShapeSpec idea generalised.
  • A parameter that is meant to be injected is declared with the sentinel default INJECTED; the validator treats it as optional, and construction fails clearly if nobody supplied it.
  • REGISTRY.build also accepts an already-constructed object, so the Python API and unit tests can assemble a detector without YAML.

docs.title: 7. Data contracts
docs.text: All structures are plain dataclasses holding tensors. They live in grasppanda/structures/ and have no dependency on any model.

docs.title: 7.1 Observation and Supervision
docs.text:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SampleKey:  # identity of one evaluation unit
    dataset: str
    scene: int
    camera: str
    frame: int


class Provenance(Enum):  # where a piece of input information came from
    SENSOR
    CALIBRATION
    PREDICTED
    GROUND_TRUTH


@dataclass
class Observation:  # everything a model may see at inference time
    key: SampleKey
    depth: Tensor | None  # (H, W) metres
    rgb: Tensor | None  # (3, H, W) in [0, 1]
    intrinsics: Tensor  # (3, 3)
    points: PointSet | None  # camera frame, metres
    point_feats: Tensor | None  # (N, C): ones / rgb / normals, as declared
    masks: dict[str, Mask]  # 'workspace', 'instance', …; each Mask carries data + Provenance
    frame: ReferenceFrame


@dataclass
class Supervision:  # training-only; never passed to predict()
    objects: list[
        ObjectGraspLabels
    ]  # per object: points, friction scores, widths, collision mask, pose
    point_labels: dict[
        str, Tensor
    ]  # 'graspness', 'objectness', 'instance', … aligned to observation.points
    extras: dict[str, Any]  # method-specific targets (heat-maps, tolerance, …)
  • A detector implements loss(observation, supervision) -> dict[str, Tensor] and predict(observation) -> list[GraspGroup]. predict receives no supervision, no evaluator handle and no dataset handle.
  • A dataset config declares its observation explicitly, including every mask and its source. A model declares required_inputs. The checker matches them (§5.5).
  • Ground-truth leakage is a named attribute, not a hidden default. The workspace crop used by the GraspNet family is derived from the GT segmentation mask at test time (§8.1). Here that is spelled workspace: {type: SegmentationBBoxWorkspace, source: ground_truth, outlier: 0.02}. Any GROUND_TRUTH provenance on an inference input sets gt_assisted: [workspace] on the run and appears as a column in result tables.
  • Batches concatenate variable-size clouds with batch offsets; fixed-size batches expose a dense (B, N, …) view without copying.

docs.title: 7.2 Points and features
docs.text:
Structure Fields Invariant PointSet coords (N,3), batch_offsets, frame, id, optional parent_id + index id is unique per set. A sub-sampled set records which parent it came from and, when it is a true subset, the index into it. PointFeatures feats (N,C), points: PointSet Features cannot exist without their set. Consumers assert the set identity they expect. VoxelMap (internal to sparse backbones) voxel coords, inverse_map, voxel_size, source_id devoxelize() returns PointFeatures bound to the source set and raises if asked to map onto any other set. An inverse_map therefore cannot be reused across backbones or point sets.

A backbone states what it returns: output = "dense" (features on the input set — sparse U-Net, PTv3) or output = "subsampled" (features on a child set — PointNet++ set abstraction). Stages that need one or the other say so; conversion between them is an explicit, configured module (FeaturePropagation), never an implicit interpolation.

docs.title: 7.3 Stage outputs
docs.text:
Structure Fields SeedSet points: PointSet (child of the scene set), feats (M,C), scores: dict[str, Tensor] with declared semantics (graspness, objectness, heatmap), valid (M,), source (how the seeds were chosen). No score is mandatory. ApproachSet direction (M,3) unit vectors, optional rotation (M,3,3), optional view_index (M,) with the ViewTemplate it indexes, optional logits. Aligned one-to-one with a SeedSet. GroupFeatures feats with named axes, e.g. (seed, channel) or (seed, depth, channel); seeds; local_frame. An axis is never squeezed implicitly. RawPredictions Method-specific tensors plus the id of the codec that can decode them. Keeps gradients.

Too few seeds, an empty heat-map or a failed segmentation produce valid = False entries, not zero-coordinate grasps. Each detector documents its padding policy.

docs.title: 7.4 GraspGroup
docs.text:
The single output type of every detector and the single input type of every post-processor and evaluator.

Field Shape Meaning translation (G,3) Grasp point in metres, in frame. rotation (G,3,3) Proper rotation (det = +1, orthonormal within tolerance). Columns: approach axis, closing axis, height axis. width, depth, height (G,) Jaw opening; finger insertion depth along the approach axis past the grasp point; finger thickness. Metres. score (G,) Ranking score, higher is better. score_kind names the semantics. object_id (G,) optional Instance association when a method provides one, else -1. frame, gripper, key Reference frame, gripper definition, SampleKey.
  • validate() checks finiteness, SO(3) membership and non-negative widths; it runs at the detector boundary in debug and test modes.
  • depth here is insertion depth, never camera-z depth. The grasp point is the benchmark's grasp origin, not a robot TCP; conversion to a TCP is a function of Gripper.
  • Scores. Raw GraspNet label scores are the minimum friction coefficient μ for force closure: lower is better and -1 means invalid. They are not confidences. μ exists only inside Supervision. A detector's score_kind is declared by its head bundle (for example predicted_quality, an uncalibrated regression of a label-derived quantity); no method's score is assumed to be a calibrated probability.
  • The GraspNet 17-D array [score, width, height, depth, R(9), t(3), object_id] appears only in GraspGroup.from_graspnet_array() / .to_graspnet_array(), i.e. at the import/export boundary.

docs.title: 8.1 What the reference methods actually do
docs.text:
Read from source at the pinned commits (Appendix A). This table, not the papers' block diagrams, drives the abstraction.

GSNet (graspness_unofficial) EconomicGrasp GraspNet-baseline / SBG HGGD Input Depth → cloud, constant-ones features Same Depth → cloud, xyz 4-channel RGB-D image 640×360 + 25 600-point cloud Workspace crop Box around GT segmentation in table frame, ±2 cm, also at test time Same Same None Scene encoder Sparse U-Net, per-point 512-d Same architecture PointNet++ (baseline) / 2 SA + 2 transformer blocks (SBG) → 1024 seeds, 256-d 2-D encoder-decoder; no 3-D scene network Proposal Objectness + graspness per point → mask → FPS to 1024 Same code 2-way "objectness" on the 1024 seeds; optional OBS needs a second segmentation network at test time (SBG) Heat-map peaks → up to 48 partial grasps (u, v, θ, width, Δz) Approach 300 view scores; train: one view sampled by multinomial from predicted scores; test: argmax Same code 300 view scores; argmax in both modes None. Rotation is Euler-factored: θ in 2-D, 7×7 learned (γ, β) anchors in 3-D Grouping One cylinder (r 0.05, 16 neighbours) among the seeds, with features; no depth axis Same grouper + neighbour self-attention Cylinders over the scene cloud, xyz only, one per depth → explicit depth axis (seed, 4); SBG adds four radii Unrotated ball of radius = predicted width around the lifted centre; 512 points; image features attached and detached Head SWAD: score and width grids (12, 4), regression Angle (13-way), depth (5-way), score (6-way) classification + width regression, with a validity mask Score, angle class, width per depth, plus tolerance 49 anchor logits + per-anchor translation offsets GT inside the training forward Label matching runs mid-forward; the crop rotation comes from the labels (object pose × template) Same Same, and crops are centred at the matched GT grasp point rather than the seed None; targets are computed after the forward from the network's own proposals Output score Max of regressed grid (unbounded) Bin-centre-weighted sum of raw logits (no softmax) score × P(objectness) × tolerance / 0.05 (SBG) Anchor sigmoid Collision filter in shipped test path Default on in test.py, shipped command turns it off Off Shipped command turns it off (SBG) On, and also rejects grasps with ≤ 2 points between the fingers Recipe Adam 1e-3, ×0.95/epoch, 10 epochs, batch 4, 15 000 points, flip + x-rotation Adam 1e-3, cosine, 20 epochs by default (README command: 10), batch 4, 20 000 points, flip SBG: Adam 1e-3, OneCycle, 18 epochs, batch 2, BN-momentum decay; "validation" on test_seen AdamW 1e-2, StepLR, 15 epochs, batch 4 × 2 accumulation, value clipping, BN-momentum decay; one optimizer over two networks

Consequences:

  1. GSNet, EconomicGrasp, GraspNet-baseline and SBG share one skeleton with a small number of real variation points (encoder output kind, proposal, view selection policy, grouping support and axes, head bundle).
  2. HGGD shares none of the four GSNet-shaped stages. It has no per-point graspness, no 3-D scene backbone, no view classification and no approach-aligned crop; its proposal stage emits partial grasps, not points. It must be its own detector.
  3. Three of four families crop the workspace with ground-truth segmentation at inference and HGGD does not. A comparison table that does not show this column is comparing different input conditions.

docs.title: 8.2 Detector families
docs.text:
Every detector implements the same outer contract and nothing more is required of it:

class BaseGraspDetector(nn.Module):
    required_inputs: ClassVar[set[str]]  # e.g. {"points"} or {"rgb", "depth", "points"}

    def loss(self, observation, supervision) -> dict[str, Tensor]: ...
    def predict(self, observation) -> list[GraspGroup]: ...
    def configure_optimizers(self, cfg): ...  # optional override

Train and eval behaviour follow nn.Module.training; there is no constructor flag (upstream models need a second instance to validate during training).

Family Methods in v1 Internal stages Seed-based (SeedGraspDetector) GSNet, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, GraspNet-baseline, SBG backbone → proposal → view → (assigner, training only) → grouper → head bundle Image-to-region (HGGD) HGGD; RNGNet later if approved image encoder → heat-map proposal → lift → region grouping → local encoder → anchor head bundle Dense contact (ContactGraspNet) Contact-GraspNet PointNet++ encoder → per-point contact head bundle

All three share structures, operators, post-processors, evaluators, engine and CLI. Only the first family uses the PROPOSALS / VIEWS / GROUPERS / ASSIGNERS slots. HGGD passes a PartialGraspSet (3-D centre, in-plane angle, width, depth offset, heat score) between its stages; it never fills a graspness field. If RNGNet later reuses HGGD's proposal or region grouping, those become registered slots at that point (principle 7).

The seed-based skeleton is extracted in M2, when EconomicGrasp becomes its second user, and re-examined in M3 against GraspNet-baseline and SBG. HGGD lands in M2 precisely to test that the outer contract, the data structures and the engine did not overfit to GSNet.

docs.title: 8.3 Stage contracts of the seed-based family
docs.text:
class Backbone(nn.Module):
    output: ClassVar[Literal["dense", "subsampled"]]
    out_channels: int

    def forward(self, points: PointSet, feats: Tensor | None) -> PointFeatures: ...


class Proposal(nn.Module):  # scene features -> seeds
    requires: ClassVar[Literal["dense", "subsampled", "any"]]

    def forward(self, feats: PointFeatures, obs: Observation) -> SeedSet: ...
    def loss(self, seeds: SeedSet, sup: Supervision) -> dict[str, Tensor]: ...


class ViewStage(nn.Module):  # seeds -> one approach per seed
    template: ViewTemplate  # e.g. Fibonacci lattice, 300 views

    def forward(self, seeds: SeedSet) -> ApproachSet: ...
    def loss(self, approach: ApproachSet, matched: MatchedLabels) -> dict[str, Tensor]: ...


class Assigner:  # training only
    def __call__(self, seeds, approach, sup) -> MatchedLabels:
        ...
        # label grids at the chosen view, crop frame, crop centre, validity mask


class Grouper(nn.Module):
    support: ClassVar[Literal["seeds", "scene"]]
    out_axes: tuple[str, ...]  # ("seed",) or ("seed", "depth")
    out_channels: int

    def forward(
        self, support: PointFeatures, centres: Tensor, approach: ApproachSet
    ) -> GroupFeatures: ...


class HeadBundle(nn.Module):  # see 8.4
    in_axes: tuple[str, ...]
    codec: GraspCodec

    def forward(self, groups: GroupFeatures, seeds: SeedSet) -> RawPredictions: ...
    def loss(self, raw: RawPredictions, matched: MatchedLabels) -> dict[str, Tensor]: ...
    def decode(self, raw: RawPredictions, seeds: SeedSet, approach: ApproachSet) -> GraspGroup: ...

What the checker does with these declarations:

Swap Verdict Reason given to the user SparseUNet14 → PTv3 (with its decoder) under GSNet Allowed Both dense; channel counts are injected. Encoder-only PTv3 checkpoints (Sonata, Concerto, Utonia) are subsampled and are a different registered type. SparseUNet14 → PointNet2 under GraspnessFPS Rejected Proposal requires dense features; the backbone returns a 1024-point subsample. Add a FeaturePropagation neck explicitly or change the proposal. CylinderGroup → multi-scale cylinder, same axes Allowed out_axes unchanged. CylinderGroup (seed,) under an operation/tolerance head Rejected Head expects (seed, depth). SWADHead ↔ EconomicHead Allowed as a bundle swap Checker also verifies the label asset each bundle needs. SWADHead → operation/tolerance bundle Allowed only with a depth-axis grouper and the tolerance asset Checker lists every missing piece at once. GraspnessFPS → object-balanced sampling Allowed if an instance mask input is configured Its provenance (predicted or ground_truth) is recorded on the run. HGGD local PointNet → PointNet++ Allowed inside HGGD Same region contract. HGGD heat-map proposal into a GSNet slot Rejected Different family: emits partial grasps, not seeds.

Any change of structure or feature distribution requires retraining or declared fine-tuning. Loading a checkpoint into a swapped architecture fails on the key report (§12.1); nothing claims a checkpoint is portable across components.

docs.title: 8.4 Head bundle
docs.text:
A head bundle is one registered class that owns four things sharing one GraspCodec: the prediction module, the target encoder, the loss, and the decoder. HEADS contains bundles only; there is no way to configure a head with another bundle's decoder.

head:
  type: SWADHead
  num_angle: 12            # the codec checks these against the dataset's label grid
  num_depth: 4
  width_target_scale: 10.0
  width_decode_gain: 1.2   # upstream applies 1.2 only in the decoder; kept as a named, documented option
  score_target: log_friction_batch_norm
  loss: {score: {type: SmoothL1, weight: 15.0}, width: {type: SmoothL1, weight: 10.0}}
  • The codec is the single owner of the angle and depth grids, the flattening order of the angle × depth grid, the width scale, and the mapping to and from GraspGroup. Upstream writes np.pi / 12 and (i + 1) * 0.01 directly in the decoder, independent of NUM_ANGLE / NUM_DEPTH; a mismatch there changes results silently.
  • Primitive losses inside a bundle are swappable where that is semantically safe (SmoothL1 ↔ L1). The structure of the targets is not.
  • A bundle may own non-gradient state. HGGD's (γ, β) anchors are learned by a shifting procedure during the first epochs and are stored in the checkpoint; they are buffers of its anchor head bundle.
  • Proposal and view stages follow the same pattern on a smaller scale: each owns its targets and its loss, and loss weights are attributes of the stage that produces the loss.

docs.title: 8.5 Training-time flow and the assigner
docs.text:
Seed-based detectors cannot compute targets before the forward pass, because targets depend on which seeds and which view the network chose. The flow, as verified for GSNet:

  1. Backbone, then proposal. Seeds are selected from predictions in training as well as in inference.
  2. View stage. Training samples one view per seed from the predicted distribution; inference takes the argmax.
  3. Assigner (training only). Transforms each object's grasp points and view grid by its GT pose, re-indexes object-frame views to the camera-frame template, matches each seed to its nearest label point, and returns the label grids at the chosen view together with the crop rotation.
