docs.title: As a YAML fragment
docs.text:
Any sampler inside either proposal; this is everything a config needs:

model:
  proposal:
    type: ScoredSeeds
    num_seeds: 1024
    select_by: graspness_and_objectness   # graspness | objectness | product
    graspness_threshold: 0.1
    objectness_threshold: 0.5
    top_fraction: null                    # e.g. 0.1: a rank cut instead of the thresholds
    too_few: pad                          # best_rest: fill with the best other points
    sampler:
      type: ScoreWeightedFPS
      gamma: 1.0

model:
  proposal:
    type: SampledSeeds
    num_seeds: 1024
    sampler: {type: FeatureFPS, metric: concat, coord_weight: 1.0}

ScoredSeeds reads point-wise graspness labels: the config needs the graspness section of the training dataset (the presets carry it; grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness --camera <camera> --config <config> builds the labels once). SampledSeeds needs no label of its own.

docs.title: The settings that matter
docs.text: Setting Choose select_by graspness_and_objectness is GSNet's rule. graspness drops the objectness test (objectness is still trained). objectness makes every predicted object point a candidate: foreground sampling with a learned mask. product cuts P(object) × graspness, MultiGraspNet's rule (arXiv 2602.06504, RA-L 2026): a soft version of the first. graspness_threshold belongs to the label definition: 0.1 for graspness normalised to [0, 1] per frame (GSNet) or per instance (FineGrasp). Change the label, change the threshold. top_fraction a rank cut: the best share of each frame's points, whatever their values. DexGraspNet 2.0 selects "object points that rank top 1%" in graspness before FPS to 1024 points. With 15 000 points per frame the share must be at least 0.07 to leave 1024 candidates; the preset uses 0.1. too_few pad (GSNet): a frame without candidates has no real seed and trains the proposal only, which happens in the first iterations of every run. best_rest: such a frame gets the best-scored other points as real seeds. sampler.gamma (ScoreWeightedFPS) 0 is FPS started at the best point, 1 is SASA's reference, large values approach top-k. distance: squared is the released kernel, euclidean the paper's formula; squared with γ equals euclidean with γ/2. sampler.metric, sampler.coord_weight (FeatureFPS, FusionFPS) concat is the squared L2 distance of [xyz, features] as in the released 3DSSD code; sum is coord_weight·|Δxyz| + |Δfeatures|, Eq. 1 of the paper. With 512 feature channels and coord_weight: 1 the coordinates (metres) hardly count; raise it or set normalize: true when the seeds cluster. sampler.voxel_size (VoxelGridSampler), sampler.min_distance (ScoreNMS) they decide how many real seeds a scene yields. Read metric/real_seeds from the probe and adapt. sampler.seed (RandomSampler, FPS with start: random) an integer makes two evaluations pick the same seeds.

docs.title: Pretrained weights
docs.text: There are none to load for a new option and none are needed: a sampler has no parameters. A checkpoint of GSNet, EconomicGrasp or FineGrasp loads strictly into a model whose proposal is ScoredSeeds (the scorer is the same score layer), so a sampler can be swapped at test time on a trained model; that is a different experiment from training with the sampler (GSNet's own sampling ablation retrains per sampler), and the config should say which one it is.

docs.title: List what is installed
docs.text:
grasppanda components --slot samplers
grasppanda components ScoredSeeds

docs.title: 5. Pitfalls met while building this
docs.text:
• fpsample 1.0.2, bucket methods, do not begin at start_idx. Measured here on 5000 random points, 256 picks: vanilla returns exactly the indices of grasppanda.ops.furthest_point_sample; bucket (QuickFPS) is repeatable and spreads as well (smallest spacing 0.138 against 0.140) but returns another seed set and does not contain the start point; the npdu methods assume points in scan order and gave a smallest spacing of 0.007 on a shuffled cloud, worse than random sampling (0.017). Use method: vanilla when the seed set must equal the reference.
  • CPU bridges are not faster here. 20 000 → 1024 points took 6 to 12 ms with fpsample (bucket, h = 3 to 9) and 10 ms with the kernel GraspPanda already ships; the bridges are for CPU-only inference and for people who want the same kernel as another code base.
  • torch_cluster.fps takes a ratio, not a count, and starts at a random point by default. The bridge converts the count, trims the result and sets random_start: false; with that it returned exactly the reference indices in the unit test.
  • Three distances are called F-FPS. The 3DSSD paper adds L2 distances with a weight λ, its released code takes the squared L2 distance of the concatenation without λ, and SASA's code adds cdist(xyz) + γ·cdist(features). metric and coord_weight name the convention; the unit test compares both with a brute-force distance matrix.
  • S-FPS: paper and kernel differ by a factor of two in γ. The released kernel multiplies the squared distance by score^γ; distance names the convention and the test pins the relation.
  • 3DSSD's fusion sampling returns 2 M points. A proposal has a fixed seed count, so FusionFPS splits the count between the two kinds (feature_fraction); that is a deviation, stated in the docstring.
  • A score above 1 must not be clamped. A first version clamped graspness to [0, 1] before the sampler; the predicted graspness is a regression output and is not bounded by 1, every value above 1 then tied, and top-k fell back to "the first k points" (caught by the unit test). The selecting score is now only kept non-negative.
  • One value read back per pick makes a sampler slow on a shared GPU. The first version of the general kernel read every pick as a Python number and measured feature distances by subtracting an N × C array: 1024 picks among 15 000 points with 512 channels took 18 s on the GPU of this machine while other jobs were running, and dense-fusion-fps probed at 14 s per iteration. Picks now stay on the device and a feature distance is one matrix-vector product per pick: 0.19 s for the same call (FusionFPS 0.5 s, ScoreWeightedFPS 0.3 s, ScoreNMS 0.2 s, plain FPS 0.01 s). Feature-space sampling over the whole scene is still the most expensive option here.
  • Probes failed with "CUDA error: unspecified launch failure" once, in two processes at the same second and at unrelated places (a loss, an assigner), while the GPU held 46 of 48 GB for other jobs. The cells were probed again and their records replaced.
  • A stage preset used to have to be a stage of a shipped reference model (a tripwire test). Options beyond the reference models are now listed in that test by component.

docs.title: 6. Not wrapped
docs.text: Candidate Link opened Reason Object-balanced seeds (quota per instance): OBS / FS of Scale-Balanced-Grasp, per-object quantile of DexGraspNet 2.0 Scale-Balanced-Grasp (an MIT licence file, on code derived from graspnet-baseline, whose terms are non-commercial), DexGraspNet2 (no licence file) needs an instance mask as a test-time input; Observation.masks is declared but no dataset or transform fills it. The sampler side would be a small wrapper around any sampler here; the missing part is the mask provider with its provenance (ground truth, a segmentation network, a height threshold are different experiments). Follow-up. GraNet's cascaded selection (object points, then ten value classes, graph convolutions between levels) GraNet@d9992e1 (MIT) not a proposal alone: it brings its own graph encoder (DGL) and a ten-class label that no dataset here builds. Its last step (top-k) is the graspness-topk option. MultiGraspNet's graspness loss (weighted binary cross-entropy on the soft target) arXiv 2602.06504 a primitive of the loss slot, not of this one; its candidate rule is the product-fps option. Written from the paper; no code of the work was used. RandLA-Net code RandLA-Net CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; random sampling needs no code from it. S4G code, Contact-GraspNet code s4g-release (no licence file), contact_graspnet (NVIDIA licence) licences; the two selection rules are small and were written from the papers (ScoreNMS, FPSThenTopK). PyTorch3D sample_farthest_points, Open3D farthest_point_down_sample, mmcv PointsSampler mmcv@d2111bd not installed in the shared environment (PyTorch3D and mmcv need a compiled build matching the local PyTorch); they would add a third and fourth spelling of the same D-FPS. Voted seeds (VoteGrasp), mask queries (M2T2), image heat-map centres (HGGD, RNGNet, KGN) none opened for this page they emit virtual seeds or a variable number of regions; the seed-based skeleton needs scene points with parent_index (label matching). Another detector family. A sampler option inside the encoders (PointNet2, FurthestPointSubsample), where 3DSSD, IA-SSD and SASA place theirs — a change to the encoders, not to this slot. The SAMPLERS registry is ready for it.

docs.title: The training recipe: optimizer, schedule, hooks, augmentation
docs.text:
Words such as seed, contract, preset, adapter, label set and point painting are explained in the slot index.

Which of these options fit a method

Every method has a page that lists the options of each of its slots with what was measured for each (the verdict, the levels composes, runs, learns and predicts, the class, the grasps, the reason of a refusal): GSNet (optimizer, schedule, hooks, augmentation, whole recipe); EconomicGrasp (optimizer, schedule, hooks, augmentation, whole recipe); FineGrasp (optimizer, schedule, hooks, augmentation, whole recipe); GraspNet-baseline (optimizer, schedule, hooks, augmentation, whole recipe); Scale-Balanced-Grasp (optimizer, schedule, hooks, augmentation, whole recipe); HGGD (optimizer, schedule, hooks, augmentation, whole recipe). In a terminal: grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --list optimizer.

Class: one run, seed 0, 20 iterations, 8 frames of one scene; a class counts verdicts, not accuracy. Where this page names a class or a measured verdict, it is one of the measured classes.

Everything on this page is around the model: how its weights are updated, how the learning rate moves, what runs before and after an epoch, and how a training sample is perturbed. None of it changes what the detector computes, so none of it is bound to one method: the same line works under GSNet and under HGGD unless the page says otherwise.

No AP is claimed for anything here. "Runs" means: grasppanda probe trained 20 iterations on 8 real frames of GraspNet-1Billion with finite losses and predicted grasps. Whether a recipe is better takes a training run and an evaluation.

docs.title: 1. The task of the slot
docs.text:
A config has four places that make up the recipe, and each is a slot you fill by name:

Config key Registry What it decides When it runs optimizer OPTIMIZERS how gradients become weight updates once per train.accumulate batches scheduler SCHEDULERS the learning rate over the run after every optimizer step or every epoch (train.scheduler_unit) hooks HOOKS anything else around the loop: weight averages, freezing, clipping variants at before_run, before_epoch, before_step, after_iter, after_epoch, after_run data.train.dataset.transforms TRANSFORMS augmentation of one training sample in the data-loader workers, per sample

Plain options of the loop need no component: train.amp (mixed precision), train.accumulate (gradient accumulation), train.grad_clip with train.grad_clip_mode (clipping), train.ema (a fixed-decay weight average), train.sync_bn.

The loop itself (grasppanda/engine/trainer.py) is short: forward and backward per batch; every train.accumulate batches before_step hooks, clipping, optimizer.step(), the weight average, the scheduler. Everything on this page plugs into those points.

docs.title: 2. Input and output
docs.text:
Optimizer. Built by build_optimizers(model, config["optimizer"]). The engine supplies two arguments a config never writes: params (every parameter with requires_grad, or what the detector's configure_optimizers returns) and, for components that ask for it, model (to name parameters). The result must be a torch.optim.Optimizer; the bridges on this page return the library's own optimizer object, so checkpoints hold its state dict unchanged. A detector may return several optimizers; each gets a scheduler of its own.

Scheduler. Built per optimizer from the scheduler node; it must be a torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LRScheduler. The trainer calls step() once per optimizer step (train.scheduler_unit: iteration) or once per epoch (epoch, the default). The engine fills in the length of the run where the schedule needs it: total_steps of OneCycleLR and TimmSchedule, T_max of CosineAnnealingLR, total_iters of PolynomialLR. scheduler: null is a constant rate.

Hook. A subclass of grasppanda.engine.hooks.Hook; every callback receives the TrainState (model, optimizers, schedulers, gradient scaler, ema, epoch and iteration counters, the resolved config). Hooks run in ascending priority; evaluation is 70, checkpointing 80, so a hook that changes the weights used for evaluation has a lower one. A weight average installs itself as state.ema, which is what evaluation.weights: ema scores and what a checkpoint stores under ema.

Transform. A PointTransform maps one PointSample to one PointSample after the label-alignment boundary. A sample holds points (N, 3) float64 in metres in the camera frame (z along the view), full_points (the cloud before sampling), per-point labels aligned with points, and objects: one 4 × 4 object-to-camera pose per instance, to which the grasp labels are attached. So an augmentation may

  • remove or reorder points only through sample.gather(index), which carries the labels;
  • move the scene only together with the object poses;
  • not move points at all when the sample carries images (rgb, depth) or camera-bound extras, as HGGD's does: the config check refuses such a transform list (a transform that moves points declares moves_points = True), and the sample refuses it again.

Scaling the scene is therefore not an allowed augmentation: grasp widths, depths and the gripper are in metres and would not follow.

What the config checker does. grasppanda print-config --check (and compose) checks every key of these nodes against the constructor signature of the named class, without importing the optional libraries. Free-form arguments of a library go into one explicit mapping, options. Whether an optimizer name exists in the installed library is known only when the optimizer is built: probe or train then names the valid ones.

docs.title: 3. Options at a glance
docs.text:
Install the optional libraries once: pip install -e ".[optim]" (timm, pytorch_optimizer, schedulefree; all Apache-2.0). Options marked "core" need nothing.

Everything is random-init: a recipe has no weights. "Measured" is the verdict of grasppanda probe per method, from the records of Measured combinations; G = GSNet, E = EconomicGrasp, H = HGGD. The records below are of two methods, not five: the last column is the class of the measured page at the level runs, counted over the methods probed (2 of 2 probed: it ran under a seed-based method and under HGGD, a detector family with its own data path, hooks and clipping), followed by the methods not probed yet. The grid now has a cell for every preset under every method it applies to (all six; the five seed-based ones for a preset that names backbone). That column is written by tools/make_method_pages.py from the records; the other levels are on the method pages.

docs.title: Recipe presets (name them after --set)
docs.text:
grasppanda compose --list optimizer (or schedule, hooks, augment, recipe) prints them; grasppanda compose --show optimizer=timm-lamb prints one file with its re-tuning notes.

Slot --set What it is Sets Needs Measured Class at runs optimizer optimizer=adamw-no-decay-1d AdamW with no weight decay on biases and normalisation weights, through ParamGroups. ParamGroups core G runs, H runs universal optimizer optimizer=adamw AdamW of PyTorch with decoupled weight decay, the default of the transformer encoders. AdamW core G runs, H runs universal optimizer optimizer=ademamix AdEMAMix (Pagliardini et al., arXiv 2409.03137): Adam with a second, slow momentum. PytorchOptimizer optim G runs, H runs universal optimizer optimizer=timm-adan Adan (Xie et al., arXiv 2208.06677): Adam with a Nesterov momentum estimate. TimmOptimizer optim G runs, H runs universal optimizer optimizer=timm-adopt ADOPT (Taniguchi et al., NeurIPS 2024): Adam that converges for any beta2. TimmOptimizer optim G runs, H runs universal optimizer optimizer=timm-madgrad MADGRAD (Defazio and Jelassi, arXiv 2101.11075): dual averaging with momentum. TimmOptimizer optim G runs, H runs universal schedule schedule=constant No schedule: the optimizer's learning rate for the whole run. train options core G runs, H runs 5 of 6 probed schedule schedule=cosine-restarts Cosine with warm restarts (SGDR, Loshchilov and Hutter, ICLR 2017): cycles of 4 epochs, each peak half the one before. ParamGroups, TimmSchedule, FreezeHook, EMAHook optim G runs, E runs most; seed-based only: it names the backbone module recipe recipe=ptv3-adamw-onecycle Pointcept's PTv3 recipe with its tenth of the rate for the transformer blocks. What did not simply run, in the words of the probe:

  • recipe/GSNet/optimizer/schedulefree-sgd, runs-unstable: 1 of 20 iterations had no real seed (iteration 3).
  • recipe/HGGD/optimizer/soap, fails: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered CUDA kernel errors might be asynchronously reported at some other API call, so the stacktrace below might be incorrect. For debugging consider passing CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 Compile with TORCH_USE_CUDA_DSA to enable device-side assertions.
  • recipe/GSNet/hooks/amp and recipe/HGGD/hooks/amp, refused: mixed precision is not supported by the detector yet (it does not declare amp_ready = True). Probed before that rule existed, GSNet stopped in the first iteration with "Index put requires the source and destination dtypes match, got Float for the destination and Half for the source", and HGGD's first loss was not finite (loss/heatmap = nan, loss/angle = inf).
  • recipe/HGGD/augment/jitter and recipe/HGGD/augment/shift, refused: RandomJitter (RandomShift) moves the points, but this dataset section also serves image-space data (rgb, depth, view_grasps), which would stay where it was.

Under HGGD the three encoder-specific optimizer and hook presets and the two encoder recipes have no cell: they name backbone, a module only the seed-based skeleton has. They have cells under the five seed-based methods; the records above are of GSNet and EconomicGrasp.

docs.title: One line with compose
docs.text:
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set optimizer=timm-lamb --set schedule=warmup-cosine --set hooks=ema+grad-clip \
    --set augment=jitter -o my_recipe.yaml
grasppanda probe my_recipe.yaml          # about a minute: does it train and predict?
grasppanda train my_recipe.yaml
  • optimizer, schedule and recipe take one preset; hooks and augment take several joined by +.
  • Recipe slots combine with stage slots (--set backbone=ptv3 --set recipe=ptv3-adamw-onecycle) and work for HGGD, which has no stage slots.
  • --opts changes single values and wins over a preset: --opts optimizer.lr=3e-3 scheduler.warmup_steps=0.1 train.epochs=20.
  • The composed file lists what each preset says must be re-tuned.

What compose writes for HGGD with --set optimizer=timm-lamb --set schedule=warmup-cosine --set hooks=ema (real output, header omitted):

_base_:
  - configs/hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e.yaml

optimizer:
  type: TimmOptimizer
  name: lamb
  lr: 0.002
  weight_decay: 0.02

scheduler:
  type: TimmSchedule
  name: cosine
  warmup_steps: 0.05              # fraction of the run
  warmup_lr_init: 1.0e-06
  lr_min: 1.0e-06

train:
  scheduler_unit: iteration

evaluation:
  weights: ema

hooks: [{type: EpochSignalHook}, {type: BNMomentumHook, initial: 0.5, decay: 0.5, step: 2, minimum: 0.001, delay: 1, module: image_net}, {type: EMAHook, decay: 0.999, warmup: true, buffers: copy}]

The two hooks of HGGD's own recipe are written out again because a list in a child config replaces the inherited one.

And a probe of GSNet with --set optimizer=schedulefree-adamw --set hooks=ema+freeze-encoder --set augment=jitter+dropout (real output, shortened):

  model       GSNet · 15,353,775 parameters
  data        8 frames of the config's dataset · 4 per iteration
  trained     20 of 20 iterations · 0.36 s per iteration (median, without data; data 0.40 s), measured on this machine now
  memory      peak 1.9 GiB on the GPU, this process
  predicted   2 frame(s) · 7, 16 grasps

✓ runs: trained 20 iterations on 8 frames of the dataset and predicted on 2 frame(s), with finite losses and real seeds in every iteration.

docs.title: Optimizers
docs.text:
optimizer: {type: AdamW, lr: 1.0e-3, weight_decay: 0.05}                    # torch.optim, by class
optimizer: {type: TimmOptimizer, name: lamb, lr: 2.0e-3, weight_decay: 0.02}
optimizer: {type: TimmOptimizer, name: lookahead_adan, lr: 1.0e-3, options: {betas: [0.98, 0.92, 0.99]}}
optimizer: {type: PytorchOptimizer, name: prodigy, lr: 1.0}
optimizer: {type: ScheduleFree, name: adamw, lr: 2.5e-3, warmup_steps: 200}
  • lr and weight_decay are arguments of the bridge; everything else the optimizer takes (betas, eps, momentum, …) goes into options.
  • Names: python -c "import timm.optim as o; print(o.list_optimizers())" and python -c "import pytorch_optimizer as o; print(o.get_supported_optimizers())". A wrong name is reported with the list of valid ones when the optimizer is built.
  • A lookahead_ prefix wraps any timm optimizer in Lookahead.
  • Learning-rate-free optimizers (prodigy, dadaptadam, …) want lr: 1.0 and usually --set schedule=constant or a cosine.
  • A schedule-free optimizer needs scheduler: null and ScheduleFreeHook; the presets schedulefree-adamw, -radam, -sgd set all three.

docs.title: Parameter groups: a pretrained encoder, layer-wise decay
docs.text:
optimizer:
  type: ParamGroups
  optimizer: {type: AdamW, lr: 1.0e-3, weight_decay: 0.05}   # any optimizer node; must set lr
  lr_multipliers: {backbone: 0.1}      # dotted prefix of the parameter name, or "re:<regex>"
  layer_decay: 0.75                    # null: off
  layer_decay_module: backbone
  layer_decay_depth: 2
  no_decay_1d: true                    # no weight decay on biases and normalisation weights

The rate of a parameter is lr × the first matching multiplier × layer_decay ** (L - i) for layer i of the L layers of layer_decay_module. A layer is a sub-module layer_decay_depth levels below that module, in registration order:

sparse-unet14 depth 1: stem, down, encoder, up, decoder, project            (6 layers)
sparse-unet14 depth 2: stem.conv, stem.norm, down.0, … decoder.3, project   (19 layers)
ptv3 depth 2: embedding.stem, enc.enc0 … enc.enc4, dec.dec3 … dec.dec0      (10 layers)
ptv3 depth 3: … enc.enc0.block0, enc.enc0.block1, enc.enc1.down, …          (32 layers)

(python -c "from grasppanda.engine.optimizers import layer_names; ..." on your own encoder.) In a U-Net the decoder is registered after the encoder and therefore counts as later layers with a higher rate. A pattern that matches nothing is an error that lists the top-level modules. OneCycleLR would overwrite all group rates with one max_lr; the engine scales a scalar max_lr per group.

To train a pretrained encoder: load the weights (runtime.load_from=<checkpoint>, with runtime.allow_weight_mismatch=true when the checkpoint does not cover the whole detector; the page of the encoder slot says which released weights fit), then --set recipe=finetune-encoder or the single parts optimizer=encoder-lr-0.1, optimizer=layer-decay, hooks=freeze-encoder.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
scheduler: {type: OneCycleLR, max_lr: 1.0e-3, pct_start: 0.05, div_factor: 10.0, final_div_factor: 1000.0, cycle_momentum: false}
scheduler: {type: TimmSchedule, name: cosine, warmup_steps: 0.05, warmup_lr_init: 1.0e-6, lr_min: 1.0e-6}
scheduler: {type: TimmSchedule, name: multistep, warmup_steps: 1, warmup_lr_init: 1.0e-4, options: {decay_t: [6, 9], decay_rate: 0.1}}
scheduler: {type: TimmSchedule, name: cosine, options: {t_initial: 4, cycle_limit: 3, cycle_decay: 0.5}}   # restarts
train: {scheduler_unit: iteration}     # or epoch: the unit of every step count above
  • TimmSchedule.warmup_steps below 1 is a fraction of the run, from 1 on a step count.
  • warmup_lr_init and lr_min are absolute rates, not factors.
  • OneCycleLR.max_lr replaces optimizer.lr; keep cycle_momentum: false unless the optimizer has betas or momentum you want cycled.

docs.title: Hooks and train options
docs.text:
hooks:
  - {type: EMAHook, decay: 0.999, warmup: true, interval: 1, buffers: copy}
  - {type: SWAHook, start_epoch: 7}
  - {type: FreezeHook, modules: [backbone], epochs: 2, eval_mode: true}
  - {type: AdaptiveGradClipHook, clip_factor: 0.01, exclude: [head]}
evaluation: {weights: ema}             # score the average (EMAHook, SWAHook or train.ema)
train: {amp: true, accumulate: 2, grad_clip: 1.0, grad_clip_mode: norm}
  • One weight average per run: EMAHook, SWAHook and train.ema exclude each other. EMAHook differs from train.ema in three ways: the decay warms up (min(decay, (1 + n) / (10 + n))), buffers are copied rather than averaged by default (batch-norm statistics and HGGD's learned anchors stay those of the trained model), and interval can skip steps. A resumed run continues either average exactly.
  • evaluation.weights: ema selects the average of a checkpoint in grasppanda test as well; model selects the trained weights of the same checkpoint.
  • FreezeHook sets requires_grad per epoch; an optimizer skips a parameter without a gradient, weight decay included, so nothing has to be rebuilt when the modules are released. With eval_mode the frozen modules keep their batch-norm statistics.
  • AdaptiveGradClipHook and train.grad_clip exclude each other (the preset agc switches train.grad_clip off, which matters under HGGD, whose recipe clips by value).

docs.title: Augmentation
docs.text:
data:
  train:
    dataset:
      transforms:
        - {type: RandomDropout, ratio: 0.2, prob: 0.5}     # before the sampling step
        - {type: RandomSample, num_points: 15000}
        # ... the label steps, flip and rotation of the base config ...
        - {type: RandomShift, shift: [[-0.1, 0.1], [-0.1, 0.1], [-0.05, 0.1]]}
        - {type: RandomJitter, sigma: 0.001, clip: 0.005}

--set augment=dropout+shift+jitter writes exactly this around the list of the base config. Units are metres in the camera frame. RandomJitter perturbs only the network input: full_points, poses and labels describe the clean scene.

docs.title: Without compose: schedule bases
docs.text: Three method-neutral files under configs/_base_/schedules/ can be inherited like the methods' own: adamw_onecycle_10e.yaml, adamw_warmup-cosine_10e.yaml, schedulefree-adamw_10e.yaml. They set optimizer, scheduler and train.epochs.

docs.title: 5. Pitfalls
docs.text:
• OneCycleLR and momentum. Its default cycle_momentum: true rewrites betas or momentum every step and raises for optimizers that have neither. The presets set false.
  • OneCycleLR ignores optimizer.lr. The peak is max_lr. Changing only optimizer.lr with --opts changes nothing.
  • Schedule-free and batch norm. The weights that are evaluated are an average; the batch-norm statistics were collected at the training point. The authors re-estimate them; this toolbox does not.
  • Schedule-free in a short probe. With warmup_steps: 200 a 20-iteration probe runs entirely inside the warm-up, so its losses fall more slowly than with Adam. That says nothing about a full run.
  • Per-epoch units and warm-up. With train.scheduler_unit: epoch a warm-up that starts at 0 spends the whole first epoch at rate 0; the preset multistep-warmup starts at 1e-4.
  • Lists replace. hooks and transforms of a child config replace the inherited list. compose writes the base's entries out again; a hand-written child must repeat them (HGGD needs its EpochSignalHook).
  • SWAHook.start_epoch must be below train.epochs; the run refuses to start otherwise ("nothing would be averaged").
  • Point augmentation next to images is refused by the config check. augment=jitter, augment=shift and the flip and rotation of the GraspNet recipes move the points; a dataset section that serves images or view_grasps (HGGD's) would keep them where they were. The message names the transform and the image-space data. augment=dropout removes points and moves none, so it runs under HGGD.
  • A wrong optimizer name passes the config check and fails when the optimizer is built, with the list of valid names: the check does not import the libraries.
  • Mixed precision is not ready for the ported methods, and is refused. hooks=amp (train.amp: true) failed under GSNet in the first iteration: the label assigner writes half-precision values into a single-precision tensor ("Index put requires the source and destination dtypes match"). Under HGGD the loss of the first iteration was not finite (loss/heatmap = nan, loss/angle = inf). The config check now refuses train.amp: true unless the detector class declares amp_ready = True, and none of the shipped ones does. The preset stays as the switch for a detector of your own; it is one of the 37 names on this page and not a usable option today.
  • SOAP fails under HGGD. optimizer=soap runs under GSNet; under HGGD the second optimizer step ends in "CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered", three times out of three. The cause was not investigated.
  • Schedule-free SGD in a short probe. Under GSNet one of the 20 iterations of the probe had no real seed (runs-unstable); the AdamW and RAdam variants did not show it.

docs.title: 6. Not wrapped
docs.text: Candidate Link Why not Normalisation and activation as config keys (GroupNorm, LayerNorm, GELU, SiLU, …) torch.nn; timm create_act.py No shared layer builder exists in the stages: norms and activations are literals at dozens of sites in grasppanda/models/, outside this package's lane. A hook that swapped modules after construction would not run at grasppanda test, so trained and tested models would differ. Needs one builder used by every stage first. RandomScale Pointcept transform.py Grasp widths, depths and the gripper are in metres; PointSample has no way to scale the label grids with the scene. ElasticDistortion same file Not a rigid map: object poses, and the grasp labels attached to them, cannot follow. Chromatic transforms (auto-contrast, colour jitter) same file The ported methods feed no colour to the scene encoder; HGGD's image pipeline is not a point transform. Mix3D scene mixing Pointcept pointcept/datasets/utils.py, point_collate_fn(mix_prob) Works in the collate function, which is fixed in the engine; two scenes' object poses and label sets would have to be merged. Sharpness-aware minimisation (SAM) pytorch_optimizer/optimizer/sam.py (class SAM) Its step() needs a closure that runs a second forward and backward pass; the loop makes one pass per batch and calls step() without a closure. ReduceLROnPlateau, timm PlateauLRScheduler PyTorch, timm Step on a monitored metric, which the trainer does not hand to schedulers. Refused by name. timm's learning-rate noise timm.scheduler TimmSchedule evaluates the closed form so that a resumed run needs no state of timm's; the noise is applied in timm's own step(). Batch-norm re-estimation after SWA (torch.optim.swa_utils.update_bn) PyTorch It iterates a loader of tensors; batches here are Batch objects and the detectors compute losses, not plain forwards.

docs.title: Scene encoders: overview
docs.text:
Words such as seed, contract, preset, adapter, label set and point painting are explained in the slot index.

Which of these options fit a method

Every method has a page that lists the options of each of its slots with what was measured for each (the verdict, the levels composes, runs, learns and predicts, the class, the grasps, the reason of a refusal): GSNet (scene encoder); EconomicGrasp (scene encoder); FineGrasp (scene encoder); GraspNet-baseline (scene encoder); Scale-Balanced-Grasp (scene encoder). In a terminal: grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --list backbone.

Class: one run, seed 0, 20 iterations, 8 frames of one scene; a class counts verdicts, not accuracy. Where this page names a class or a measured verdict, it is one of the measured classes.

The slot model.backbone of the seed-based methods (GSNet, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp). It has more options than any other slot, so its documentation is split by family. This page says what all of them share and where each option is explained; the slot index has the class of every option.

No grasp accuracy is claimed for any encoder that is not the one a ported method ships with. Each option was composed and probed on real frames under all five methods; that shows it builds, trains for 20 iterations and predicts.

docs.title: The task, and input and output
docs.text:
The scene encoder is the first learned stage: it turns one depth-camera view of a cluttered table (15 000 to 20 000 points, about 5 mm apart) into one feature vector per point. Everything after it reads those features. Its receptive field and its resolution decide what a seed knows about its surroundings before the grouper takes a crop.

input a PointSet (coords (N, 3) in metres in the camera frame, all clouds of the batch concatenated with batch offsets) and per-point features (N, in_channels): constant ones, coordinates and normals, or nothing, as the method feeds output dense PointFeatures with one row per input point output subsampled PointFeatures on a sub-sample of the points, the same number for every cloud of the batch; those points become the seeds out_channels the width of the features, injected into proposal, view stage and grouper

Three contracts tie an encoder to its neighbours, and grasppanda compose resolves each of them or refuses with the fix:

  1. Where the features live. A proposal requires dense or subsampled features. When the encoder returns the other kind, compose wraps it in the adapter FeaturePropagation (sub-sampled to dense) or FurthestPointSubsample (dense to sub-sampled) and says so. On the measured page such a cell reads runs in that adapter.
  2. The point features. Compose sets the encoder's in_channels to what the method feeds.
  3. The width. An encoder declares the width it returns for its options (Backbone.output_channels) and a grouper the width it needs; the config check compares them without building anything. Compose sets out_channels where the encoder has that option and otherwise, under Scale-Balanced-Grasp, puts the projected grouper in place (Grouper, section 5).

No contract checks the unit of length. Most of these networks were published for rooms or street scenes; the presets restate radii and grid sizes for a table top and say in their header what was derived from what. They are starting points, not tuned values.

docs.title: The three pages
docs.text:
Page Families Options (--set backbone=) Point-based networks set abstraction, residual MLPs, graph convolutions, random sampling; released weights for PointNet++ and PointNeXt pointnet2-msg, pointnet2-msg-dense, pointnext, pointnext-b, pointnext-l, pointnext-xl, pointmetabase, pointmetabase-xl, pointvector, pointvector-xl, assanet, pointmlp, dela, dgcnn, dgcnn-static, randlanet, pyg-pointnet, pyg-edgeconv, pyg-point-transformer, pyg-pointgnn Sparse-voxel networks and released weights sparse U-Nets (the MinkUNet family, SpUNet), and released weights for them and for the serialised transformers PTv3 and LitePT minkunet18a, minkunet34c, minkunet34c-pointcontrast, minkunet18a-openscene, spunet, spunet-gaussiancross, ptv3, ptv3-scannet200, ptv3-ppt, ptv3-encoder, ptv3-sonata, ptv3-sonata-small, litept, litept-structured3d Transformers, state-space models, pretrained 3-D encoders point transformers, a plain volume transformer, octree attention, point-patch tokens (ViT, Mamba, Uni3D) point-transformer-v1, point-transformer-v2, volt, octformer, point-vit, point-mamba, uni3d Scene encoders of the model zoo the encoders the ported methods ship with and those ported earlier, with the evidence against their reference implementations sparse-unet14, pointnet2, pointnet2-dense, pointnet2-transformer, oacnns, ptv3-utonia

grasppanda compose --list backbone prints all of them with one line each; grasppanda components --slot backbones adds the contract, the source, the status and the optional library of every class.

docs.title: How to choose
docs.text:
• To change as little as possible, take an encoder of the kind the method already has: dense for GSNet, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp, subsampled for GraspNet-baseline and Scale-Balanced-Grasp. No adapter is inserted then.
  • To start from released weights, read section 3.2 of the sparse page and section 5 of the point and transformer pages: they list which files load into which class, their licences (several are non-commercial) and what does not load (usually the first layer, which reads the input).
  • On a small GPU, the tables of the pages give the peak memory of the probes; the point-based encoders with graph convolutions over the whole scene are the most expensive.
  • Optional libraries: the sparse networks need a spconv extra, the PyTorch Geometric bridge torch_geometric, OctFormer ocnn, PointMamba mamba-ssm (CUDA only), Uni3D timm. A config that names a missing library passes the config check and stops when the model is built, with the pip install line.

docs.title: Try one
docs.text:
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=pointmetabase \
    -o gsnet_pointmetabase.yaml
grasppanda probe gsnet_pointmetabase.yaml

Under Scale-Balanced-Grasp a probe ends as wired (a synthetic scene, exit status 3) unless it is given the reference's width histogram, which cannot be built from the eight frames of a probe; the runs of that method in the tables of these pages were measured with

grasppanda probe <config> --opts data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.source=legacy_import \
    data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.reference_sha256=<SHA-256 of the reference's file>

(configs/scale_balanced_grasp/README.md says how to import the file once.)

The measured verdict of every encoder under every method, with the adapter compose inserted and the numbers of the probe, is in Measured combinations; the explorer shows the same per selection.

docs.title: Scene encoders: point-based networks
docs.text:
Words such as seed, contract, preset, adapter, label set and point painting are explained in the slot index.

Which of these options fit a method

Every method has a page that lists the options of each of its slots with what was measured for each (the verdict, the levels composes, runs, learns and predicts, the class, the grasps, the reason of a refusal): GSNet (scene encoder); EconomicGrasp (scene encoder); FineGrasp (scene encoder); GraspNet-baseline (scene encoder); Scale-Balanced-Grasp (scene encoder). In a terminal: grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --list backbone.

Class: one run, seed 0, 20 iterations, 8 frames of one scene; a class counts verdicts, not accuracy. Where this page names a class or a measured verdict, it is one of the measured classes.

Options for the slot model.backbone of the seed-based methods that work on the raw point cloud: set abstraction (PointNet++ and its descendants), residual MLPs, graph convolutions, random-sampling networks and point-wise networks on a grid pyramid. Sparse-voxel CNNs and serialised transformers have pages of their own.

Everything on this page comes from existing code: a library bridge, source adapted from a permissively licensed repository, or released weights for a class that already existed. No grasp AP is claimed for any option here. What was checked is stated per option: the contract on tiny clouds in the unit suite, and grasppanda compose plus grasppanda probe on real GraspNet-1Billion frames under the five seed-based methods.

docs.title: 1. The task of the slot
docs.text:
The scene encoder is the first learned stage of a seed-based detector (GSNet, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp). It turns one depth-camera view of a cluttered table, 15 000 to 20 000 points, into a feature vector per point. Everything after it reads those features: the proposal picks seeds from them, the view stage chooses an approach direction per seed, the grouper crops the scene around each seed and adds the seed's feature, and the head predicts the grasp. The encoder decides what a seed "knows" about its surroundings before any crop is taken, so its receptive field and its resolution are what matter for this task.

depth frame -> points (N, 3) -> [ backbone ] -> proposal -> view -> grouper -> head -> grasps
                                  this slot

HGGD is a detector family of its own (image encoder plus region network) and has no scene point encoder to replace.

docs.title: 2. Input and output
docs.text:
class Backbone(nn.Module):                # grasppanda/models/base.py
    output: "dense" | "subsampled"        # where the returned features live
    in_channels: int
    out_channels: int
    def forward(self, points: PointSet, feats: Tensor) -> PointFeatures: ...
points A PointSet: coords of shape (N, 3), metres, camera frame, all clouds of the batch concatenated, with batch offsets (points.sizes, points.batch_index). Clouds of a batch may differ in size. Point spacing on a table top is about 5 mm. feats (N, in_channels). GSNet and EconomicGrasp feed constant ones (point_features: ones, 3 channels); FineGrasp feeds coordinates and normals (6 channels); GraspNet-baseline and Scale-Balanced-Grasp feed nothing (in_channels: 0). With point_features: ones the detector builds ones(N, backbone.in_channels), so any in_channels works. result, output = "dense" PointFeatures(feats, points): one row per input point, bound to the same PointSet. result, output = "subsampled" PointFeatures(feats, points.subset(index)): features on a child set that records which input rows it holds; every cloud of the batch must yield the same number of rows (the seeds). out_channels Read by the detector after the encoder is built and injected into proposal, view stage and grouper as their in_channels.

What the neighbours require, and what the config checker does with it:

  • GraspnessFPS (GSNet, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp) scores every scene point, so it requires dense. SubsampledSeeds (GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp) takes the encoder's own subsample as seeds, so it requires subsampled.
  • The checker compares backbone.output with proposal.requires and refuses a mismatch. grasppanda compose then inserts the adapter that converts: FeaturePropagation (subsampled to dense, one interpolation level) or FurthestPointSubsample (dense to subsampled, keeps npoint furthest-point samples), and says so in its output.
  • When an encoder has an out_channels option, compose sets it to the width of the encoder it replaces (512 for the sparse U-Net methods, 256 for the PointNet++ ones), so the other stages keep their width. When the width is fixed by the architecture, the other stages are built that wide.
  • The width of the seed features is a contract too. The crop of Scale-Balanced-Grasp adds the seed feature to a 256-channel crop feature (seed_residual: gated). An encoder declares the width it returns (Backbone.output_channels), the grouper the width it needs, and the config check compares the two without building anything. For an encoder of another width compose puts DepthCylinderProjectionGroup in place (the same crop with a linear layer in front of the residual) and says so; --no-adapter leaves the pair refused (Grouper, section 5).
  • No contract checks the unit of length. Every published configuration of these networks is for rooms (first radius 0.1 m, grids from 4 cm). The presets below restate radii and grids for a table top and say what they were derived from; all of them are choices by analogy, not tuned values.

docs.title: 4. How to use each option
docs.text:
The pattern is the same for all of them:

grasppanda compose --list backbone                        # what exists
grasppanda compose --show backbone=pointmetabase          # one preset with its notes
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set backbone=pointmetabase -o gsnet_pointmetabase.yaml
grasppanda probe gsnet_pointmetabase.yaml                 # trains 20 iterations on 8 frames
grasppanda train gsnet_pointmetabase.yaml

Real output of the compose step (2026-10-13):

slot      component             from
────────  ────────────────────  ──────────────────────
backbone  PointMetaBase         preset `pointmetabase`
proposal  GraspnessFPS          base config
view      TemplateViewStage     base config
assigner  NearestLabelAssigner  base config
grouper   CylinderGroup         base config
head      SWADHead              base config

contracts
  ✓ backbone · proposal
  ...
config check
  ✓ valid  (hash 7c25e7980f79)

Under a method whose proposal needs the other kind of output, compose adds the adapter and says what it did (grasppanda compose graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e --set backbone=randlanet):

backbone  RandLANet in FurthestPointSubsample  preset `randlanet`, in the adapter FurthestPointSubsample

  • wrapped RandLANet in the adapter FurthestPointSubsample (preset `furthest-point-subsample`):
    SubsampledSeeds requires 'subsampled' scene features, but RandLANet returns 'dense' ones (one
    feature per scene point). An adapter changes the model; its notes below say how.
  • FurthestPointSubsample.npoint: 1024, the number of seeds of the proposal
    (`model.proposal.num_seeds`): the points the adapter keeps are the seeds.

Options are overridden with --opts model.backbone.<option>=<value>; the path addresses the encoder wherever an adapter put it. In a config written by hand the fragment is the model.backbone node of the preset, for example:

model:
  backbone:
    type: PointMetaBase
    in_channels: 3        # constant ones
    radius: 0.04

docs.title: PointNet++ with multi-scale grouping: pointnet2-msg, pointnet2-msg-dense
docs.text:
grasppanda compose graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --set backbone=pointnet2-msg -o baseline_msg.yaml
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set backbone=pointnet2-msg-dense -o gsnet_msg.yaml

model:
  backbone:
    type: PointNet2MSG
    in_channels: 0
    npoints: [2048, 1024, 512, 256]
    radii: [[0.02, 0.04], [0.05, 0.1], [0.1, 0.2], [0.2, 0.3]]    # one list per level
    nsamples: [[32, 64], [16, 32], [16, 16], [16, 16]]
  • PointNet2MSG is a drop-in for the GraspNet-baseline encoder: the same level sizes, the same 1024 seeds and 256 channels, two balls per level. Use it where the method takes seeds from the encoder; PointNet2MSGDense where the proposal scores every point.
  • radii, nsamples and sa_mlps take one list per level with one entry per scale; a level's width is the sum over its scales. fp_mlps (coarsest first) decides where the output lives: k entries stop k levels above the coarsest.
  • Choosing radii: the larger ball of a level is what a single-scale network would use; the smaller one helps where points are dense (near the camera). Cost grows with the sum of nsamples over the scales.

docs.title: PointNeXt sizes: pointnext, pointnext-b, pointnext-l, pointnext-xl
docs.text:
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=pointnext-b -o gsnet_pointnext-b.yaml
preset blocks width sa_layers / sa_use_res parameters with the official segmentation head pointnext (S) 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 32 2 / true 0.792 M pointnext-b 1, 2, 3, 2, 2 32 1 / false 3.828 M pointnext-l 1, 3, 5, 3, 3 32 1 / false 7.125 M pointnext-xl 1, 4, 7, 4, 4 64 1 / false 41.576 M

The presets set radius: 0.04 (room value: 0.1). Depth costs ball queries: every inverted residual block runs one on the reference operators. Released weights: section 5.

docs.title: PointMetaBase and PointVector: pointmetabase[-xl], pointvector[-xl]
docs.text:
grasppanda compose economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set backbone=pointmetabase-xl -o economicgrasp_pointmetabase-xl.yaml
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set backbone=pointvector -o gsnet_pointvector.yaml

model:
  backbone:
    type: PointVector          # or PointMetaBase
    in_channels: 3
    radius: 0.04
    blocks: [1, 4, 7, 4, 4]    # XL; the default 1-3-5-3-3 is L
    width: 64
  • Both take the arguments of PointNeXt (blocks, width, strides, radius, radius_scaling, nsample). PointMetaBase also has expansion (1 as published); PointVector has block_nsample (8, fixed in the official code).
  • PointMetaBase is the cheap one: its blocks share one ball query and one offset embedding per stage. The unit suite pins its size to the published ones (2.738 M for L, 15.284 M for XL, 19.672 M for XXL = blocks: [1, 5, 9, 5, 5], width: 64, with the segmentation head).
  • PointVector here is the scene network of the official code (flag: 1: sum over neighbours, ReLU). The object-classification variants of that code are not built.
  • Output width is width (32 or 64): under Scale-Balanced-Grasp see section 6.

docs.title: ASSANet: assanet
docs.text:
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=assanet -o gsnet_assanet.yaml
  • radii, nsamples, mlps: per level and scale, as for multi-scale PointNet++, but the two scales of a level run one after the other. reduction: mean (published), max or sum. fp_mlps lists the propagation widths finest first; the first entry is the output width (the preset uses 256, the published network 64).
  • use_xyz: true (set by the preset) appends the coordinates to the input features. Without it the stem batch-normalises features that are the same on every point (the constant ones GSNet, EconomicGrasp, GraspNet-baseline and Scale-Balanced-Grasp feed), and the normalised value of a constant is zero: the encoder returned zeros and learned nothing, which a 20-iteration probe did not show (the first records of this option were made that way and have been replaced). The class now refuses constant features without use_xyz in training, and the probe reports a part that received no gradient.
  • The unit suite pins the default network to the published size (2.425 M with the segmentation head).

docs.title: PointMLP: pointmlp
docs.text:
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=pointmlp -o gsnet_pointmlp.yaml
  • Neighbourhoods are by count (k_neighbors), anchors by ratio (reducers): nothing to convert from rooms to a table top.
  • gmp_dim appends a max-pooled vector of the whole frame to every point (0 turns it off). embed_dim: 32 with res_expansion: 0.25 is the authors' small setting.
  • It reads the coordinates itself as its first three input channels; with FineGrasp it also receives coordinates and normals as features (the official model reads coordinates and normals).

docs.title: DeLA: dela
docs.text:
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=dela -o gsnet_dela.yaml

model:
  backbone:
    type: DeLA
    in_channels: 3
    grid_size: [0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04]   # first entry: the point spacing of the input
  • grid_size[0] is the spacing of the input cloud and sets the unit of the offset encoding; the other entries are the cells the cloud is subsampled to. Keep the factor of 2 between levels of the official pyramid unless you also change k.
  • Level sizes depend on the frame, so DeLA is dense only; under GraspNet-baseline and Scale-Balanced-Grasp compose wraps it in FurthestPointSubsample.
  • Not built: the auxiliary relative-coordinate loss and the stochastic depth of the official recipe (a backbone of this slot returns features only).

docs.title: DGCNN: dgcnn, dgcnn-static
docs.text:
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=dgcnn -o gsnet_dgcnn.yaml
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=dgcnn-static \
    --opts model.backbone.k=48 -o gsnet_dgcnn-static_k48.yaml
  • k: neighbours per point. dynamic: true rebuilds the graph in feature space for layers 2 and 3 (the paper); false keeps the spatial graph. emb_dims: width of the frame-level max-pooled vector, 0 to leave it out. knn_chunk: queries per block of the neighbour search (memory against speed).
  • coords_as_features: true (default) puts the coordinates in front of the input features. Leave it on with point_features: ones, otherwise the network sees constants only.
  • No subsampling: memory is proportional to N x k. Under FineGrasp the probes peaked at 30 GiB (dgcnn) and 36 GiB (dgcnn-static, k: 32); under GSNet at 8 to 11 GiB.

docs.title: RandLA-Net: randlanet
docs.text:
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=randlanet -o gsnet_randlanet.yaml
  • sub_sampling_ratio and dim_output take one entry per level; num_neighbors is by count. Among the cheapest encoders on this page (3 to 4 GiB in the probes under GSNet, EconomicGrasp and GraspNet-baseline).
  • Sampling is random in training and a fixed permutation in evaluation (seed), so inference is repeatable and a frame gives the same result alone or in a batch.
  • A cloud needs at least num_neighbors x prod(ratios[:-1]) points (1024 at the defaults).

docs.title: PyTorch Geometric layers: pyg-pointnet, pyg-edgeconv, pyg-point-transformer, pyg-pointgnn
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[torch_geometric]"
grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set backbone=pyg-point-transformer -o gsnet_pyg-pt.yaml

model:
  backbone:
    type: PyGPointEncoder
    in_channels: 3
    conv: point_transformer     # pointnet | edge | point_transformer | pointgnn
    channels: [64, 64, 128]     # one layer per entry
    k: 16
    conv_args: {}               # further arguments of the library layer
preset conv library layer pyg-pointnet pointnet torch_geometric.nn.PointNetConv pyg-edgeconv edge torch_geometric.nn.EdgeConv pyg-point-transformer point_transformer torch_geometric.nn.PointTransformerConv pyg-pointgnn pointgnn torch_geometric.nn.PointGNNConv (all channels equal)

Only the layers are the library's. The stack around them is not a published network: it is the quickest way to try a message-passing layer in a grasp detector. The graph is built by GraspPanda, so torch_geometric alone is enough (no pyg-lib, torch_cluster). Without the library the class says how to install it:

The backbone PyGPointEncoder needs 'torch_geometric.nn', which is not installed. Install it with: pip install -e ".[torch_geometric]"

docs.title: 5. Released weights that fit existing classes
docs.text:
tools/convert_backbone_weights.py cuts the encoder out of a released checkpoint, checks it strictly against the class (every tensor present, right shapes; anything left over must be a part the format is known to carry) and writes a file whose keys start with backbone.. Nothing is downloaded by the tool or by a test.

--format Source file Fits Tensors Trained on Code licence, weight licence Size pointnext-s (-b, -l, -xl) ..._ckpt_best.pth in the S3DIS folders linked from PointNeXt docs/modelzoo.md (Google Drive) PointNeXt(in_channels=4, ...) of that size S: 106 S3DIS area 5, rooms at 4 cm, colour + height MIT; weights: not stated S: 9.6 MB votenet pretrained_votenet_on_sunrgbd.tar, pretrained_votenet_on_scannet.tar in votenet_pretrained_models.zip linked from the VoteNet README (Google Drive) PointNet2(in_channels=1, radii=[0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2]) 96 SUN RGB-D single-view scans; ScanNet MIT; weights: not stated 11.5 MB each csc-pointnet2 partition8_4096_15k_pointnet.pth, the PointNet++ pre-training linked from the Contrastive Scene Contexts README PointNet2(radii=[0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2]), i.e. the GraspNet-baseline layout, coordinates only 96 (the file's fp3, fp4 are left behind) ScanNet frame pairs, self-supervised MIT; weights: not stated 6.4 MB csc-pointnet2-dense the same file PointNet2Dense with the GraspNet-baseline level sizes and fp_mlps 256-256 / 256-256 / 256-128 / 128-32 120 as above as above as above

The dataset terms of S3DIS, SUN RGB-D and ScanNet apply to weights trained on them; none of the files states a licence of its own, so treat them as research-only until you have checked.

What was verified on 2026-10-13 with the real files: pointnext-s, both votenet files and both csc formats convert and load with strict=True, and a converted file loads into a full detector through the engine (matched 96, unexpected 0, mismatched 0, the 66 missing tensors are the stages after the encoder). The B / L / XL formats use the same code path with the options the unit suite pins to the published sizes; their files (46 to 500 MB) were not downloaded. Activations were not compared with the upstream implementations, so the classes keep their status (PointNeXt: tested). The integration tests of strict loading skip when a file is absent, and the files are not kept on the machine the suites run on: the check above is that of the day it was made, not one that is repeated.

python -m tools.convert_backbone_weights --list
python -m tools.convert_backbone_weights partition8_4096_15k_pointnet.pth csc_pointnet2.pth \
    --format csc-pointnet2

wrote 96 tensors to csc_pointnet2.pth
source sha256: a6812612720295ff2625537aa1c5c88c0ba9748de2e4b4f501c84e86730c482e
model.backbone: {'type': 'PointNet2', 'radii': [0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2]}

Then start a training from it; the other stages start from random weights and the key report lists them as missing:

grasppanda train graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --opts runtime.load_from=csc_pointnet2.pth runtime.allow_weight_mismatch=true

Read before you rely on such an initialisation:

  • Radii are not stored in a checkpoint. The VoteNet and CSC networks were trained with room radii (0.2 to 1.2 m). They load under the GraspNet-baseline radii (0.04 to 0.3 m) without complaint; because offsets are divided by the radius, the network then sees a table top enlarged about five times. Whether that helps is untested. Printing the room radii, as the tool does, is the honest default; choosing table-top radii is an experiment.
  • Input channels are part of the weights. PointNeXt checkpoints read colour and a height above the floor (4 channels); VoteNet reads one height channel. A camera-frame table-top cloud has no floor height: define what you feed (zero, or height above the table plane) and keep in_channels as printed.
  • The integration test tests/integration/test_backbone_released_weights.py repeats the strict loading when the files lie in $GRASPPANDA_WEIGHTS/components/released_backbones/, and is skipped otherwise.
  • Some research checkpoints pickle their experiment config next to the weights (the CSC file holds an omegaconf object). The tool reads tensors with PyTorch's restricted loader and replaces every other class the file names by an inert stand-in; nothing of the file is executed.

docs.title: 6. Pitfalls met while building this page
docs.text:
• The grouper of Scale-Balanced-Grasp wants 256 channels from the encoder. pointnext*, pointmetabase* and pointvector* end on their stem width (32 or 64). When this page was first written such a config passed the check and failed at build; the width is a contract now, and compose puts the projected grouper in place (section 2). The model is then a variant of Scale-Balanced-Grasp, not the paper's. The presets of the encoders whose width is free (assanet, pointnet2-msg-dense, and every class with out_channels) are 256 wide for this reason.
  • Probing Scale-Balanced-Grasp needs its width histogram. Without --opts data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.source=legacy_import data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.reference_sha256=<sha> the probe falls back to a synthetic scene and reports wired, not runs (docs/user_guides/combinations.md, "The width histogram").
  • Constant input features starve encoders that read geometry through features. With point_features: ones, an EdgeConv or a point-wise MLP sees constants. DGCNN, PyGPointEncoder, RandLANet, PointMLP therefore read the coordinates themselves; the set-abstraction encoders get geometry through grouped offsets and do not need it.
  • Absolute coordinates. RandLA-Net's published neighbourhood encoding contains the absolute positions of both points, and DGCNN / PointMLP / the bridge read camera-frame coordinates as features: their features are not translation invariant.
  • Frame-level vectors. dgcnn (emb_dims) and pointmlp (gmp_dim) append a max-pooled vector of the whole frame to every point, so features depend on the workspace crop. Both can be switched off.
  • Padded balls under mean or sum. A ball query pads a sparse ball by repeating its first hit. Under max-pooling that is invisible; assanet (mean) and pointvector (sum) count the repeated point several times, as their upstream code does.
  • torch_geometric 2.8 without pyg-lib. Its knn_graph raises 'knn_graph' requires 'pyg-lib>=0.6.0'; the bridge builds the graph itself.
  • Memory. The last column of the table in section 3 is the peak of the probes. The upper end is always FineGrasp, whose own stages are heavy; there the full-resolution encoders (dgcnn*, pyg-pointgnn) reach 30 to 36 GiB. On a GPU shared with other jobs these probes ran out of memory several times before they went through alone.

docs.title: 7. Not wrapped
docs.text: Candidate Opened Why not KPConv (ICCV 2019), rigid and deformable HuguesTHOMAS/KPConv-PyTorch (MIT per the GitHub licence record; model files read), Open3D-ML (MIT) Not a thin adaptation: it needs kernel-point dispositions (an optimisation whose results the upstream caches as files), radius neighbourhoods with a shadow point, a grid pyramid with barycentre subsampling, all computed in the upstream data pipeline with compiled code; the deformable form also owns loss terms, for which the slot has no channel. A follow-up of its own. KPConvX / KPConvD (CVPR 2024) licence file of apple/ml-kpconvx (MIT, Copyright 2024 Apple Inc.); the code was not read Expected to have the same prerequisites as KPConv (not checked). Not attempted. RandLA-Net, authors' repository licence file of QingyongHu/RandLA-Net CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (and TensorFlow); the MIT implementation of Open3D-ML was adapted instead. Contact-GraspNet's PointNet++ MSG layout and weights not opened for this page NVIDIA Source Code License (non-commercial): no code taken. Its three-scale layout can be written as a PointNet2MSG config by hand; its checkpoints were not converted (the TensorFlow original and the PyTorch port are two different networks). torch_geometric.nn.XConv (PointCNN), GravNetConv torch_geometric 2.8.1 They build their neighbour graph inside the layer through knn / knn_graph, which needs pyg-lib in this version of the library. PointNeXt checkpoints of the Hugging Face organisation torch-pointcloud not opened for this page Third-party conversions with their own key layout; the official files fit directly. DeepLA-Net, LinNet, PointMixer not opened for this page Earlier notes found no licence file in the repositories; venues and licences were not re-checked. SPoTr, X-3D, HPENet V2, PAConv, RepSurf, PVCNN, DeepGCN, BAAF-Net not opened for this page Not reached. Their licences were not re-checked; SPoTr, X-3D and HPENet V2 are forks of the same code base as PointMetaBase and would follow its pattern.

docs.title: Scene encoders: sparse-voxel networks and released weights
docs.text:
Words such as seed, contract, preset, adapter, label set and point painting are explained in the slot index.

Which of these options fit a method

Every method has a page that lists the options of each of its slots with what was measured for each (the verdict, the levels composes, runs, learns and predicts, the class, the grasps, the reason of a refusal): GSNet (scene encoder); EconomicGrasp (scene encoder); FineGrasp (scene encoder); GraspNet-baseline (scene encoder); Scale-Balanced-Grasp (scene encoder). In a terminal: grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --list backbone.

Class: one run, seed 0, 20 iterations, 8 frames of one scene; a class counts verdicts, not accuracy. Where this page names a class or a measured verdict, it is one of the measured classes.

This page is about one config line, model.backbone, for the encoders that run on a voxel grid (sparse convolutions, and the point transformers that serialise voxels), and about starting them from published checkpoints. Point-based encoders (PointNet++, PointNeXt) and image encoders have their own pages.

Nothing here is a grasp-detection result. Every option below was built, loaded (where it has weights) and probed for twenty training iterations on real GraspNet-1Billion frames; no option has been trained to convergence in GraspPanda and no AP is claimed for any of them.

docs.title: 1. The task of the slot
docs.text:
The scene encoder is the first learned stage of a seed-based grasp detector (GSNet, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp). It receives the partial point cloud of one depth view, a cluttered table top seen by one camera, and returns one feature vector per point. Everything after it reads those features: the proposal stage scores every point ("is there a grasp here?") and picks about a thousand seeds, the view stage chooses an approach direction per seed, the grouper crops a neighbourhood per seed and the head regresses the grasp. The encoder is therefore the only stage that sees the whole scene, and the only one that can know that a point lies on the rim of a bowl next to a box.

depth view ─► points ─► [ backbone ] ─► proposal ─► view ─► grouper ─► head ─► grasps
                          this page      seeds      approach   crops     6-DoF

docs.title: 2. Input and output
docs.text:
Read from grasppanda/models/base.py (Backbone) and grasppanda/models/detectors/seed_based.py.

Call backbone(points, feats) -> PointFeatures points PointSet: (N, 3) float coordinates in metres, camera frame, of all clouds of the batch packed one after another, with batch offsets. N is 15 000 per frame under GSNet and 20 000 under the other methods. feats (N, in_channels) float. With point_features: ones (GSNet, EconomicGrasp, GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp) it is a constant 1 in every channel: the network sees geometry only, through the voxel grid. With point_features: observation (FineGrasp) it is the 6 real channels of the dataset, and compose sets in_channels: 6. Returns PointFeatures: (N, out_channels) bound to the point set they live on. output "dense": one feature for every input point (all encoders of this page), or "subsampled": features on a child set of about 1024 points (PointNet++). Attributes in_channels, out_channels: the detector builds proposal, view stage and grouper with in_channels = backbone.out_channels.

What the neighbours require:

  • A proposal states requires = "dense", "subsampled" or "any". GraspNet-baseline and Scale-Balanced-Grasp take seeds from a sub-sampling encoder; compose then wraps a dense encoder in the adapter FurthestPointSubsample (and tells you).
  • The width is free, with one exception: the grouper of Scale-Balanced-Grasp (DepthCylinderGroup with a gated seed residual) adds seed features to 256-channel crop features. Encoders with a free out_channels (SparseUNet14, SpUNet, MinkUNet) are set to the width of the encoder they replace. PTv3 and LitePT have a fixed width; for them compose puts DepthCylinderProjectionGroup in place of that grouper and says so (the width is a contract the config check compares; Grouper, section 5).

What a sparse-voxel encoder does with this input, in all classes of this page: it quantises the coordinates to a grid it owns (voxel_size or grid_size, 0.005 m in every preset, the grid of GSNet), runs on one feature per occupied voxel and hands the feature of a voxel back to every point in it. The grid is the encoder's unit of length: a network whose weights were trained on rooms at 0.02 m sees, at 0.005 m, a quarter of the extent per kernel. Sparse convolutions go through the facade grasppanda.ops.sparse (spconv underneath; extra spconv-cu118 and siblings).

docs.title: 3. Options
docs.text: "Route" says where the code comes from: A = adapted from a permissive repository (listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md), W = released weights loaded into a class the toolbox has, own = written for this code base earlier (see Scene encoders). "Measured fit" is the verdict of grasppanda probe on real frames, in the vocabulary of Measured combinations: runs, runs in FurthestPointSubsample when compose inserted that adapter, runs-unstable. Every option composes under all five seed-based methods; at the level runs the class of each is in the method pages and the measured page (an option whose run was runs-unstable and not repeated is not counted there yet).
