The lines losses, gradient and changed are what tells a stage that learns from one that is only wired in: a flat term, a unit without a gradient or a part that did not change is reported in every verdict and never hidden by a falling total.

fails is a combination that passed the config check and then broke. The probe says where. The config check compares what components and datasets declare; what it cannot know is whether options suit your data. An encoder named by its type instead of its preset is built with its own defaults, and compose says so:

$ grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=OACNNs -o gsnet_oacnns_bare.yaml
...
what compose did
  • backbone: OACNNs with its constructor defaults; no preset was named. Its options are the
    component's own defaults, not a recipe for table-top clouds; that is what its preset holds:
    `--set backbone=oacnns`.
...
$ grasppanda probe gsnet_oacnns_bare.yaml
...
✗ fails: at loss (iteration 1), in the backbone OACNNs: ContractError: OACNNs: cloud 0 of the batch has no voxel left after 4 of 4 down-sampling steps. With crop_odd_extent=True the sparse grid is the bounding box of the cloud and loses the last cell of an odd axis at every level, so a cloud has to span at least 16 voxels along every axis. Use a smaller grid_size, or set crop_odd_extent=False to keep every voxel.

The default grid of OA-CNNs is 2 cm, for rooms; the preset sets 5 mm. That is what a preset is for, and the probe is what tells you in a minute instead of after a queue.

A combination that fails for a reason the contracts could have known is a bug of the contract rules: it should be refused before anything is built, or run. Two such families were found by probing and are refused now, by two rules shown in Compose above: a model on a data recipe that does not serve its labels (which compose resolves for the label set of the head), and an encoder of another width under a grouper that fixes one (which compose resolves with the grouper's projected variant). If a probe shows you a third, please report it.

A probe that ends with CUDA out of memory is fails too, with a note: on a shared machine that is a statement about the device at that moment, not about the combination.

docs.title: What a probe needs
docs.text:
The dataset and the label assets of its split sample. They are small; for GraspNet-1Billion, RealSense:

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels --split sample
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness --camera realsense --split sample
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --compact-labels --split sample \
    --config economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e     # EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness --camera realsense --split sample \
    --config finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e             # FineGrasp
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --tolerance --split sample \
    --config graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --view-grasps --camera realsense --split sample \
    --config hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e                         # HGGD

The width histogram of Scale-Balanced-Grasp is the exception. It is a statistic of a whole training split, and eight frames leave bins of it empty, which its generator refuses. So a config that reads it (scale_statistic in its training dataset: every config composed from Scale-Balanced-Grasp, or with --set assigner=scale-balanced) is probed with the reference's own file, which does not depend on the split. Import it once. The import needs a config that names the file by its SHA-256, which compose writes:

SHA=$(sha256sum <reference repository>/statistic/scale_distribution.npy | cut -d' ' -f1)
grasppanda compose scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --opts data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.source=legacy_import \
           data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.reference_sha256=$SHA -o sbg_reference_histogram.yaml
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --scale-statistic --import-legacy \
    --scale-statistic-file <reference repository>/statistic/scale_distribution.npy \
    --config sbg_reference_histogram.yaml

From then on, either compose with those two --opts, or hand them to the probe:

grasppanda probe <config> --opts \
    data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.source=legacy_import \
    data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.reference_sha256=$SHA

Without it the probe of such a config says exactly this, runs the synthetic check and ends wired (exit status 3). Training on the full split does not need the import: grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --scale-statistic --config <config> builds the native histogram of that split (about 3200 frames).

Without the dataset, or without an asset, the probe says what is missing and how to build it, falls back to a wiring check on a synthetic scene and reports wired, never runs:

$ grasppanda probe gsnet_pointnet2_multi-scale.yaml --opts data.train.dataset.root=/data/not-mounted
  config      gsnet_pointnet2_multi-scale.yaml  (hash 3f3ae3d710e7)
  overrides   data.train.dataset.root=/data/not-mounted
  model       GSNet · 4,730,280 parameters
  dataset     NOT READ: the dataset is not on this machine. GraspNet-1Billion not found at /data/not-mounted. Set `root` in the dataset config, or the environment variable GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT.
  data        SYNTHETIC scene with random labels: a wiring check, not a result
  device      cuda
  note        wiring check: model.proposal.graspness_threshold was lowered so that the untrained proposal lets points through to the stages behind it.
  trained     2 of 2 iterations · 0.15 s per iteration (median, without data; data 0.00 s), measured on this machine now
  memory      peak 3.9 GiB on the GPU, this process
  losses      first → last
    loss/objectness             0.9192 → 0.831
    loss/graspness              2.883 → 1.578
    loss/view                   16.27 → 13.15
    loss/score                  1.915 → 1.383
    loss/width                  1.982 → 1.154
    loss                        23.97 → 18.1
  seeds       supervised: 1.00 → 1.00, min 1.00
  predicted   2 frame(s) · 1024, 1024 grasps

✓ wired: trained 2 iterations on a synthetic scene with random labels and predicted on 2 frame(s), with finite losses.
  Real frames were not probed; `wired` says only that the stages connect.
  (5 s)

The synthetic scene is the ray-cast table top of grasppanda demo; its labels are noise. grasppanda probe <config> --synthetic asks for that check directly, for example in a project without data. --json prints the whole report for scripts; --iters, --frames, --predict-frames, --split, --device and --workers change what is run. A count below one or a split the dataset does not have is a wrong request, not a verdict: the command says so and exits with status 2. grasppanda probe --help repeats the verdicts, the exit statuses and what a probe needs.

docs.title: 4. Train
docs.text:
grasppanda train gsnet_pointnet2_multi-scale.yaml

The composed config is an ordinary config: everything in Training and testing applies. What it is not is a tuned recipe. The optimizer, schedule, batch size and point budget are the base method's, chosen by its authors for its own stages; the header of the composed file lists what to re-tune first, and metric/real_seeds and metric/supervised_seeds in the training log are the first numbers to compare with a run of the reference config. A number from such a run has no paper to be compared with: report it as trained here, next to the reference under the same recipe, and call it experimental.

configs/experimental/ holds eight such configs. They are compose's output for the command in their header and are regenerated with the presets (python -m tools.make_combination_docs).

docs.title: Reading the measured page
docs.text:
Measured combinations is steps 2 and 3 run for a grid: every scene encoder under every seed-based method, every other stage with one stage replaced at a time, a sample of the legal sets of stages (each composed onto the method whose data recipe serves its labels), HGGD as it is and with every image-encoder preset, every post-processing preset under all six methods, every recipe preset under every method it applies to, every loss preset in one term of every kind it accepts, and a few requests that replace several slots at once. Grid probes run with --schedule constant, so that the trends of different methods compare. The explorer shows the same records per selection. Every cell is a recorded outcome; its two commands are in the measured file beside the page. Typing them repeats the experiment: the same config (hash for hash), the same parameter count, the same first losses. It does not repeat the later numbers: a cell is one run. In the tables

  • ✓ is runs; ✓ own is the method's own component (the cell composes to the shipped config, hash for hash); ✓ in Adapter ran after compose inserted that adapter; † means compose also set out_channels or in_channels to fit the method;
  • ∅ is runs-empty (it ran and predicted no grasp on either frame), ≈ (n) is runs-unstable, ✗ (n) is refused (the config check's verdict: nothing was built) and fails (n) passed the config check and broke; n points to the reason below the table;
  • below the mark of a probe: the grasps it predicted per frame and, for a record of judge 2, the range of the fall of its loss terms and the levels it did not reach; a probe that predicted no grasp on any frame is greyed;
  • the last column is the class of the component, level by level. A cell is decided at four levels from its record: composes (the config check accepts it), runs (the probe ran clean: runs or runs-empty; runs-unstable counts as not running only when a repeat of the probe was unstable too, and stays unstable, not repeated until then), learns (every loss term active in at least half of the iterations fell by at least 5 %, none flagged flat, rising or constant, every unit reached by a gradient, every part changed) and predicts (grasps on every predicted frame, scores not all the same). The last two need judge 2: a record of the first judge says not checked. The class counts the methods under which the option reached a level: universal (all five seed-based methods), most (three or four), some (two), specific (exactly one), none; an option probed under fewer methods, or with undecided cells, reads N of M probed with the rest named after it (+1 not checked). A refusal by policy (remote code) waits for your consent and is never counted as none;
  • the columns Fall per loss term and Learns, predicts of the numbers below a table say what judge 2 saw in a run and what kept it from a level; a record made before that judge says not checked. The sections Judges and Measured classes of the page define every field and every threshold, from grasppanda.combine.levels.

The tables Measured classes near the top of the page list every component under its class, one table per level: that is the short answer to "what works where". Every class is "one run, seed 0, 20 iterations, 8 frames of one scene": it counts verdicts, not accuracy.

A class is a statement about that grid: those presets, the methods' own recipes, one stage replaced at a time. specific for a head bundle means that it cannot be swapped in alone, because it needs its assigner and its labels; the table Sets of stages shows combinations in which it runs (the sets are too many to probe each: the page says how many were, and how they were picked), and Several slots at once a few requests that also replace the encoder, a loss or the recipe. A set that reads dense label grids is refused under EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp, whose recipes serve compact labels, and the reverse; the page does not hold those cells, the config check says it when you compose one. And a class says nothing about accuracy: universal at runs means "builds, trains and predicts under every method", not "is a good idea under every method".

Whether an option that runs also learns like the stage it replaces is the next level: Learns like the reference? trains the cells that run for 250 iterations and compares every loss term with the method as shipped under the same settings (on a par, worse, diverging). One run per cell, eight frames of one scene: a statement about training dynamics, still not about accuracy.

The section Passed the check, failed afterwards lists the gaps this grid met: combinations the config check accepted and a component then refused to build or run. The toolbox treats each as a bug of its contract rules. An empty list says that no cell of the grid is such a case; it is not a proof about configs outside the grid.

docs.title: Adding a preset
docs.text:
# One sentence that says what this is.
#
# Free text: where it comes from, what it is not.
#
# What must be re-tuned, and why:
# * option: value, and the reason it will have to change
model:
  backbone:
    type: MyEncoder               # a comment that travels with the line
    grid_size: 0.005

Save it as grasppanda/presets/<slot>/<name>.yaml. A registered scene encoder without a preset, a stage without a preset or a stated reason, and a component without measured cells each fail a unit test that says what to run (tests/unit/test_combine_presets.py, tests/unit/test_combine_grid.py).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: A GraspPanda config is a YAML file. It describes the whole experiment: model, data, optimisation, evaluation and runtime. No behaviour is reachable only through a command-line flag.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Every component is written as {type: Name, ...arguments}:

model:
  type: ToyDetector
  backbone: {type: ToyBackbone, out_channels: 64}
  head:     {type: ToyHead, num_angle: 12, num_depth: 4}
optimizer: {type: Adam, lr: 1e-3}
scheduler: {type: ExponentialLR, gamma: 0.95}

type names a class in the registry that owns that slot: model is resolved in DETECTORS, model.backbone in BACKBONES, optimizer in OPTIMIZERS (every torch.optim optimizer is available), and so on. List what is registered with:

grasppanda print-config --list backbones
grasppanda print-config <config> --list all      # also shows the config's custom imports

grasppanda components shows the same registries as a catalogue: each component with its contract, status, source and the shipped configs that use it, and grasppanda components <name> its options and what it can be combined with. The Components page is that catalogue; which component can replace which is in Swapping components.

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text:
The top level is a closed set. An unknown key is an error.

Key Content _base_ Parent files to inherit from. custom_imports Out-of-tree modules to import before validation. model The detector. data train, val, test: each {dataset, batch_size, num_workers, shuffle, drop_last}. optimizer, scheduler Optimisation. train epochs, amp, accumulate, grad_clip, grad_clip_mode, ema, sync_bn, scheduler_unit. evaluation interval, evaluator, variants, save_best, split, weights, num_workers. hooks Extra training hooks. runtime work_dir, run_id, device, seed, deterministic, resume, allow_config_mismatch, load_from, allow_weight_mismatch, checkpoint, log, ops.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
_base_:
  - ../_base_/default_runtime.yaml
  - ../_base_/schedules/gsnet_10e.yaml

train:
  epochs: 20        # overrides the schedule

An entry of _base_ is a path relative to the file. When there is no such file, it is the name of a shipped config, with or without .yaml: _base_/default_runtime.yaml for a building block, gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e for a whole method. This works from any directory and from an installed wheel, so a config of your own can start from a shipped one:

_base_: [gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e.yaml]   # uses both levels (rule 1)

train:
  epochs: 20

A file next to the config comes first. A base that is neither is an error reported at the file that names it (set in: <that file>).

docs.title: Merge rules
docs.text:
1. At most two levels. A config may inherit from a file that itself inherits from _base_/ building blocks. A third level is an error.
  2. Sibling bases must not disagree. If two files of one _base_ list set the same value, loading fails and names both files. There is no "last one wins" to remember.

  3. Mappings merge deeply — unless type changes. When a child sets a different type, the inherited node is replaced:

    # base:   optimizer: {type: Adam, lr: 1e-3, betas: [0.9, 0.99]}
optimizer: {type: SGD, momentum: 0.9}
# result: optimizer: {type: SGD, momentum: 0.9}     (lr and betas are dropped)

    Arguments of the old component can never leak into the new one. The dropped keys are printed. 4. _delete_: true replaces a mapping that has no type. 5. Lists replace wholesale.

docs.title: Interpolation
docs.text:
${path.to.value} refers to another value. It is resolved after all merging and all overrides, so changing the source changes every reference:

runtime:
  work_dir: work_dirs/${config_name}/seed${runtime.seed}

${config_name} is the file name of the config without its extension.

docs.title: Command-line overrides
docs.text:
grasppanda print-config <config> --opts train.epochs=20 optimizer.lr=3e-4 hooks.0.interval=5
  • Values are parsed as YAML, so true, null, 1e-3 and [1, 2] mean what they mean in a file.
  • Overrides go through exactly the same validation as file contents.
  • Overriding type follows merge rule 3.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Validation runs before any dataset is opened or any module is built, and reports every problem at once.

Layer Checks Example message Schema Top-level and fixed-structure keys and their types. unknown top-level key 'runtim'. Did you mean 'runtime'? Component signatures Each {type: X} node against X.__init__: the name exists in the right registry, every key is a parameter, required parameters are present, value types match. ToyHead has no parameter 'num_angles'. Did you mean 'num_angle'? Cross-field rules Contracts between components and between sections. ToyDepthGrouper emits features with axes ('seed', 'depth', 'channel'), but ToyHead expects ('seed', 'channel'). 
grasppanda print-config <config> --check                # validate, print a summary
grasppanda print-config <config> --for train --check    # also require what `train` needs
grasppanda print-config <config> --no-check             # print a broken config to debug it

docs.title: Out-of-tree components
docs.text:
custom_imports:
  - my_package.my_heads          # an importable module
  - ../my_components.py          # or a file, relative to this config

A .py path is loaded as a standalone module, so a single-file plugin next to its config works without installation. See Add a component.

docs.title: What a run records
docs.text: config.resolved.yaml (everything above, expanded, defaults written out), the original files and overrides, the git commit and diff, a code archive and the environment. The config hash printed by --check identifies the experiment; it ignores runtime.work_dir, runtime.run_id, runtime.resume and runtime.allow_config_mismatch, so that moving, naming or resuming a run does not change its identity. What each key does is described in Training and testing.

docs.title: Notes on YAML
docs.text:
• lr: 1e-3 is a number here. (Plain PyYAML reads it as a string.)
  • Duplicate keys in one mapping are an error rather than "last one wins".

docs.title: Cross-dataset evaluation
docs.text: How a model trained on GraspNet-1Billion is tested on GraspClutter6D, what such a comparison keeps fixed, and what has been measured so far. The facts about the two datasets are in Dataset preparation.

docs.title: One command
docs.text:
grasppanda test gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_10e --weights <checkpoint>
Method Transfer config Weights it takes GSNet gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_10e gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e EconomicGrasp economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_10e economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e EconomicGrasp economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-kinect-to-gc6d-d435_10e economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-kinect_10e GraspNet-baseline graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_18e graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e Scale-Balanced-Grasp scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_18e sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e HGGD hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_15e hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e

Author checkpoints are converted first, exactly as for GraspNet-1Billion (the commands are in each configs/<method>/README.md). Useful overrides:

--opts data.test.dataset.split=test_mini           # 24 scenes, 312 frames: minutes, a check only
--opts data.test.dataset.camera=zivid              # realsense-d415 | realsense-d435 | azure-kinect | zivid
--opts evaluation.num_workers=8                    # processes of the evaluator

The whole test split is 235 scenes × 13 views = 3 055 frames per camera. No derived asset is needed to test.

docs.title: Why a config and not a list of overrides
docs.text:
A transfer config inherits the method's GraspNet-1Billion config and replaces two nodes, data.test and evaluation.evaluator:

_base_:
  - gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e.yaml

data:
  test:
    dataset:
      type: GraspClutter6D
      camera: realsense-d435
      split: test
      load_labels: false
      preprocess:
        - {type: DepthToCloud}
        - {type: SegmentationRectWorkspace, margin: 0.1}
      transforms: ${data.val.dataset.transforms}
      keep_full_points: true
      seed: 0

evaluation:
  evaluator: {type: GraspClutter6DEvaluator}
  • What the weights depend on cannot drift. The model, the point count, the input features and both post-processing variants are not restated; they are the inherited values, and transforms is an interpolation of the recipe's own evaluation transforms. A unit test compares every other section of each transfer config with its parent.
  • The same change as --opts would be about ten overrides including two lists, because a changed type replaces a node and all its arguments must be given again. That is easy to get wrong and leaves no name to quote in a result table.
  • The config has a name, a hash in every result record, and is validated by grasppanda print-config --check in the test suite.

A transfer config is a test config. Its evaluator cannot score the inherited GraspNet-1Billion validation loader, so it sets evaluation.interval: 0; to train, use the config it inherits from.

docs.title: What changes with the dataset, and what must not
docs.text:
In the transfer config Why Frames changes: GraspClutter6D, realsense-d435, test The benchmark. The D435 is the camera of the paper's table and the sensor model of GraspNet-1Billion's realsense. Intrinsics, depth scale changes, read per image Nothing in a model or a transform holds a camera constant; DepthToCloud and HGGD read the calibration of the frame. Workspace crop changes to SegmentationRectWorkspace (margin 0.1) The crop of the official tool, and of the authors' released baseline code. GraspNet-1Billion's crop (SegmentationBoxWorkspace) is a box in a table frame that this dataset does not have; see the measured effect below. HGGD has no crop on either dataset. Evaluator changes to GraspClutter6DEvaluator Width clip 0.14 m, foreground filter, no table: the protocol of the benchmark. Model, including every length fixed Voxel size (5 mm), ball-query and cylinder radii, depth bins and the 300 views are the units the weights were trained in. Gripper of the model (0.10 m) fixed It bounds the labels the model learnt from and clamps its decoded widths. See "The gripper" below. Points per cloud (15 000 / 20 000 / 25 600), input features fixed Part of the recipe; fewer or more points change the density the encoder was trained on. HGGD network image (640 × 360) fixed The 1920 × 1080 image is reduced by 3 instead of 2; the focal length of the network image comes out nearly the same (465 to 472 px against 464 px). Post-processing (raw, cd) fixed The collision filter of each reference, with its own voxel size, approach distance and threshold. Point-sampling seed fixed (0) The same points every run.

What shifts without being a setting, and is therefore not corrected:

  • Distance. Objects are 0.70 m from the D435 in the median (0.36 to 1.04 m), against 0.44 m (0.31 to 0.52 m) in GraspNet-1Billion. The image is larger, so a pixel covers about the same length on an object (0.50 mm against 0.47 mm); how much noisier the depth is at that distance was not measured. No depth range is clipped on either dataset.
  • Extent and density. The reference crop here spans 0.91 × 0.57 × 0.81 m, about twice that of GraspNet-1Billion in each direction (0.48 × 0.35 × 0.26 m), and a scene holds 14.5 object instances instead of 9.0. With the same point budget an object gets roughly half the points.
  • Objects. All 68 test objects are unseen, also by a model trained on GraspClutter6D.

docs.title: The gripper
docs.text: The benchmark gripper opens to 0.14 m and the evaluator clips widths there. A model trained on GraspNet-1Billion was supervised with grasps up to 0.10 m and clamps what it decodes to 0.10 m. On the 68 test objects, 38 % of the valid label grasps are wider than 0.10 m (4 % are wider than 0.14 m); for 18 objects more than half are, for 3 objects more than 90 %. This part of the transfer gap is structural. --opts model.gripper.max_width=0.14 only moves the clamp of the decoder (which multiplies the regressed width by 1.2); it is a controlled variant, measured below, not the default.

docs.title: Subset results
docs.text:
Subset numbers

Everything in this section was measured on test_mini: 24 of the 235 test scenes, 312 frames per camera. These are not benchmark results and do not enter the model zoo. Per-scene AP ranges from below 1 to above 60 for one model, so the mean over 24 scenes has a scene-clustered standard error of about 3 AP (given per row). The full-split commands are at the end of this page.

AP / AP0.8 / AP0.4 in percent, RealSense D435, protocol graspclutter6d-sv-v1, 312 of 312 frames scored. raw: predictions as emitted; cd: with the reference's model-free collision filter. Provenance of the weights: author is the authors' released GraspNet-1Billion RealSense checkpoint, converted; local is a checkpoint the maintainers trained with the upstream code on their own variant of the graspness labels (epoch 18), used because no usable author checkpoint of GSNet is at hand.

Method Weights Input crop raw cd SE of AP (raw / cd) Reported, whole test split GraspNet-baseline author ground-truth rectangle 8.71 / 10.48 / 7.01 17.39 / 20.99 / 13.03 1.5 / 2.7 17.95 / 21.54 / 13.53 Scale-Balanced-Grasp author ground-truth rectangle 20.92 / 25.50 / 15.89 23.03 / 27.86 / 17.61 2.8 / 3.2 22.69 / 27.57 / 16.95 EconomicGrasp author ground-truth rectangle 22.38 / 27.45 / 16.62 23.10 / 28.29 / 17.00 3.3 / 3.4 21.67 / 26.62 / 15.90 GSNet local ground-truth rectangle 27.62 / 33.67 / 21.50 28.74 / 35.11 / 22.12 3.7 / 3.9 none published HGGD author none (gt_assisted: none) 15.40 / 19.67 / 8.84 16.67 / 21.30 / 9.39 2.0 / 2.2 none published

Reported is Table IX of the GraspClutter6D paper (arXiv 2504.06866 v3): models trained on GraspNet-1Billion, tested on the 235 test scenes with the D435, "workspace-cropped inputs", collision filter not stated. HGGD is not like-for-like with the other rows: it reads the whole image and no ground truth shapes its input.

docs.title: Against the reported numbers
docs.text:
• GraspNet-baseline: the reported number is reproduced by cd and not by raw. cd is 0.56 AP below the reported value (0.2 standard errors), and AP0.8 and AP0.4 agree as closely; raw is 9.2 AP below (6 standard errors). The reference test script filters collisions by default, and the one baseline whose code the GraspClutter6D authors released (Contact-GraspNet) is run with the same filter values (voxel 0.01 m, approach 0.05 m, threshold 0.01 m). The evidence says that number was produced with the collision filter.
  • Scale-Balanced-Grasp and EconomicGrasp: consistent, but the subset cannot say which variant was reported. raw and cd differ by 0.7 to 2.1 AP, both lie within 0.6 standard errors of the reported value, and the subset resolves about 3 AP.
  • What cannot be checked from here: which checkpoints the authors evaluated (the GraspNet-1Billion column of their table equals the published numbers of Scale-Balanced-Grasp and EconomicGrasp to two decimals, 44.85 and 51.63, which suggests the public RealSense weights); their point sampling; and their input code for three of the four methods, which is not public.
  • GSNet and HGGD have no published GraspClutter6D number. The GSNet row uses a local checkpoint (on 120 frames of GraspNet-1Billion test_seen it scores 68 / 71 AP raw / cd, a subset number as well), so it says how this checkpoint transfers, not how the published model does.

docs.title: Controlled variants on the same 312 frames
docs.text:
Each row changes one thing. The last column is the change of raw AP against the first row of the method, with the standard error of the per-scene differences: rows of one method are scored on the same frames, so their difference is resolved far better than the 3 AP of a single number.

Method Variant raw AP cd AP Change of raw GraspNet-baseline as above 8.71 17.39 GraspNet-1Billion crop 8.91 18.76 +0.2 (cd: +1.4 ± 0.4) Scale-Balanced-Grasp as above 20.92 23.03 GraspNet-1Billion crop 24.04 26.88 +3.1 ± 0.9 EconomicGrasp as above 22.38 23.10 GraspNet-1Billion crop 23.20 23.84 +0.8 ± 0.6 camera realsense-d415 25.30 25.70 +2.9 ± 1.7 camera zivid 29.76 30.81 +7.4 ± 1.8 Kinect weights (...g1b-kinect-to-gc6d-d435...) on the D435 21.52 22.10 −0.9 ± 0.9 Kinect weights on azure-kinect 15.72 16.31 −5.8 ± 2.0 against the row above GSNet as above 27.62 28.74 GraspNet-1Billion crop 28.23 29.29 +0.6 ± 0.4 model.gripper.max_width=0.14 28.38 29.47 +0.8 ± 0.2

"GraspNet-1Billion crop" is the crop the weights were trained with, applied in the world frame of the rig:

--opts "data.test.dataset.preprocess.1={type: SegmentationBoxWorkspace, margin: 0.02, invalid_depth_foreground: include}"
  • The crop matters for some methods and not for others. The official crop keeps a wide margin of table and background: on view 0 of the subset scenes 30 % of its points are on objects, against 46 % for the box. Scale-Balanced-Grasp gains 3.1 AP from the tighter box and GraspNet-baseline 1.4 AP with the collision filter; for EconomicGrasp and GSNet the change is within its error. A table that mixes crops would rank methods by their input.
  • The sensor moves the result as much as the choice of method. The same EconomicGrasp weights score 22.4 AP on the D435 and 29.8 on the Zivid.
  • The sensor a model was trained on does not carry over by name. The Kinect weights score 21.5 AP on the D435 and 15.7 on the Azure Kinect of this dataset, whose 3840 × 2160 frames give a crop of 2.4 million points of which a quarter are on objects. Why that pairing is the weakest was not investigated.
  • The width clamp costs GSNet 0.8 AP. Letting the decoder open to 0.14 m raises raw from 27.62 to 28.38. The larger part of the gripper mismatch is in what the model learnt, which no test-time setting changes.
  • The collision filter is worth 8.7 ± 1.4 AP for GraspNet-baseline and 0.7 to 2.1 AP for the other four methods.
  • The subset cannot rank Scale-Balanced-Grasp against EconomicGrasp (−1.5 ± 1.3 AP raw; the paper has Scale-Balanced-Grasp 1.0 AP ahead). The GSNet checkpoint is ahead of EconomicGrasp by 5.2 ± 1.4 AP, with the caveat on its provenance above.

docs.title: The whole test split
docs.text:
Run so far for five methods, 3 055 of 3 055 frames scored each: GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp and HGGD with the authors' converted checkpoints (author-ckpt), and GSNet with the model trained from scratch by this toolbox (reproduced; its weights are not published yet). AP / AP0.8 / AP0.4 in percent, RealSense D435; the rows, with the reported numbers beside them, stand in the model zoo and the result records in configs/<method>/records/.

Method Weights Input crop raw cd Reported GraspNet-baseline author-ckpt ground-truth rectangle 8.69 / 10.35 / 6.96 17.14 / 20.60 / 12.86 17.95 / 21.54 / 13.53 Scale-Balanced-Grasp author-ckpt ground-truth rectangle 21.77 / 26.49 / 16.46 22.71 / 27.61 / 17.01 22.69 / 27.57 / 16.95 EconomicGrasp author-ckpt ground-truth rectangle 21.69 / 26.64 / 15.79 22.25 / 27.30 / 16.06 21.67 / 26.62 / 15.90 GSNet reproduced ground-truth rectangle 25.58 / 31.38 / 19.42 26.87 / 33.00 / 20.04 none published HGGD author-ckpt none (gt_assisted: none) 14.25 / 17.41 / 9.23 14.56 / 17.79 / 9.33 none published

HGGD is not like-for-like with the other rows: it reads the whole image, and its cd is its own filter followed by NMS. The GSNet row is one training run with one seed; its weights are another model than the local checkpoint of the subset table above.

What the whole split adds to the subset: the reported value lies 0.81 AP above cd and 9.26 above raw for GraspNet-baseline, 0.02 AP below cd and 0.92 above raw for Scale-Balanced-Grasp, and 0.02 AP below raw and 0.58 below cd for EconomicGrasp. So the reported table is closest to the filtered run for two methods and to the unfiltered run for the third. The paper does not state the collision filter, and whether it was applied to some methods and not to others was not investigated. The controlled variants above (crops, cameras, Kinect weights, gripper width) exist for the subset only.

A run took 8 to 12 minutes per method on the development machine (one GPU, four evaluator processes, shared with other jobs):

for CONFIG in \
    economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_10e \
    graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_18e \
    scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_18e \
    hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_15e \
    gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense-to-gc6d-d435_10e
do
    grasppanda test $CONFIG --weights <the converted checkpoint of that method> \
        --opts evaluation.num_workers=8
done

A result of such a run is an author-ckpt number of the transfer config, stamped with the protocol, the split, the camera, the variant and gt_assisted. It enters the zoo with its result records:

python -m tools.record_result <work directory of the run> --method <directory below configs/>

checks that every frame was scored by clean code with hashed weights, copies the records to configs/<method>/records/ and prints the rows for the method's metafile.yaml.

docs.title: Checking a run against the official tool
docs.text:
grasppanda test writes predictions/<variant>/scene_NNNN/<camera>/<view>.npy. The official tool names files by image id. To score a dump with graspclutter6dAPI, link it into that layout:

from grasppanda.datasets.graspclutter6d import GraspClutter6D
from grasppanda.evaluation.graspclutter6d import export_official_layout
from grasppanda.utils.paths import dataset_root

keys = GraspClutter6D.load_manifest(dataset_root("graspclutter6d")).keys("test", "realsense-d435")
export_official_layout("<run>/predictions/raw", "official_dump", keys)
# then: GraspClutter6DEval(root, "realsense-d435", split="test").eval_all("official_dump")

The other way round, evaluation.evaluator: {type: GraspClutter6DEvaluator, layout: official} scores a dump that was written for the official tool. One difference is deliberate: the official tool scores a frame without a file as zero, GraspPanda reports it as missing and gives no headline number for an incomplete run.

docs.title: Training on GraspClutter6D
docs.text:
gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e and economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e carry the GraspNet-1Billion recipe over and change the gripper to 0.14 m. They are this toolbox's choice, not a reproduction: no GSNet or EconomicGrasp recipe for this dataset has been published. Each has run for 20 iterations on one scene (the loss fell from 20.1 to 1.9 and from 28.6 to 2.5); no model has been trained. The assets and their cost are listed in Dataset preparation.

grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --labels
grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --graspness --camera realsense-d435
grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --compact-labels --config economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e
grasppanda train gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e
grasppanda train economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e

docs.title: Dataset preparation
docs.text:
GraspPanda reads two benchmarks: GraspNet-1Billion and GraspClutter6D. Both are read in place, and everything derived from them is built by one command, grasppanda prepare.

  • Raw datasets are never modified. Nothing is written into a dataset tree.
  • Derived labels (the grasp-label store, point-wise graspness and the label assets of individual methods) live in a separate asset store under $GRASPPANDA_CACHE. Each asset records its generator, its parameters and the preprocessing it assumes, and is found by a hash of those. A config that asks for other parameters asks for another asset; it can never read misaligned labels.
  • Splits are explicit sets of (scene, camera, frame). Validation data is a scene-level hold-out from the training scenes, never a test split.

docs.title: Where things are looked for
docs.text: What Resolved from, in this order GraspNet-1Billion root in the dataset config, $GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT, $GRASPPANDA_DATA/graspnet1b, ./data/graspnet1b GraspClutter6D root in the dataset config, $GRASPPANDA_GRASPCLUTTER6D_ROOT, $GRASPPANDA_DATA/graspclutter6d, ./data/graspclutter6d Derived assets $GRASPPANDA_CACHE

docs.title: grasppanda prepare
docs.text:
grasppanda prepare <dataset> --check                 # what the tree and the assets lack
grasppanda prepare <dataset> --labels                # dense grasp labels as a memory-mapped store
grasppanda prepare <dataset> --graspness --camera C  # point-wise graspness maps
grasppanda prepare <dataset> --compact-labels --config <config with compact_labels>
grasppanda prepare <dataset> --tolerance      --config <config with tolerance>
grasppanda prepare <dataset> --view-grasps --camera C --config <config with view_grasps>
grasppanda prepare <dataset> --scale-statistic --config <config with scale_statistic>

Every action reads a dataset config: the shipped base config of the dataset and camera, or the one named with --config. What is built is exactly what that config later asks for. --split and --scenes 5,9,13 restrict the scenes; generation is resumable and finished shards are skipped. Evaluation needs none of these assets: a test loader reads depth (and, for the reference workspace crop, the segmentation) only.

Asset Flag Read by Depends on the camera Grasp-label store --labels every training recipe, and every other generator no Point-wise graspness --graspness GSNet, EconomicGrasp yes, and on the preprocessing Compact grasp labels --compact-labels EconomicGrasp no Grasp tolerance --tolerance GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp no Per-view grasps --view-grasps HGGD yes Scale statistic --scale-statistic Scale-Balanced-Grasp yes

docs.title: GraspNet-1Billion
docs.text:
The official download, 190 scenes with 256 frames per scene and camera:

scenes/scene_XXXX/object_id_list.txt
scenes/scene_XXXX/{realsense,kinect}/{rgb,depth,label}/NNNN.png
scenes/scene_XXXX/{realsense,kinect}/meta/NNNN.mat          intrinsics, depth factor, poses
scenes/scene_XXXX/{realsense,kinect}/annotations/NNNN.xml   poses, four decimals
scenes/scene_XXXX/{realsense,kinect}/{camera_poses,cam0_wrt_table}.npy
grasp_label/NNN_labels.npz
collision_label/scene_XXXX/collision_labels.npz
models/NNN/nontextured.ply,  dex_models/NNN.pkl

Splits (shipped in grasppanda/datasets/splits/graspnet1b.yaml): train (scenes 0 to 99), test_seen (100 to 129), test_similar (130 to 159), test_novel (160 to 189), test (their union), train_dev / val_dev (90 and 10 training scenes) and sample.

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --check
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness --camera realsense

The method-specific assets are listed with their commands in each method's configs/<method>/README.md.

docs.title: GraspClutter6D
docs.text:
GraspClutter6D (RA-L 2025, arXiv 2504.06866, data licence CC BY-SA 4.0) holds 1 000 scenes in BOP layout. Its grasp labels have the format of GraspNet-1Billion, which is why every label generator of this toolbox runs on it unchanged. Download and unpack it as its README says; the reader needs

split_info/grasp_{train,test}_scene_ids.json    the grasp splits (authoritative)
split_info/obj_ids_per_scene.json
scenes/<scene:06d>/{rgb,depth,label}/<image:06d>.png
scenes/<scene:06d>/{mask,mask_visib}/<image:06d>_<instance:06d>.png
scenes/<scene:06d>/scene_camera.json    per image: cam_K, depth_scale, cam_{R,t}_w2c
scenes/<scene:06d>/scene_gt.json        per image and instance: cam_{R,t}_m2c, obj_id
grasp_label/obj_<object:06d>_labels.npz
collision_label/<scene:06d>.npz         one array per instance, in scene_gt order
models_m/obj_<object:06d>.ply           object models in metres
dex_models/obj_<object:06d>.pkl         force-closure data of the evaluator

grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --check counts all of this for the 648 scenes of the grasp splits and then reports the derived assets of every camera.

docs.title: Cameras
docs.text:
A scene has 13 annotated views, and every view was taken by four cameras. All 52 images of a scene share the directories; the camera is encoded in the image id, image = 4 * view + c. A SampleKey holds the camera name and the view (0 to 12).

Camera (camera:) c Image Raw depth unit Focal length (px) Base config realsense-d415 1 1920 × 1080 1 mm 1404 or 1429 graspclutter6d_d415.yaml realsense-d435 2 1920 × 1080 1 mm 1394 or 1415 graspclutter6d_d435.yaml azure-kinect 3 3840 × 2160 0.1 mm 1996 or 2112 graspclutter6d_kinect.yaml zivid 4 1920 × 1200 0.1 mm 2790 graspclutter6d_zivid.yaml

Intrinsics and depth scale are read per image from scene_camera.json. Three of the cameras have two calibrations in the grasp splits (in the scenes inspected, view 0 has one and views 1 to 12 the other), so one constant camera matrix per camera, as GraspNet-1Billion pipelines often hard-code, would be wrong here. The depth scale was the same on all 8 424 images of each camera. The paper reports its benchmark on the RealSense D435.

docs.title: Splits
docs.text:
Split Scenes Frames per camera Object models Source train 413 5 369 123 (ids 69 to 198) split_info/grasp_train_scene_ids.json test 235 3 055 68 (ids 1 to 68) split_info/grasp_test_scene_ids.json all 648 8 424 191 union of the two sample 1 (scene 5) 13 6 first training scene, for smoke tests test_mini 24 312 66 of the 68 every tenth test scene by rank; shipped val_dev 41 533 110 of the 123 every tenth training scene by rank; shipped train_dev 372 4 836 123 train without val_dev
  • The test objects are all unseen. No object model occurs in both splits: the benchmark has no "seen" part, unlike GraspNet-1Billion.
  • The three subsets are fixed scene lists in grasppanda/datasets/splits/graspclutter6d.yaml. They exist only when the split files of the tree contain them. test_mini is for quick checks; a number measured on it is a subset number, not a benchmark result. Per-scene AP varies widely on this dataset (from below 1 to above 60 for one model), so the mean over 24 scenes carries a standard error of about 3 AP.
  • All objects of val_dev are training objects, so it measures fit to new arrangements, not to new objects.
  • The other 352 scenes of the dataset are in neither grasp split and are not read.
  • The paper states 132 training objects. The split files give 123: object ids 112 to 117, 191, 199 and 200 occur in no scene of either grasp split.

docs.title: What a frame holds
docs.text:
• Scenes are denser than in GraspNet-1Billion: 14.5 object instances per scene on average (5 to 20), and in 84 % of the scenes at least one object model occurs more than once. The label image stores object ids and cannot tell two copies apart, so the reader builds the instance map from the per-instance visibility masks (mask_visib), and grasp labels, collision labels and compact labels are keyed by instance (position in scene_gt.json), not by object id.
  • The instance list and its order are the same for all 52 images of a scene (checked on all 648 scenes). The reader and the evaluator refuse a frame for which that fails.
  • Lengths in the JSON files are millimetres; poses leave the reader in metres.
  • cam_R_w2c / cam_t_w2c hold the camera pose in the world frame (camera to world), contrary to what the names say. The world frame is fixed to the rig, not to the table: bounds of a TableBoxWorkspace are world coordinates here.
  • scene_camera.json also has entries -4 to 0; they have no image and are ignored.

docs.title: Derived assets
docs.text:
Built on three training scenes (5, 9 and 13; 11 object models, 49 instances) on the development machine while it was heavily loaded, so the times are upper bounds:

Asset Command (add --scenes 5,9,13 for the three scenes) Three scenes Whole train split, extrapolated Grasp-label store grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --labels 2.8 GB about 55 GB (236 MB per object model, 62 MB per scene) Graspness, one camera ... --graspness --camera realsense-d435 2.2 MB, 3 min with 3 workers about 0.3 GB, 5 h with 4 workers Compact labels ... --compact-labels --config economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e 24 MB, 11 s about 3 GB, 25 min Tolerance ... --tolerance --config _base_/datasets/graspclutter6d_d435_tolerance.yaml 332 MB, 1 min with 4 workers about 4 GB, 10 min Per-view grasps, one camera ... --view-grasps --camera realsense-d435 --config _base_/datasets/graspclutter6d_d435_hggd.yaml 96 kB, 1 min with 3 workers about 15 MB, 1.5 h with 4 workers

The whole-split figures are extrapolations from the three scenes, not measurements. The label store is the large one; only training reads it. The evaluator keeps a cache of its own, extracted from dex_models/ and models_m/ on first use: about 7 MB per object model, 0.5 GB for the test objects.

Two facts measured on those scenes that matter for training:

  • Only 9.6 % of the annotated grasp points keep a collision-free grasp of friction ≤ 0.4 (10 401 of 108 094); on GraspNet-1Billion 39 % do. The scenes are far more cluttered, so EconomicGrasp's compact labels supervise far fewer seeds per frame.
  • The per-view labels of HGGD come to 17 to 67 per frame (GraspNet-1Billion scene 0: 59), from 471 to 1 964 candidate grasps per scene.

docs.title: Dataset configs
docs.text:
Config (configs/_base_/datasets/) Recipe carried over from Cloud Assets it reads for training graspclutter6d_{d415,d435,kinect,zivid}.yaml Graspness (GSNet) 15 000 points, official workspace crop label store, graspness graspclutter6d_d435_tolerance.yaml GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp 20 000 points, official workspace crop label store, tolerance graspclutter6d_d435_hggd.yaml HGGD colour and depth images, 25 600 points, no crop per-view grasps EconomicGrasp: configs/economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e.yaml EconomicGrasp 20 000 points, official workspace crop compact labels, graspness

These carry the GraspNet-1Billion recipe of each method family over and change only what the dataset fixes. None reproduces a published GraspClutter6D training recipe: none exists for the ported methods. HGGD's network image is 640 × 360, and the detector takes any sensor image that is an integer multiple of it: the D415, D435 (×3) and Azure Kinect (×6) images fit, the Zivid images (1920 × 1200) do not.

docs.title: What differs between the two benchmarks
docs.text:
Measured values are medians over 20 test frames of GraspNet-1Billion (two frames of every ninth test scene, RealSense unless a camera is named) and over 104 test frames of GraspClutter6D (all 13 views of every third test_mini scene).

GraspNet-1Billion GraspClutter6D Scenes, frames 190 scenes × 256 frames per camera 648 scenes in the grasp splits × 13 views per camera Cameras realsense (D435), kinect (Azure Kinect), one directory each D415, D435, Azure Kinect, Zivid, interleaved by image id Image 1280 × 720 1920 × 1080, 3840 × 2160 (Kinect), 1920 × 1200 (Zivid) Intrinsics one calibration per camera per image; two calibrations for three of the cameras Raw depth unit 1 mm 1 mm (RealSense), 0.1 mm (Azure Kinect, Zivid); per image Camera to objects 0.44 m (0.31 to 0.52) 0.70 m (0.36 to 1.04) on the D435; the paper states 0.31 to 1.37 m over all cameras Size of a pixel on the objects 0.47 mm (RealSense), 0.74 mm (Kinect) 0.50 mm (D435), 0.47 (D415), 0.36 (Kinect), 0.26 (Zivid) Object ids 0 to 87; the segmentation stores id + 1 1 to 200; the segmentation stores the id Instances an object occurs once per scene repeated objects; instances from mask_visib Label files grasp_label/NNN_labels.npz, collision_label/scene_XXXX/collision_labels.npz grasp_label/obj_NNNNNN_labels.npz, collision_label/NNNNNN.npz Label grid 300 views × 12 angles × 4 depths the same Label widths gripper of 0.10 m up to 0.15 m; gripper of 0.14 m Object poses meta/*.mat or annotations/*.xml scene_gt.json (millimetres) Table frame cam0_wrt_table.npy, z up, origin on the table the rig's world frame; the table is not at z = 0 Reference workspace crop 3-D box around the ground-truth segmentation, 2 cm margin (SegmentationBoxWorkspace) image rectangle around the ground-truth segmentation, 10 % margin (SegmentationRectWorkspace) Cloud in that crop 554 000 points, 0.48 × 0.35 × 0.26 m, 39 % on objects 908 000 points, 0.91 × 0.57 × 0.81 m, 32 % on objects (D435) Splits train / seen / similar / novel train / test, disjoint objects Evaluator GraspNet1BEvaluator, protocol graspnet1b-sv-v1 GraspClutter6DEvaluator, protocol graspclutter6d-sv-v1 Ranks and frictions top 50; μ = 0.2, 0.4, …, 1.2 the same Width clip 0.10 m 0.14 m Foreground filter none grasps 5 cm or more from every object model are dropped before NMS Collision scene object models and a synthetic table object models only

Both reference crops are derived from the ground-truth segmentation, at test time too. Results on them are stamped gt_assisted: [workspace].

The evaluator constants are those of the official tools (graspnetAPI 1.2.x and graspclutter6dAPI at ddb2ee7). For GraspClutter6D the equality is checked stage by stage on label-derived grasps for all four cameras and on the dumps that grasppanda test wrote for several detectors (tests/integration/test_eval_clutter_parity.py). How a model trained on one benchmark is tested on the other is the subject of Cross-dataset evaluation.

docs.title: Inference and visualisation
docs.text:
Four tools take a trained detector off the benchmark:

Tool What it does grasppanda demo grasps on one frame, as numbers, a picture and an animation grasppanda explore the same in a browser page: pick a method and a weights file, run it on the example scene or on your depth image GraspInferencer the same from Python: a depth image or a point cloud in, a GraspGroup out grasppanda analyze says where the AP of an evaluation comes from, and how two evaluations differ

All command output on this page was produced by the commands shown, on the development machine (one RTX A6000, shared). Paths are as printed.

You bring the weights

The model zoo has no weights to download yet: the one model trained with GraspPanda so far (GSNet) is not published, and the checkpoints the authors of the methods released are under their own, mostly non-commercial, licences. No grasp checkpoint is downloaded for you (only an image-encoder preset with pretrained: true fetches backbone weights, through its library, and says so). You download an author checkpoint yourself, convert it once with tools/convert_checkpoint.py, and pass the result with --weights. Each method's page walks through it in five minutes, with the file, its licence, the commands and what they printed when they were measured: GSNet, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, HGGD.

docs.title: Without downloading anything
docs.text:
The example project trains a toy detector on a CPU in about a second. It predicts nothing useful, but it goes through every step a real method goes through, so it tells you that your installation works:

grasppanda train projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml --opts runtime.run_id=toy
grasppanda demo  projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml \
    --weights work_dirs/toy_train/toy/checkpoints/best.pth --example

--example is a synthetic table-top scene that ships with the package: six geometric primitives on a table, ray-cast into a 1280 x 720 depth image in millimetres, a colour image, the camera matrix and an object mask. It is computed from formulas, so it needs no dataset and carries no dataset licence. It is not a camera image: surfaces are perfectly smooth and there is no noise, no missing depth and no reflection.

docs.title: With a real method
docs.text:
Take GraspNet-baseline: it needs no sparse-convolution library and runs on a CPU. Get checkpoint-rs.tar from the link in its page (non-commercial research licence), then:

python -m tools.convert_checkpoint checkpoint-rs.tar baseline_realsense.pth \
    --source-format graspnet-baseline --camera realsense
grasppanda demo graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --weights baseline_realsense.pth --example --collision-filter

ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ  GraspPanda 0.1.0  ·  6-DoF grasp detection in clutter

  model     GraspNetBaseline on cuda, reads points
  pipeline  data.test: DepthToCloud() -> SegmentationBoxWorkspace(margin=0.02, invalid_depth_foreground='include') -> RandomSample(num_points=20000)
  variants  raw (no post-processing), cd (ModelFreeCollisionFilter)
  input     synthetic example scene: 1280 x 720, 6 primitives on a table, no sensor noise (not a camera image); workspace from the scene's own object mask

wrote  work_dirs/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e/demo/grasps.npy  (285, 17) float32, GraspNet layout, best first
       work_dirs/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e/demo/grasps.png  the cloud and the 30 best grasps, red (lowest shown) to green
       work_dirs/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e/demo/grasps.gif  24 frames swinging around the scene
       work_dirs/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e/demo/example  the scene as files: depth.png, rgb.png, mask.png, intrinsics.txt

What the lines say:

  • pipeline is the test pipeline of the config, step by step. The demo runs exactly these steps on the input; it has no preprocessing of its own.
  • cloud: the workspace crop left 316,254 points and the model was given 20,000 of them.
  • grasps: how many the model emitted, and how many the collision filter kept. The time is that of the first call, which includes loading GPU kernels; later calls are faster. On the CPU of the same machine (--device cpu) this call took 1.0 s.
  • The picture draws the 30 best grasps (--top-k) as wire-frame grippers, coloured by score rank. --show opens the same scene in an interactive Open3D window if you have a display and pip install -e ".[vis]".

What the result does not say: how good the method is. The scene is synthetic and outside the training distribution of every model here; whether a grasp would hold is not checked. For numbers, see Training and testing and Reading an analysis.

docs.title: The five methods
docs.text:
Every shipped method runs through the same command. What differs is what each reads and how its authors' checkpoint is converted:

Method Config Reads --source-format Needs GraspNet-baseline graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e points graspnet-baseline nothing extra Scale-Balanced-Grasp scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e points scale-balanced-grasp nothing extra HGGD hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e (or -kinect_) colour and depth images, intrinsics, points hggd a colour image GSNet gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e points graspness-unofficial an spconv extra EconomicGrasp economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e (or -kinect_) points economicgrasp an spconv extra

All five were run with --example --collision-filter and on a GraspNet-1Billion frame while this page was written. Weights for a RealSense config were trained on RealSense D435 images, weights for a Kinect config on Azure Kinect images.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A depth image: single-channel, 16-bit PNG or TIFF (or a .npy). An integer image is read as millimetres, a float image as metres; --depth-scale N says otherwise (N depth units per metre).
  • The intrinsics of the depth camera in pixels: --intrinsics fx,fy,cx,cy, or a file holding those four numbers or the 3 x 3 camera matrix. They must be the intrinsics of the resolution the image has.
  • For HGGD, the colour image registered to the depth image, pixel for pixel (--rgb). Point-cloud methods ignore it, except to colour the picture.
grasppanda demo graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --weights baseline_realsense.pth --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8 --collision-filter --out work_dirs/camera_baseline

  input     camera/depth.png: 1280 x 720 uint16, read as millimetres
  cloud     20,000 points to the model, sampled from 445,990 in the workspace
  grasps    942 predicted in 3.51 s (first call, includes warm-up); 240 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter

(The files here are the example scene, written to disk by --example. They stand in for a camera so that the command can be shown with its output.)

docs.title: The workspace matters
docs.text:
The point-cloud methods were trained and tested on clouds cropped to the objects: the GraspNet-1Billion pipelines crop to a box around the ground-truth segmentation, at test time too (which is why their results are stamped gt_assisted: [workspace]). Your camera has no ground truth. The inferencer does not pretend otherwise; it does what the input allows and says what it did:

You pass What happens --workspace XMIN YMIN ZMIN XMAX YMAX ZMAX only points inside this box of the camera frame are kept (metres; x right, y down, z forward) --mask FILE (object pixels non-zero, from any segmentation) and --table-from-camera FILE the config's own provider runs, with your mask in the place of the dataset's segmentation --mask FILE alone the same kind of crop with the box aligned to the camera axes instead of the table; a note says so nothing every pixel with depth is used, and a note says what that means

The note of the last case, as printed:

  note      The test pipeline of this config crops the cloud with SegmentationBoxWorkspace, which reads a ground-truth segmentation; the weights were trained and tested on clouds cropped that way. No mask was given, so every pixel with depth is used. Expect grasps on the surroundings too and fewer points on the objects; pass mask=... (object pixels) or workspace=... (a box in the camera frame) to restrict the input.
  cloud     20,000 points to the model, sampled from 699,022 in the workspace

HGGD is the exception: its pipeline has no workspace (NoWorkspace), it reads the whole image.

grasppanda demo hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e --weights hggd_realsense.pth \
    --depth camera/depth.png --rgb camera/rgb.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 --collision-filter

  model     HGGD on cuda, reads depth, intrinsics, points, rgb
  pipeline  data.test: DepthToCloud() -> NoWorkspace() -> RandomSample(num_points=25600)
  variants  raw (no post-processing), cd (ModelFreeCollisionFilter + GraspNMS)
  input     camera/depth.png: 1280 x 720 uint16, read as millimetres; colour camera/rgb.png
  cloud     25,600 points to the model
  grasps    470 predicted in 4.09 s (first call, includes warm-up); 72 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter + GraspNMS

docs.title: The usual mistakes
docs.text:
Each ends with exit code 1 and one line that says what to change. Verbatim:

$ grasppanda demo ... --depth camera/depth.png
✗ InputError: --depth needs --intrinsics fx,fy,cx,cy: the focal lengths and the principal point of the depth camera in pixels. Without them a depth image cannot become a point cloud. Your camera's SDK reports them (RealSense: rs-enumerate-devices -c).

$ grasppanda demo ... --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 --depth-scale 1
✗ InputError: the depth image (median value 545, depth_scale=1) has a median range of 545 m. The values are probably millimetres: pass depth_scale=1000 (--depth-scale 1000).

$ grasppanda demo ... --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 --workspace -0.2 -0.2 1.5 0.2 0.2 2.0
✗ InputError: the workspace is empty: no pixel with depth lies inside it (CameraBoxWorkspace). The cloud spans x -0.45 to 0.45, y -0.19 to 0.16, z 0.42 to 0.84 metres in the camera frame (x right, y down, z forward).

$ grasppanda demo hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e --weights hggd_realsense.pth --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360
✗ InputError: HGGD reads the colour image; pass the colour image registered to the depth image: rgb=... (--rgb FILE)

Intrinsics of another resolution, a colour image of another size than the depth image, a colour-mapped picture of depth instead of a depth image, and a cloud in millimetres are refused in the same way.

docs.title: Point clouds and dataset frames
docs.text:
--points cloud.npy|.ply|.pcd takes a cloud in the camera frame, in metres, that you have already cropped to the workspace. The image-space steps of the pipeline do not apply to it; sampling and input features do. A method that reads images refuses it and lists what it needs instead.

--frame graspnet1b:scene_0100/realsense/0000 reads a frame of the dataset the config names, through the config's own dataset reader:

  input     dataset frame graspnet1b:scene_0100/realsense/0000, read by the config's dataset reader
  cloud     15,000 points to the model, sampled from 519,612 in the workspace; ground-truth-assisted inputs: workspace
  grasps    1024 predicted in 2.58 s (first call, includes warm-up); 816 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter

The grasps are those grasppanda test dumps for that frame. This is tested, not assumed (tests/integration/test_inference_api.py): for GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, GSNet and EconomicGrasp the arrays are bit-identical to the engine's dump on all eight frames compared, raw and collision-filtered, and the same holds for GSNet on GraspClutter6D frames. HGGD draws random numbers while it predicts (it jitters its regions). A test run seeds once and draws frame after frame; a call here seeds per call. HGGD therefore reproduces the first frame of a run (within 1e-5; two runs of the same GPU kernels differ by 2e-7) and gives another, equally valid, draw for later frames.

docs.title: Run in the browser
docs.text:
grasppanda explore serves the combination explorer on your machine. Give it weights and its tab Run a method runs a ported method in the page, with no code:

grasppanda explore --weights-dir ~/grasppanda_weights   # every .pth, .pt, .tar, .ckpt under it
grasppanda explore --weights gsnet=work_dirs/gsnet/<run>/checkpoints/epoch_0010.pth \
    --weights hggd=hggd_realsense.pth                   # or files by name (repeatable)

The panel has four steps and a button:

  1. Method: one of the six ported methods. When you have changed slots in Build a combination, the panel also offers with your changes (or press Run this selection on a scene there): the composed config runs, so the weights must fit the composed model. A change of post-processing or of the training recipe keeps the model; a new stage needs weights trained with it.
  2. Weights: the files the server was started with. A file whose name suggests the method is chosen for you (gsnet, hggd_author_realsense.pth); the run says whether it fits.
  3. Input: the built-in example scene, or your depth image: a 16-bit PNG in millimetres or a .npy in metres, at most 20 MB and 4096 pixels a side, with the intrinsics fx, fy, cx, cy in pixels (pasting 925,925,640,360 into one box fills all four), an optional colour image (HGGD needs it) and an optional workspace box in the camera frame.
  4. Post-processing: the collision filter, the config's cd variant, as --collision-filter applies it.

Run shows each step while it happens (building the model and loading the weights, reading the input, predicting, post-processing, drawing), then the picture grasppanda demo draws, the best ten grasps, the counts through the post-processing chain, two downloads (every grasp as the (G, 17) array of grasps.npy, and the picture), the lines demo prints under What ran, and the commands that do the same in a terminal. On the development machine (one RTX A6000, shared) the first run after the server started took 7.9 s for GSNet on the example scene, most of it building the model, loading 176 MB of weights and the first CUDA calls; switching to HGGD took 2.3 s, and GraspNet-baseline on the example scene uploaded as depth.png with the workspace box of Your own camera 1.0 s, with the same 942 predicted and 240 kept as the command there. Running the same method again keeps its model in memory.

When a run cannot go ahead, the panel says why in the words of grasppanda demo: weights that do not fit the config (WeightMismatchError with its list of keys), a missing optional library (MissingDependencyError with the pip install line), an input the inferencer refuses (InputError: no intrinsics, a colour-mapped picture instead of a depth image, an empty workspace, HGGD without a colour image), a GPU without free memory, another run in progress.

What the server allows, and nothing more:

  • It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, answers requests addressed to a loopback name, and takes a run only from its own page (Host and Origin are checked; a run is JSON, which a page of another site cannot send without the server's consent).
  • It reads weights only from the files its command line named: under --weights-dir (resolved, so .. and links that leave the folder are refused) and each --weights NAME=PATH. The page picks one of those; a path it sends is never opened as it is.
  • An upload is limited to 20 MB, checked against the format its name claims, and decoded into a temporary directory that is removed when the run ends. A run writes nowhere else and downloads nothing (a composed selection is built with pretrained: false, since the weights file supplies every parameter). The only other file the server ever writes is a composed config you ask it to save, into the working directory.
  • One run at a time: a second request is answered with "another run is in progress".
  • A run predicts on one frame. Nothing is trained.

--device cpu runs on the CPU. On the documentation site the tab is greyed, with the command that enables it, since a run needs your weights on your computer.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image

from grasppanda import GraspInferencer

inferencer = GraspInferencer(
    "graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e", "baseline_realsense.pth"
)
depth = np.array(Image.open("camera/depth.png"))  # (720, 1280) uint16, millimetres
grasps = inferencer(
    depth=depth,
    intrinsics=(925.0, 925.0, 640.0, 360.0),  # fx, fy, cx, cy in pixels
    depth_scale=1000.0,  # depth units per metre
    workspace=(-0.25, -0.2, 0.35, 0.25, 0.2, 0.8),  # a box in the camera frame, metres
    collision_filter=True,
)
best = grasps.sort_by_score()[0]
print(len(grasps), "grasps in frame", repr(grasps.frame), "score:", grasps.score_kind)
print("grasp point   ", best.translation[0].tolist())
print("approach axis ", best.rotation[0, :, 0].tolist())
print("width, depth  ", float(best.width), float(best.depth))
print("array         ", grasps.to_graspnet_array().shape, grasps.to_graspnet_array().dtype)

240 grasps in frame 'camera' score: predicted_quality_x_tolerance
grasp point    [-0.23671351373195648, -0.01879783719778061, 0.6439999938011169]
approach axis  [0.022774772718548775, 0.4925254285335541, 0.8700000047683716]
width, depth   0.10000000149011612 0.009999999776482582
array          (240, 17) float32

The call takes exactly one kind of input: depth= with intrinsics= (and rgb=, mask=, depth_scale=, table_from_camera=, workspace=), or points=, or frame=. It returns a GraspGroup:

Field Meaning translation (G, 3) the grasp point between the fingers, metres rotation (G, 3, 3) column 0 the approach direction, column 1 the closing direction, column 2 the finger-height direction width (G,) jaw opening, metres depth (G,) how far the fingers reach past the grasp point along the approach, metres score (G,) higher is better; score_kind says what it is. It is not a calibrated probability frame camera: the optical frame of the depth sensor, x right, y down, z forward

to_graspnet_array() gives the 17 columns other GraspNet tools read: [score, width, height, depth, R (9, row-major), t (3), object_id]. To move the grasps into your robot's base frame, apply your hand-eye calibration as a 4 x 4 tensor: grasps.transform(base_from_camera, frame="base").

Things worth knowing:

  • Order. Grasps come in the order the detector emits them. Use sort_by_score().
  • Repeatable. Point sampling and the detector's random draws are seeded per call, from the config (data.<split>.dataset.seed, runtime.seed), so the same input gives the same grasps. seed= changes both.
  • Post-processing. collision_filter=True applies the config's variant that holds a collision filter (cd in the shipped configs); variant="name" applies any chain of evaluation.variants. The filter tests the gripper against the observed points only; it knows nothing about what the camera did not see.
  • Two halves. inferencer.observe(...) returns the Observation the model reads (the sampled cloud, the cloud before sampling, the images), inferencer.predict(observation) the grasps. Use them to look at what the pipeline did to your input.
  • Warnings. Differences from the conditions of the test pipeline (no mask where the pipeline crops with one, a cloud that cannot be checked for a crop) are raised once per inferencer as InferenceWarning.

docs.title: What is not claimed
docs.text: The weights were trained on GraspNet-1Billion: two cameras, 1280 x 720, objects on a table 0.4 to 0.7 m away. Nothing here has been measured on another camera, another resolution or a real robot. HGGD needs an image whose size is a multiple of its 640 x 360 network input, with the same aspect ratio. Treat grasps on your own data as predictions of a model outside its test conditions until you have checked them on your setup.

docs.title: The header
docs.text: The first block is everything a number needs before it may be quoted: protocol, split and camera, how many frames were scored, which inputs were derived from ground truth, the post-processing chain, and the weights and code that produced it. extent compares the frames of the record with the split it names. This run scored every 64th frame, so it is a subset, and the report says so in capitals. The weights are the authors' RealSense checkpoint, converted (provenance author-ckpt), and the collision filter ran. Its AP of 0.4867 is a measurement on 120 frames; it is not the AP of GraspNet-baseline on the seen split.

docs.title: Where the precision comes from
docs.text:
AP is the mean of a precision table with one column per friction threshold μ. The first table gives the mean of each column; their mean is the AP. Here a grasp that needs μ ≤ 0.2 is rare (0.18), and most of what can be earned is earned by μ ≤ 0.8.

The second table attributes the AP. A frame's AP is a weighted sum over its 50 ranks: rank 1 owns about 9 % of it, rank 50 owns 0.04 %. Every rank either earns its share, or loses it for exactly one reason: the gripper collides with the scene (checked against the ground-truth models), nothing is between the fingers, the grasp is free but not force-closed at this μ, or the rank was never filled. The columns add up to one. In this run 29 % of the AP is lost to collisions although the model-free collision filter ran, and at μ ≤ 0.8 another 12 % to grasps that are free but do not hold.

By object applies the same split to the object each ranked grasp belongs to. The numbers are percentage points of AP: object 0 earns 3.07 points and loses 4.99 to collisions, more than any other object. success is the share an object's ranks earned of what they held. Object ids are the dataset's.

By scene lists the scenes at both ends. Scenes, not frames, are the unit to think in: the four frames of a scene show the same objects.

Grasps follows the predictions through the post-processing chain. For a chain with two steps each step has its own row. HGGD's cd variant on the same frames:

Grasps
  stage                           grasps  per frame  removed by this step  left of the predicted
  ──────────────────────────────  ──────  ─────────  ────────────────────  ─────────────────────
  predicted                       53,917  449.3
  after ModelFreeCollisionFilter  25,908  215.9      51.9 %                48.1 %
  after GraspNMS                  7,954   66.3       69.3 %                14.8 %
  frames with an empty prediction: 0

The split by cause and object and the per-step counts are stored in the record by grasppanda test (fields breakdown and grasp_counts). Records written before these fields existed are read as before; the report then gives the total the chain removed, from the grasp counts of the run's records, and says that the rest is not recorded.

A:cd picks a variant of a run; --variant picks one for both. The two records must share protocol and dataset. Whatever else differs between them (split, cameras, ground-truth-assisted inputs, post-processing, weights, code) is listed under differs, so that a difference in the numbers is not credited to the wrong cause.

The summary pairs scenes. The interval is a bootstrap over the paired scenes and the sign test counts in how many scenes each side is ahead; both treat a scene as one observation. On this subset Scale-Balanced-Grasp is ahead in all 30 scenes. Both are author checkpoints scored on 120 frames; the statement is about these 120 frames.

--plot draws the report: for one record the precision per friction threshold, the share earned and lost, and every scene; for a comparison the difference of every scene around zero. It uses Pillow only, like the renderer of grasppanda demo.

docs.title: Training and testing
docs.text:
grasppanda train, grasppanda test and grasppanda infer take a config and nothing else. Every setting of a run lives in the config; the few flags the commands accept are shorthand for overrides and end up in the run snapshot like any other override.

What you can run today

The engine is implemented and tested on synthetic data. The dataset readers, the detectors and the benchmark evaluator arrive with their own milestones, so the examples below use the example project: a toy detector, a synthetic dataset and a toy evaluator that exercise every code path on a CPU in seconds. No benchmark number has been produced with this engine yet.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
CFG=projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml

grasppanda train $CFG --opts runtime.run_id=demo
grasppanda test  $CFG --weights work_dirs/toy_train/demo/checkpoints/best.pth
grasppanda infer $CFG --weights work_dirs/toy_train/demo/checkpoints/best.pth \
                      --input val --output out/toy_val
